• QUICK AT FIGURES—The dancing-master. 3.'HY friend has a friend, and thy friend's friend has a friend therefore, be discreet. A PETRIFIED clock was recently found in Rome which, it is thought is an indieation of hard times. "WE were both victims of a too heavy load," as the burst gun said to the staggering sports- man. A FRENCH gourmand says—" Appetite is the most ungrateful thing in the world; the more you do for it the sooner it deserts you." Art art-critic, describing a collection of bric-a- brae, says, "The visitor's eye will be struck on entering the room with a porcelain umbrella." IN a druggist's window a notice was exhibited, recommending a certain patent medicine, with the very dubious heading, "Try one box; no other medicine will ever be taken by you." "Is that dog of yours a cross-breed?" asked a gentleman recently of a countryman. "No, sir," was the reply ; " his mother was a gentle, affection- ate creature.' "DID you do nothing to resuscitate the body ?" was recently asked of a witness at a 'coroner's inquest. " Yes, sir; we searched the pockets," was the reply. "You du not seem to relish wit much this morning," said a would-be wag to John Randolph. "You haven't tried me yet,' was the cutting re- , PIY• AT a travelling agency.—To clerk, " Did you ever realise anything in the German lotteries?" "Yes, sir. I tried five times, and realised that I was an idiot I " A GENTLEMAN, asking Pr. Johnson why he hated • the Scotch, was vaiewered—" I don't hate them, air, neither do I hate frogs, but I don't like to have either hopping about my chamber." A GENTLE3IAN in company with Foote, at the Smyrna coffee-house, took up a newspaper, saying, " Ile wanted to see what the Ministry were about." Foote replied, "Look among the robberies." LORD NORBURY, the Irish Judge, dining at a table where corned beef formed a dish, was asked if he chose a slice. "I would try it," said he, "if it were hung." "If you were to try it,' observed Curran, "it would be sure to be hung." " True ! " cried a lady when reproached with the inconsistent marriage she had made, "1 have often said I never would marry a parson, or a Scotchman, or a Presbyterian; hut I never said I would not marry a Scotch Presbyterian parson." "WHY, Franky," exclaimed a mother at the summer boarding-house, "I never knew you to ask for a second piece of pie at home." "I knew 'twan't no use,' said Frauky, as he proceeded with his pie-eating. "Is there anything wrong in kissing?" he asked her, as they stood together at the garden gate. "Certainly there is," she briskly replied; then slowly and softly added, after a pause: "if there's any one looking." THE latest definition by a boarding-school young lady: -" Omniscient; a four-wheeted carriage." Teacher (surprised)—" Why Miss Jones, you must be thinking of an omnibus 1' Miss J.—" Well, an omnibus will carry almost anything." DURING the investigation before a coroner of a case by burning, a witness who claimed to have been present was asked: "What was the last scene of all ?" He promptly replied: "The servant girl, a fire, and a can of kerosene." WeDow (at evening party)—"Do you unflerstand the language of flowers, Dr. Crusty ?" Dr. Crusty (an old bachelor)—" No, !mem." Widoin "You don't know if yellow mimes jealousy?" Dr. Crusty —"No, ma'm. Yellow means biliousness." "CAPTAIN," said a cheeky youth, "is there any danger of disturbing the magnetic current if I examine that compass too closely?' And the stern mariner, loving his little joke, promptly responded: "No, air; brass has no effect whatever on them." Too Mum 'YANK."--=A Yankee woman recently married a Chinese leundryinan, and in three days thereafter the unhappy Celestial appeared at a bar- ber's shop and ordered his pigtail to be cut off, say- ing, in explanation, "Too muchee yank." A Dereree..—Studeut (to his pri,fessor)—" In bringing my theme over, lecofessor, I got it wet, as , I had no umbrella. De yon want me to recopy it ?" Professor G. (soinetteng of a weg)—" Oh, no, not at all. I dare say I shall find it dry enough when I read it." LAWYER. (to vsitness, sharply)—" What did the prisoner co next ? ' IVitnees (hesitatingly)—" I think—" faawyer—" Stop there; you are not to say what you think." Witness—" That's lucky for you; you might hear something you wouldn't con- sider flatterieg." e • A 'BOASTER, in a hotel was telling of the many sections of oeuutry that he had visited. A man at his elbow asked " liave you ever been in Algebra t" "On, yes," seid the boaster. "1 passed threneh there on the top of a stage-coach about a yE:al• His IDEA OF :TUFeING —" Well, my man," said a military docter to a patient who had been on "low diet" for a long time, "how are you ? " "Much better, sir." "Could you eat a small chicken to-day?" "That I could, sir." "What would you like it stuffed with ? " "Please, your honour, replied the hungry patient, "I would like it stuffed with another chicken." ELDERLY GENTLEMAN (to little boy who is buying candy)—" My young friend, don't you think that, instead of spending all the pennies you get, it would be better to put some of them away for rainy day?" Little .134—" New. What's the good of money on a rainy day? Ma never lets ate stir out of the house." A SCOTCH dominie, after relating to his scholars the story of Ananias and Sepplara, asked them "why God did not strike everyuody dead who told a lie." After a long silence, one little fellow got to his feet and exchomed : "Because, sir, there wadna be oeybody left." " Meoeme, you are growing more beautiful every day," gallantly said a gallant to an actress now pest her pi ime. "Every day? Oh, Monsieur," protested the very vain and aged party, "you flitter me 1" "Well," gallantly and accommodat- ingly replied Hasselbriuk, "let's say every other day! PARENT—" Who is the laziest boy in your class, Joheily ? " Johnny—" I dunno.' "I should think you would know. When all the others are 'industriously writing or studying their lessons, who is he sits idly iu his seat and watches the rest, Instead of working himself ? " "The teacher." WHEN Sir Elijah Impey, the Indian Judge was on his passage home, as he was one day walking the deck, it having blown pretty hard the preced- ing day, a shark was playing by the aide of the ship. Having never seen such an object before, he celled to one of the sailors to tell him what it was. "Ah 1" replied the tar, "I don't know what name they know them by ashore, but hete we call them sea-lawyers. GARRICX, one day dining with a large company, 1100 n after dinner left the room, and it was supposed that he had left the house; but one of the party, on going into the area to seek him' found Gerrick fully occupied in amusing a negro buy, who was a servant in the family, by mimicking the manner and noise of a turkey-once, which diverted the boy to such a degree that he was convulsed with laughter, and only able now and then to titter, "0, Massa Garrick I you will kill me, Massa Garrick !" LITTLE WILLIE had a habit when he went to his aunt Bessie'e of asking for an apple. His mother, hearing of this, cautioned him sternly against doing so. When next he set out for his aunt's house his mamma made him promise that he would not ask for an apple. He had scarcely set foot inside the door however, when he blurted out : " I'm going to be a good boy, Auntie Bessie, and do as mamms told me, I'm not asking you for an apple, auntie, am I? " The hint was taken, and the coveted huh was produced as asked. AN American contemporary says :—" If you drop your collar sted sometimes—and the moat "stud- iously " careful man is liable to do so—here is an infallible way of finding it again. After you have hauled the chest of drawers, and the bed, and the rest of the heavy furniture across the room to look under them, you replace all the articles care- fully, and put on a pair of heavy shoes. Thin start to walk across the room, and before you have taken three steps you will have inevitably stepped on the caller-ate-I atel ,oseotted it ?"

div.head: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
Among the birthday gifts to the Prince of Wales is 1,000 cigars, specially manufactured in Bavaria. It is calculated that the choice weeds will be of the value of 10s. apiece.

Mrs. BesantN visit to America is for the .puopose of settling a difficulty that has arisen between the Theosophists there and Mr. Judge, the most promin- ent American leader of the sect. Not even the apostles of brotherhood can always agree. Mrs. Besant's visit will be very brief; she will return as soon as this matter is settled.

RAl(lyard Kipling, on arriving at the Antipodes to pay his respects to Robert Louis Stevenson, was offered by a leading Australian manager £5,000 for a three months' reading tour of selections from his stories. But he was too bashtul to strike out into the line that yielded such immense profits to Charles Dickens. "I jib at the platform," was his plaintive confession.

The Duke of Edinburgh will not bola the com- mand at Devonport for the usual period, and his resignation may be expected in the spring. The whole thing has become a tolerable ibore to the Duke, who, moreover, is of course annoyed and embarrassed by the positive refusal of the Duchess to join him at Devonport. The Duke and Duchess will reside permanently in Germany after he leaves Devonport.

Miss Annie Abbott, "the little Georgia Magnet," is an obvious American, and although her normal temperature is ten degrees lower than that of the ordinary human being, she seems to enjoy good health and high spirits. She is young and pretty, and well-proportioned, except in the matter of her hands and feet, which are noticeably large. The other day the Electric Lady went down to Sand- ringham, and it may be taken for granted that she fairly electrified the Prince.

They are telling a good story about Prince George of Wales, the sailor, whose progress towards health I am glad to note, and who is said to be a very in- telligent, pleasant boy, though somewhat bump- tious. Being recently in the company of one "Billy," a famous journalist, who was talking about his old school, the Prince said cheekily." Was that were you were sent to-learn to write for the Times '? " " No," said " Billy," quietly, " I was sent there to learn manners " ; and the young gen- tleman grinned and collapsed.

An amusing incident mentioned in the files by Tuesday's Australian mail, points the moral that there are some colloquial expressions which medi- cal M.P.'s would do well to avoid. In the "one man one vote "debate in the Legislative Assembly of Victoria, Dr. L. L. Smith interrupted a speaker with the Conservative shibboleth, "Why not leave well alone ? " The retort was a crusher: 'Where would the hon. member's profession be if that idea were always carried out? The inquisitive doctor collapsed amidst roars of laughter.

Justice Wills is, one may confidently say, un- doubtedly the most gently courteous and even- tempered judge on the Bench. Beneath the polished suavity of Lord Coleridge one is conscious of a power of keen east-wind sarcasm that is sometimes used with withering effect ; but nothing of this kind detracts from the mild gentlemanliness of Sir Alfred Wills. About a fortnight after he was made a judge, Sir Alfred Wills was seen carrying a hod of coals upstairs for his charwoman, whom he had met struggling painfully with the load.

Dr. Broadbent, who is now attending Prince George of Wales, is one who has made his own way from the start. He is a recognised authority on zymotic diseases, and has served on several commis- sions appointed to investigate them. His chief characteristics are a strikingly irregular physiog- nomy, a-soothingly confidential manner towards his patients, and an almost inspired infallibility in diagnosis. He has long been spoken of among in- timates us a probable successor to Sir William Jen- ner. His present " case " will certainly bring him a knighthood, and should improve his chances of be- coming Queen's:Physician. He resides in Seymour- street.

When the Rev. Nevile Sherbrooke was a young man, and still in the Army, he devoted much of his time to religious services among his men. On one occasion, while standing on a barrel preaching to a large company, near Bournemouth, Lord Cairne,then Sir Richard, stood by and listened attentively. At the close of the discourse he entered into conversa- tion with the martial young preacher. "1 will not say you have mistaken your vacation in being a soldier," he said, "but should you ever change your work for that of the Church, come.to me, and I will use my influence." The time arrived shortly when he was called on to redeem his promise,and the earl not only gave him a living, but in due time his daughter Lady Lilias also.

The " superior person" has got his deserts at last. The Hon. George Nathaniel Curzon is to be Under- Secretary for India, vice Sir .John Gorst It is a compliment to Mr. Curzon, but hardly to Sir John Gorst--especially when it is borne in mind that the young gentleman who succeeds him was the indi- Vidual who took upon himself to rebuke Sir John for his cynical defence of the attempted arrest of the Senaputty. Mr. Curzon has qualified for a salary at the India Office by undry Asiatic trips on the scale of Cook's excursions, but it has yet to be seen whether his travels have brought him more than that "little knowledge" which is just as dangerous a thing in Government offices as any- where else.

A vast7deal has been said in praise or blame of the, German scheme of pensions in old age. and we are frequently reminded that the Swiss and French Governments are at work on the same problem. But a really novel and interesting experiment now being made in Denmark has, for some reason or other, escaped notice. Not many months ago the Danish Government proposed to put a new tax upon lager beer. To this the Radicals replied that if the poor man's beer was to be tared tile poor man ought in some way to get the advantage, and for this purpose they proposed the establish- ment of an old age pension scheme. The Govern- ment persisted in their beer tax, but took over the Radical pension scheme, and made it even more Radical, inasmuch as under their plan no cohtribu- tions were to be required.

Lord Crawford and Balcarres, on whom has been conferred the vacant Collar of the Thistle in succes- sion zo the Earl of Mint°, who died recently, is a nobleman of four-and-forty who has taken but a small part in politics, devoting himself to scientific pursuits. He has held the position of president of the Royal Astronomical Society, and is a Fellow of the Royal Society. Lord Crawford has large estates in Aberdeenshire, but his income is greatly derived from coal mines on his Lancashire property—Haigh Hall. The earl succeeded to the title on the death of his father in 1880, and early in the following year people were startled by the report that the late earl's body, had been stolen from the family vault at Dunecht House. The body was afterwards found hidden in a wood, but though one of the culprits was brought to justice, the mystery was never satisfactorily explained.

Professor Crookes at the annual meeting of the Institution of Electrical Engineers discussed the practicability of turning to account the store of electrical force universally abundant in space. It has been computed that "in a single cubic foot of ether which tills all space there are locked up 10,000 feet of energy which have hitherto escaped notice." Professor Crookes now tells us that the latest re- searches warrant the expectation that this vast and hitherto hopelessly inatessible storehouse of power will ere long be made readily available. He leads us to hope that we may have our rooms illuminated by electricity without the instrumentality of wires, and that this is only one of a series of prospective marvels. A fine flame, he states, can now be pro- duced without chemical aid. Should the inferences of Professor Crookes be confirmed by further experi- ment, the outlook presented to us is "the bewilder- ing possibility of telegraphy without wires, posts, cables, or any of our present costly appliances."

To-day (Saturday) the Archbishop of Canterbury will sclemnise the marriage of a young Australian with the sister of Lord Randolph Churchill at St. George's Hanover-square. The bridegroom, Mr. Gordon Wilson, of the Royal Horse Guards, is the son of Sir Samuel Wilson, M.P. for Portsmouth,who began life in a linen manufactory in his native county, Antrim, Ireland. In 1852 he emigrated to Australia, and for some time worked as a gold digger at Ballarat and Bendigo. Ile. invested all the capital he could get in a sheep station in the north- west of Victoria, and this was .the .beginning of a ewer that has culminated in his becoming a

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATIMPAY, NOVEMBER 21, 1891.

squatter-millionaire, one of the wealthiest wool- kings in the world. -Bis gift of .£35,000 to the Uni- sky of bielborne won him a knighthood,and now his family connection with the house of Marlborough together with six years' steady voting for the Government in the Commons, is expected in some quarters to gain him a peerage. He succeeded Lord Beaconsfield in the,ownership of linghenden Manor.
IS AMERICA AHEAD? No. 2.
BY H. WHITHAM.

Sir James Kitson, president of the British Iron and Steel institute, writing in a recent issue of the "Contemporary Review," states some of the im- pressions he received during a recent visit to this country. He says, speaking of American artizans, "their productive power is greater than that of the English workers in the same time, and their work- ing hours are longer, their remuneration greater," " but " he says, " the pace is too quick to last. The extreme physical effort results in greater produc- tion, but it saps the vital energies, and cuts short the career." After reading this very interesting article, one is tempted to ask, what are the causes of this unwearied devotion to productive industry in America? And the answer must be, simply the worship of the almighty dollar. Mammon sits en- throned where the people thought the goddess of Liberty was reigning queen. At his call, the judges created by his power decide momentous questions, but always in accordance with his wish. Legisla- tures fawn and cringe before him, making only such laws as he approves. It is always with an eye to business that juries frame their verdicts ; all are the tools of this almost almighty power. When , slavery was abolished, Capital took care that the ' duty to care for Labour should go with it. To control labour, and the price of property, were for the future the chief objects of capital. A great debt .was made by the war, and the capitalists have seen to it that this was made the means to control , the volume of money. While one monopoly was being destroyed in the South a tight grip was being secured on another in the North. This grip which was fastened at the time on the Government has never been released. It has been said that "men who are housed like pigs can pray like Chris- tians ; and where life is a long flight from starva- tion,it is not a flight that takes the fugitive towards heaven." This statement may some day be accep- ted and acted upon; as yet, it is only taken, as the restless moan of the dead-beat, and the cry of the agitator and reformer, and therefore worthless. What is

Twenty cents a day is big money to them. Thousands of them stand ready to come, too, only too glad of the chance. " Probably it looks a little odd and mysterious that we should wish to bring this kind of labour to the islands," said Mr. Marsden ; " but the fact is, we've got to. There is no other way. The McKinley bill has made it hard for -sugar growers, and, under the old cost of labour, with the duty imposed by the bill, it is a case of shut up shop. There is no alternative but to get cheaper labour than the Chinese and Japanese now mainly employed. These Indians are great workers. They will flourish in our climate, and having never known such prices as we pay them and yet Make a profit, they think them munificent. Who knows but what they will rise in time to become among the most energetic and foremost citizens? We will need several thousands of them. How- ever, some sort of a treaty, or at least a tangible under- standing, will have to be had with Great Britain before we can bring over these people. That is the first thing now which Hawaiian sugar-growers will give their attention to:"

div.head: TEE HOME OF THE CALIFORNIAN WORKER?
div.p: TEE HOME OF THE CALIFORNIAN WORKER?

Compare it with the English -workman's home, and see which 4s ahead. This city is one vast lodging-houae. In every street are large saloons, to which are attached a large number of very small fireless rooms,in each of which one or two "roomers" find their bed. Cheerless places they are, and their occupants spend as little time as possible in them. From their room to the restaurant, which is always handy, the workers go for breakfast at 6.30. Ilaif- an-hour is allowed for lunch at noon. At six p.m. all the restaurants are again full; after this the saloons are filled, or the roomers sit out on the side walks. In the main streets, all over the great stores, are rooms again, entered by a private door, which is fixed between the shop windows. The roomers enter when they like, and take in with them whom they like. This sort of life is the rule, hot the exception,with both sexes. Marriage is al- tocrether at a discount. If a Californian girl does condescend to marry, she must be kept as a lady, or there is a divcrce ; inability to maintain is quite enough. If a return could be had of the people now living in this city, rich and poor alike, who have been divorced, or who aro living on alimony, or who have simply left each other, because they were tired of each other's company, it would cause a sensation. I know quite well what the English labourer's home is. Ido not ignore his brutality as manifested in his drunken fits. The same class of men here keep single, and maintain scores of streets through which decent people may not walk. The-police reports each morning tell of his bruta- lity in the underground dives. When all this is fairly weighed, say, is America ahead? In England workingmen have a tolerably fair trust in the em- -1)103 ers, and with this trust in mind they marry and settle down, knowing their situations are fairly safe if they themselves are sober and indus- trious. Here it is nothing of the kind. Employers care nothing about the workmen. An old face is of .no account. Employers insist upon being ft ee; the supply of labour is so great they can always have a full supply on hand. It naturally follows that in every city there is a large transient population float- ing about.

div.head: TRADE UNIONISM IS VERY STRONG
div.p: TRADE UNIONISM IS VERY STRONG

and makes itself very obnoxious. There is no love, indeed no respect between employer and employe. The city is kept in a state of turmoil with strikes and boycotts. One large furniture store,the largest in the city, is now closing out, bringing all under the hammer, on account of constant strikes. The workmen have just been to the boss, begging him to open his doors, but he says" No." Several trades- men have recently put the question, ." Why should they pay higher wages here than they do in the east? ' Eastern goods are boycotted here, however, whenever possible. You must not buy eastern clothes, eastern furniture, eastern cigars. It is wrong to buy eastern machinery, or eastern wools, and so the fight goes on. A good test of America's progress is to be found in the test of things purchased. Ask a carpenter which he would sooner have, American or English edged tools. He will scarcely think it worth while to answer you. There is scarcely anything manufactured here but bears with it signs of having been made in a hurry. The firm I ,recently and last worked for, after trying all manner of native steel, h ad to fall back upon Stubbs's steel. Ido not deny but what America might and ought to be a very long way ahead of any other nation. What I assert is her citizens are so selfish and so thoroughly unpatriotic that they would, nay indeed, every day, sell, their birthright for a mess ot pottage. They themselves confess that what England could not do with her armies she is now doing with her money bags.. Let her ask her- self, who does the selling? There are whole States here owned by English capitalists. How is America ahead with her

div.head: PRISON MANAGEMENT?
div.p: PRISON MANAGEMENT?

The sentence of hard labour here simply means industrial labour, and this in its turn means open competition with free labour. There are in the United States, near upon 58,000 convicts who are daily engaged in competing with free labour, and over one half are skilled labourers. From this source the industry of the entire country is affected. Every prison is entirely an immense factory, with a daily output competing against free and honest labour. All kinds of productive labour is found in American prisons. Convicts build railroads, and keep the high- ways in repair; they raise.cotton in Mississipt, and in New Yoyk, and in Tenessee they work in mines'. They make agricultural tools in New York. In Phila- delphia they make shoes, weave, and do tailor work. In Massachusetts they do cabinet work, brush, shoe, and machine work. In Illinois, they do wire-draw- ing, wire-weaving, brushes, stoves, edge tools, car wheels, machinery axles, chairs, saddlery, and a host of other trades. The two methods employed are : (1.) The contract system. (2.) That of leasing the prison for a certain period, the lesee assuming entire ccntrol of both discipline and industries, and fur- , nishing food, clothing, and medicine. The contract system obtains in most of the. prisons. It is less ' expensive to the Government. This is not to be wondered at where party politics dominate, and where owing to the change of parties, new and in- experienced men are also often put in charge of the prisons. There is always a power behind the throne. a power that makes and unmakes officers, improves and remitS`fines through agents whom it bends to its will. Years ago prison labour was done away with in England, long sentence prisoners only work- ing in public works. The contractor secures the services of criminals at low rates of wages; he is thus enabled to place the products of that labour at ruinously competitive prices in the markets. I have no wish to pose as a general grumbler. What I wish to point out is, that America is not going ahead so fdst as she might and would do, were it not for her politicians, and that there are forces at work which will soon put THE LABOUR QUESTION

on a new footing. There is a steady and persistent opposition being carried on to the present rate of immigration. New corners largely, settle in the cities now. The extraction of the public domain, and the unbought homestead are features that hitherto attracted; they attract no longer. The public domains where they exist are inaccessible and worthless. Homesteads all over the land are gett- ing into the money-lenders' hands. The great cry heard on all hands is cheaper labour. The Hawaiian Islands are our nearest neighbours, being only a week's voyage away. Chinese and Japanese labour is too dear for sugar growing, therefore Mr. Maisden a member of the Legislature says He has found that native Indian labour, such as would be well adapted to Hawaii, cat be got for not more than 20 cents a day. In India they do not make that much.

div.head: DARING IMPOSTOR
div.p: A DARING IMPOSTOR
THE STORY OF AN INNOCENT COIiVICT.
BY ALFRED It CALHOUN.
CILiPTER XXVI. FRANK LEFFERTS'S SURROUNDINGS.

"And so tha old gentleman is dead," said Rey- bold, without seeming to see or to notice his partner. " Ah, deah boy, what old gentleman do you refer to ?" asked Hyde. "Frank's father." "You amaze me." "That young lady came here to find Frank—" "And the old gentleman, I am told, had no end of money," said Hyde. " Yes ; he was rich. I'd give a hundred dollars to see a ,copy of his will. But that will be public property after the funeral. It is safe to say he did not leave Frank a cent. However, it iamy duty to see Miss Lefferts at once," said Reybold ; and he at once went to his own room, and dressed for the street.

When he was about: to leave his lodgings, Reybold told his partner that he expected toibe very irregu- lar in his movements till after the funeral. "Miss Lefferts and I have had a tiff, as I told you, Jack, but she has no one else to lean on in her trials but myself. Now, I shall be a model of all the proprieties, and if I am not re-instated in her favour before many days, it will not be my fault." But, I say, deah boy; what about rrank 7 Can rou get him into shape, don't cher know ? " asked Hyde, with a twitching of the right eye-lid, in- tendel to mean a great deal. "That is one of the worst features of the case. Of course, Frank is in no condition to be seen. But, I shall simply say that I have not seen him for weeks, and am quite in the dark as to his whereabouts." "Oh," laughed Hyde, "I'll trust you to make a plausible story. What I Are you off? Well, deah boy, I wish you no end of good o:ck. They say the gentle se 2 are never so woonble as when they are sad. So take the first chance to kiss and make up." Reybold called a hack, and was driven at once to the Lefferts mansion. He sent up his card by a servant, and received the reply that Miss Irene was lying down. "What gentleman has charge of the affairs about the place sA this time ? " asked Rebold. "The undertaker," said the girl, who not only knew Mr. Reybold very well, but was also au are that many days had• passed since he had been a welcome visitor at that house.

"Say to Miss Lefferts that I shall call again in a few lours, and that I am now trying to find her ,brotbdr," said Reybold, as he turned to go down to the hack still waiting before the door. The girl made no reply, but she sent a 'look of scorn after Reybold teat indicated the esteem in which bhe held him.

As it was now growing dark, Reybold dismissed the hack; and though it was a warm spring evening, he buttoned Up his tight overcoat, to hide his watch chain and his diamond studs, and hurried to Third Avenue.

Down Third Avenue to Ninth-street, and here he turned towards the East River, and after doubling through a number of narrow, unlit streets, he stopped before a little two storey bricic house, that seemed dwarfed into a toy by the towering tene- ments on either side.
A rap at the door of the little house, and it was opened, after much drawing of bolts and rattling of chains on the inside.
"Hello, Cash! is that you?" asked itcybold, catching sight of a man in the doorway. • "You, Mr. Farley ?" said the man. "The same." "Come in."

The door was opened a little wider, and aftel Reyhold had darted in, it was closed again with the same grating, of locks and rattling of chains. -'Cash, holding a little, smoking lamp in his hand, led the way back through a long, narrow hall, and as they went on, Reybohl asked, in cautious tones : "How is he to-night r
"Mingo ?" "Curse Mingo! No—Frank." " He's just 'bout as I spected he would be," said Cash, coming to a halt before a door at the ends the hail. "How is that?" He's got them.

"Got 'hat ?" "The deliriums. But come in and see for yerseL If we don't let up on his toddy he can't last long, and it would never (LI to have him play out here." , Cash opened, the door, and Reybold followed him into a dirty little bedroom, the air in which was so foul that both men were seized with a fit of coughing. " Wait ! I can't stand this unless the window is opened !" gasped Reybold. . "There he is," said Cash, setting the lamp on a little stand, where the light shone on the bed, re- vealing the bloated form of a man, dressed in soiled garments and with one boot on. There were foam flecks on the lips, and the blood- shot eyes glared with the frenzy of a madman. "There he is, what's left of him," and he waved his arm towards the bed, and watched the effect on his visitor's face. " I—l wouldn't know him. I've seen him pretty far gone after many a spree, but never so low as that," said Reybold, drawing back with a gesture of horror. "Why, you seem skeered, Mr. Farley." "I must confess I am. That sight is enough to turn the most .confirmed drunkard against the cursed. stuff." "Well, the whiskey is pretty bad, and he's got one of them heads that a little upsets. Funny what a difference- there is that way in men. Now you and me could drink ten times as much and not feel it."

"Speak for yourself, Cash." "That's what I'm a'doin', and I know something, about your strength that way. But it aint the whiskey so much; you see, his stomach turned agin that a few days ago, but to keep his head off, I had to fix him up with morphine." "Let me out !" groaned the wretch on his bed, as he began to roll his head from side to side and to toss his arms violently. "Put your chains on Rey- hold and drag him down! He made me do it. He got the paper and the pens. He called up all the devils, and told, them to' live in my heart. Don't knock, don't knock so, but let me out. Ha! who murdered Allen Lee—who crushed him? Who cursed him? Don't lie, Mott Reybold ! don't he! All is discovered. Fire ! Fire ! Fire! I'm all ablaze. Water! give me water. Water ! water, and stop that pounding on my brain !" .The delirious man sat up and stared wildly about him. He could not distinguish the figures by the bed from the forms haunting his disordered brain. Another instant, and he would have leaped to the floOr, but Cash, filled a tumbler from a black bottle, threw one arm about Frank's neck, and said, coaxingly, as he held the glass to his foaming lips: "Here is water. Drink, and you will be better." __ _

With the frantic eagerness of one burning with thirst. Frank drained the contents of the glass, and then fell back on the bed, and panted like one after a hard run from a great danger. Gradually the swollen lids fell over the blood-shot eyes, and he looked as if he never might open them again._ _ _ _

Take me out of this place, Cash. I can't stand it," said Reybold backing to the door, "But that's your work. That's the job you give me to do. If you can't stand it for a few minutes, what do you think of me and the old woman havin' to be near it all the time 2" asked Cash, as he picked up the lamp, and followed Reybold into the hall. "But I pay you for the work, considerin' the danger. And then, I guess, you wouldn't be for pay,n' me a great sight, if it wasn't that you was goin' to make out of it yersel'. But here's a place where we kin talk over all them pints." Cash opened another door and let his visitor into a room in which there was a kitchen stove and a strong smell of boiled cabbage. "We can talk here without danger, Cash 7" said Reybold, laying his hand on a chair, and glancing about him.
" You're safer here than if you was in the Tombs," laughed Cash ; adding, as he sat down: "Now, how long have I got to keep up this funny busi- ness ?"

"Only a few days more. The truth is, lam doing this for Frank Lefferts's good." "No doubt," chuckled Cash. "He would get into trouble if he was allowed his liberty. He has been writing other men's names to papers.'' "That's a weakness of his." "Yes, Cash; but I'll get matters fixed i so as to save him, and then we can get him out." "If we don't let him out very soon be won't be in no condition to care whether he's saved or not."
"I understand; but you have good judgment, Cash. I have faith in you. Keep him about as he is; and, let me say, if you do your part well I'll double your pay, and I'll be your friend as long as I

"Oh! I'll not go back on my word; but if I see he's bound to die I'll drop him out in the streets some night, then the officers will pick him up, club him if he gets shoutin', and fling him into a cell, where he'll be found dead in the mornin'. That's the way it's been with scores of cases, to my cer- tain knowledge. What a pity 'tis men can't drink in moderation, like me and you." And Cash looked as if he had said something very commendable. "Where is Mingo 7" asked Reybold, anxious to change the subject of their conversation. "He's hiding." " Where 7 " "Oh, that's tellin'," laughed Cash. "His house was burned 2" "So they say." "And his wife?"
"Well, Mr. Farley, I've a wife of my own, and so it ain't proner for me to be interested in other men's?
"But do you know what has become a the woman ? "
"No, I don't.

"If you should run across Mingo, tell him that the best thing he can do is to leave New York for a year or so—by that time his little troubles will be forgotten; and say to him that I'll help him with money if he needs it." "Then you're just the man I want to see.".
As these words were uttered by a strange voice a door behind the stove opened, and Mingo appeared, disguised as when he fled from the building he had set on fire.

Raybold sprang to his feet and threw his hand behind him, for he never ventured into these dens without being armed. "This is a trick 1" he shouted to Cash, who sat laughing in huge enjoyment of the situation. "No, it ain't no trick, Mr. Farley," said Mingo. "I didn't knowit was you when I hid. Why, you an' me ain't got no secrets; we know each other, we do. But when I heard you say you was willin' to help me I couldn't hold in no longer, so here an.. Now where's your help ? "
CHAPTER XXVII.
AFTER THE WILL WAS READ.
Three days after his sudden death Mr. Lefferts was buried in Greenwood beside his wife.

Being well known and highly esteemed, the old man's funeral was largely attended; and if any of t 1..) friends and relatives noticed that Frank was not present, they said nothing about it. From first to last Irene bore up with a fortitude that won the respect of those Who knew her inti- mately, but which led those less acquainted to think she was wanting in feeling, forgetting that the sorrow that finds expression in tears is already half healed. On her father's side Irene had no near relatives except her brother. She had heard her father speak once or twice about a half-sister of his, who had, married against the wishes of her family, and al- though the alliance was in no way disreputable, he said that he had never seen her afterwards.
Florence and Dr. Putnam forgot their own pres- sing cares in their devotion to Irene during these days of bitter trial.
It was at her request that they came to the house, after the funeral, to hear the will read.

The old lawyer who had draws up the will— Irene had known him . from her childhood— appeared to be very nervous. He breathed on his glasses and rubbed them again and again before hd could make up his mind to open the paper and read.

The will was in the customary form. It cancelled all wills previously made, and then left a number of bequests to charitable institutions, and certain yearly allowances to a number of old employees. "To my son, Franklin Lefferts, I will and bequeath the sum of one hundred and fifty dollars per annum." "To my daughter, Irene, the remainder of my estate, dmditional on her pledging herself not to marry Allen Lee. Should she refuse to make this pledge and to keep it, then she shall be paid by my executors the sum of five hundred dollars per annum, and, save so much of my estate as shall be invested to meet the aforesaid annuities and bequests, I leave all the property of which I may die possessed to my half sister, Julia Craft, or to her heirs, if she should not survive me."

The foregoing was the substance of the will, which surprised evdry one but Irene and the lawyer. Three merchants with whom Mr. Lefferts had been long acquainted were named as the executors of this very remarkable will. The lawyer explained that his client had not seen his half sister in thirty years, and that he was not at all sure that Julia Craft or any of her heirs were living, or if living, that they could be found. Florence stayed back with Irene till after the witnesses to the will and all the others had left; then kissing her heart-crushed friend, she said: "I can say nothing but what is good of the dead. Why 'should I blame your father for coming to the same conclusion about my brother that so many others have who do not know him ? But the past cannot be undone, and Allen, who would gladly give his life to help you, is himself more Mple.',s than the weakest. Oh, I often ask myself in what way have I and those novo insulted Heaven, that we must ever suffer, ever stand in the storm and the darkness Without any promise of calm and light." "Florence, I cannot ask you to stay with me to-night, and yet I do not want to be out of the reach of your hand, or the sound of your voice. You have set me the example of patience, and taught me to see my duty, and to do it. May Igo home with you I" For reply, Florence caught her in her arms, and said, as did Ruth to Naomi: "Whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Irene told the old housekeeper that she was going away with her friend for the night, and then to the surprise of the servants' she let fall the long black veil and went out with Florence.

Dr. Putnam, like all earnest men, did nothing by halves. When he told Florence that he was ping to get a trained nurse to take charge of her motner, he did not mean that he, would. carry out this idea at some indefinite :time in the future. The trained nurse, an excellent woman, was in- stalled in the tenement house quarters at once. Mrs. Lee was still very weak, and though she took but little notice of what was going on about her, still she missed Allen, and called for him every hour in the day. Poor woman, her son had been the ruling thought In her mind for maw, many bitter years, so it was not to be wondered at that she should think of him now, to the exclusion of everything else. Florence and Irene slept together that night, and after they had partaken of their humble break- fast the next,morning, the latter said: "I feel that my only hope is in keeping busy. If I should sit still and think, I am sure my mind would become a wreck. I shall go to Allen at once. I shall resume the task I have set myself; and, if the dead can see the acts of the living, he who judged me so harshly and hastily, but whose memory must ever be enshrined in my heart, will approve my course." "From my heart, Irene I thank you for your faith. Already my family I;as been like a curse to yours—" "Hush, Florence, hush !" whispered Irene, her white, upraised face looking the whiter in contrast with iter mourning dress. "Itis my family that has cursed yours. It is my brother—l know it, I feel it—my brother, through his vile associates, who has brought all the woe to you and yours." "Then, Florence, we shall bear our sorrows to- gether." , They took each other's hands, and stood with bowed heads, as if invoking the blessing of Heaven on their compact. a Irene was right; action, work, was now as .essen- tial to her own safety, as it was to the safety of the man whose rescue she had made the one object of her life.

The possible loss of a great fortune did not affect her; laced, she never gave it a thought, except in connection with her regret for the bitterness of the dead man's feelings when he dictated that clause in his will.
By ten o'clock she was again in the office of the Tombs.

"Lee aint feeling very well this morning, Miss," said the sergeant in charge, when Irene had given him her card and told him her purpose. • "But he will see me?" she said The officer, for reply, summoned a turnkey, and whispered something to him. The turnkey stared' hard at Irene, then went off, with the air of a man not quite sure of his mission.

In a few minutes he came back, and said: "I guess it 's all right; but be 'pears worse." Irene followed the man, the same man who guided her to the sane cell on a former occasion. "The doctor thinks, Miss, that Lee is in for a heavy fever or S omethin' of that kind. He 's gone all back on his grub, and that's mostly a bad sign here." The man, while talking, inserted his key in the door and it swung heavily in.

div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

"The Children's Garland" is the title of one of the most interesting volumes of the Golden Treasury 1 series, published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co. It is a selection from the best poets, made by Mr. Coventry Patmore, who is himself a poet. By way of showing that the compilation has not been made at random, it may be stated that no selection has been given which has not been put to the test in having actually pleased intelligent children It is a matter of course to say that the reader will find a great many old favourites. It should also be added that there are many new poems which are certain to become favourites with children. The volume is especially valuable for reference, as there is not only a list of contents, but an index of first lines. "The Text Book of Deductive Logic for the use of Students," published by the same firm, is from the pen of Mr. P. K. Ray, Ptofessor of logic and philosophy in the Presidency College, Calcutta. It is suggestive of the value of this publication as a text book, that it has al- ready reactid a fourth edition. The author has been careful to give attention to various criticisms and sugges- tions arising out of previous editions, and the result is a treatise which is ow almost perfect of its kind. It is in three parts, and Iffeats successively of terms, proposi- tions, and deductive 'reasoning. It may be mentioned as a special feature of the volume that it contains a large number of examples, many of them selected from well- known authors.

A new edition of Gray's Poems is edited,with introduc- tion and notes, by Dr. John Bradshaw, editor of Milton's Poetical Works, and of an English Anthology. Gray Was not a prolific writer, but all that he wrote was good, and his "Elegy written in a Country Churchyard" will live as long as the English language endures. Dr. , Bradshaw's introduction is, in brief, a life of Gray, while 1 his notes are of the fullest kind, with a view to elucida- ting and ensuring an accurate text. Messrs. Macmillan and Co. have rendered a service in another direction by publishing a "Tennyson for thel young." It is issued with an introduction and notes by Mr. Alfred Ainger, and there is every reason to believe that it will become popular with young readers. The selections have been well made, and the notes contain a variety of information with regard to the poems selected, which are of interest alike to old and young. sThe second part is to hand of Green's "Short History of the English people "published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co. The frontispiece is a beautiful reproduction in !colours of St. John the Evangelist from the Lindisfarne I Gospel book M.S. The illustrations and reproductions are perfect in thei,r way, while paper and printing are all that can be desired. The publication of this stand- ard work in parts ought to ensure it a large sale. In the Camelot Series published by Mr. Walter Scott, we have "The handbook of Swindling and other papers by Douglas Jerrold, with an introduction by Mr. Walter Jerrold. Douglas Jerrold was born in 1803 and died in 1857. He led a somewhat eventful life, and his biography is therefore of more than ordinary interest. He was enga,aed.in various commercial adventures con- nected with the starting of magazines, and in 1852 he was offered and accepted the post of editor of" Lloyd's 'Weekly Newspaper," at a salary of £l,OOO per year. In addition to this he was, it is well-known, a regular contributor to" Punch." The volume to hand includes, in addition to "The handbook of Swindling." "Tale of a Tiger," and "The moth with the golden wings;" besides several brightly written papers on Shakespeare, anti other lively sketches. , Readers who are not familiar with the works of Henry Thoreau, the American writer, cannot do better than spend a shilling in Mr. Walter Scott's issue ef his Essays and other writings: They will find much to interest and "set them a-thinking. Thoreau was, above all things, original,and never hesitated to express his extraordinary thoughts in powerful and picturesque language. To readers wearied of conventional forms of expression, it is exceedingly refreshing to read his Essays. It is said of Wordsworth that wiaen a traveller once asked his ser- vant to show him her master's study, she answered, " Here is his library ; his study is out of doors;" and the truth underlying this observation certainly holds good of Thoreau. "Sir Ralph's Secret : or, the Horned Cat," is the title of a novel by Mr. J. McLaren Coban, author of "The Missing Partner," &c. It is published by Messrs. F. Warne and Co., as a shilling volume, and it is due to the writer to say that it is much above the average of this class of publications. The interest commences with the first page, and it is sustained to the end, the plot be- ing well conceived and well worked out. " Winter's Annual," published by Messrs. F. V. Wright and Co., is a story by Mrs. John Strange Winter, author of " Bootle's Baby." Its title is " Lumley the Painter," and though it cannot be said to be strong as to plot, it is certainly strong in character, and, like all this lady's works, it is written in a fresh and wholesome style.

---"Magnetism and Mystery ; or a Life's Romance," is a shilling novel, by Mr. Louis Creswick, the publishers being Messrs. Simpkin, Marshall, and Co. There is not as much magnetism in the story as the title might sug- gest, but it is none the worse for that. The treatment is considerably out of the common, and the novel is in every respecta readable one. The interest is throughout' of a strong and dramatickincl. " The last great Naval War " is an historical retros- pect by Mr. A. Nelson Seaforth. A full account is given of the battle of Tenerife, and of much that preceded and has followed it. A diagram is given which explains the movements of Admiral flornby's fleet ; and there is also a Map showinss the movements of our fleet before the battle and a map of the world. The writer deals with the whole subject as-an historian and a specialist; and his observations cannot but be of great interest to all who are desirous of our maintaining the position which Eng- land holds as the greatest naval power in the world. The volume is published by Messrs. Cassell and Co., price 2s. Cassell's "Illustrated Almanack" (6d.) for 1892 has just been issued, and the best thing that can be said of it is that it is in no wise inferior to its predecessors. The story which runs through it is called "The fate of Sister Jessica," and in addition to the usual almanack informa- tion a good deal of space is devoted to British sports with portraits of champions. " Newbery House Magazine" for November leads off with a paper by the Rev. Father Black, which is strongly in support of "Sacramental Confession." The stery " compromise"No is continued up to the 16th chapter, and there is a complete story by Allen Adair. Amongst other interesting papers We have the conclusion of "Church Progress in America"; "The founder of a peculiar sect"; "English monuments and epitaphs," and "Wells and well worship." The" Strand "sustains the capital reputation which it has acquired as a high class sixpenny illustrated mag- azine. There is a continuation in the current issue of the portraits of celebrities at different times of their lives. The short stories and sketches are, as usual, of a kind well adapted to meet the tastes of readers of all classes. Hood's "Comic Annual," price is., is " here again," bright, comical, and original, as of yore. The sketches and odds and ends in prose and verse are innumerable; and many of them are by writers of established fame. It is sufficient to say of the illustrations that they are fully equal to the text. In their preface Messrs. Dalziel an- nounce they make their " 24th bow to the public, and to those talented artistes and authors who have enriched its pages with their work." 'rho" Pictorial World "has been reduced in price from i3d. to 3. The numbers to hand indicate no reduction in quality, and it is therefore a matter of course to ex- Peet that the bold venture will result in an enormous in- crease of circulation. We have also to hand Weldon's "Ladies' Journal of Dress, Fashion, and Needlework," price 3d. Weldon's " Practical Crochet," price 2d. ; and 'Mrs. Leach's "Family Dressmaker," price 21. Cheap as are these publications, they give a large number of illustrations and a great quantity of reading matter.

THE THEATRE AND ITS MORALITY.
REMARKABLE CORRESPONDENCE AT ST. HELENS.

The denunciations of the drama and theatre-going by the Rev. J. T. Wardle Stafford, Wesleyan minis- ter, St. Helens, to which reference was made last. week, have aroused a remarkable expression of antagonistic opinion. In addition to the letter from. Mr. Henry Irving, a summary of which appeared in the .Ex-aminer, communications from several actors. and dramatists of.position have been received,

Mr. Wilson Barrett writes that Mr. Stafford's. words at first were couched so as to suggest fair ness and a striving for truth, but,as they multiplied ran, he regretted to say, into bigoted excess. "But, added Mr. Barrett, " I feel that it is but advertising Mr. Stafford to reply to him. He has said nothing new that is true—advanced nothing fresh. All his. arguments have been replied to again and again and his sermon can no more 'harm the drama. as an institution than can the mud thrown by mischievous boys against St. Paul's Cathedral. harm the Christian religion." In concluding„ Mr. Barrett says There is too much striving for persatial fame in the religion of the pre- sent day. The preacher is as eager to adver- - tise himself as Mr. Beecham is his pills—what-- ever will secure him uotority he will discourse upon. Cant exists among us—always has existed—. always will exist; but, above it and beyond it.-- - as far as the empyrean blue from the acid, smoke-- tainted atmosphere of St. Helens—is an eternal: truth—which no Rev. J. T. Stafford, no nor ten hun- dred thousand such, can ever sweep away. That truth is—that God made man to laugh and to weep, to mourn and to rejoice, to wake and to sleep, to and to die."

Mr. Arthur W. Pinero writes—" In all intelligent, communities the theatre of to-day holds a useful and respected place. Those who from bigotry, or - prejudice, or jealousy, Or mere ignorance, stilt kick. against the wholesome drama, and its reputable ex- ponents, are simply behind the times. They are of consequence, and may safely be allowed to go.. their way." Mr. Wallace Revill, the proprietor of the St. . Helens Theatre Royal, writes that his first impulse - was to treat the ungracious pastor with profound silence, but" the extreme severity of li•Li condem- nation, the unguarded, the unfounded, and broad- - cast charges flung at curhapless heads seems to be. a matter for wonder and pity, not for meeting and‘ confuting." Mr. Revill continues—" The highest- minded, the most unquestionable of Christians, the best of families in town and couety, clergymen, magistrates, aldermen, councillors, and tradesmen • patronise my theatre, and as yet, .I can honestly • assert, no word has reached my ears from them • which would lead me to suppose that my beautiful art temple is a place where anyone need fear for their morals, or cause a blush to the most innocent.. If Mr. Stafford knows to the contrary, why not be explicit, give bona-tide instances,and prove his case so that he might have the credit of discovering the foul spot, .and I have the Pleasure of eradicating it ?"

div.head: MINISTER DECLINES TO REPLY.
div.p: THE MINISTER DECLINES TO REPLY.

The Rev. J. T. Wardle Stafford preached on Sun- day, in Sutton-road, Wesleyan Chapel, St. Helens. It was generally expected that Mr. Stafford would make some allusion to the Correspondence in the local newspapers, but he did not do so. In conver- sation with a press representative, Mr. Stafford intimated that his intention. was to take no notice of the letters in answer to his recent sermon. He felt that his remarks had not been replied to argu- mentatively, but the correspondence consisted of personal abuse of himself. Under such conditions, he intended to treat the correspondence with con- tempt, He added that he personally referred to no individual in his sermon' and the only actor he referred to Was Henry Irving, whom. he did not mention in a deprecatory spirit.

Preaching at the Congregational Chapel, St. Helens, on Sunday, the Rev. J. R. Ward referred to the body of man being the temple of the Holy Spirit. He said he would not dwell upon the res- ponsibility placed upon man as to where he should .take that temple. He would not refer to the theatre controversy than to say that he stood by his brother, the Rev. J. T. Wardle Stafford. He (Mr. Ward) might not agree with every word Mr. Staf- ford used, but he agreed with him in the main, for "The stage as it is to-day is an unclean thing." If men had the spirit of God within them, tlit.t spirit would lead them to the places Where they should go.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLARS' CONVENTION.
div.p: GOOD TEMPLARS' CONVENTION.

The Quarterly Session of the No. 1 Convention, South West Lancashire, connected with the Good Templar Order,was held in the Good Templar Hall, 31 arket-st., Hindley, on Saturday afternoon. Bro. Col. Sergeant T Mantle CC T of Warrington, pre- sided. All the officers responded to Roll Call with two exceptions; there was also an excellent atten- dance of Lodge DepOes and Representatives front Warrington, St: Helens, Earlestown, Ashton, Wigan, and Hibeley. The usual Committees on credential. and press were appointed, after which the reports of offieers were received. Bro. Mantle, C.C.T., dealt with various interesting matters referring to visits he had paid to various Lodges. He had found them working well; as D.C.T. oi the Military Distiict he had recently instituted a new lodge at Ashton Barracks. He urged special attention to mission work and public meetings during winter months, in order that we might be able to show our increased mem- bership next February. The report of Bro. R. Kean Cor. Sec., was eminently satisfactory, indicating general activity; good work had been done and was in prospect. A scheme of Temperance Education was being floated which would help very materially towards the improve- ment of the members; a mission band of speakers,singers, &c., was also in course of formation. There were 519 members in 15 lodges, an increase of one lodge and 107 members on the quarter. Bro. R. Skaife, C.S.j.T., of St. Helens, dealt with matters affecting the ripterest of the Juveniles. One new Temple had been opened at Wigan, and another would be started at Sankey Bridges, and there were pros- pects of others. The report on electoral work was read by Bro. John Taylor, C.E.S., of Earlestown, and vva of a very interesting character, indicating general activity at the various Municipal Contuts.—Bro. J. Brockbank,Convention treasurer of St. Helens, reported on. Financial m a tters. —The reports of representatives and visiting officers showed the Lodges, almost without exception, to to in good order, and manifesting an earnest Spirit. It was resolved' that Bro. Pay-Master- Sergeant J. W. Roberts, C. Co., be asked to prepare a suitable " Paper" to be read at the next session of the Convention. The " Firs-lane " Prosperity Lodge was on motion received into affiliation with the Convention. Several of the distinguished visitors then gave earnest and encouraging addresses, and the thanks of Conven- tion were heartily accorded them. The same compliment' was paid to the Hindley .friends for their excellent arrangements for the session.—Bro. D. Houg,liton, responded, and a very interesting session was closed at 6-20 p.m. The members then formed into procession, and marched to St. Paul's schoolroom, where a very nicely arranged tea was partaken of by a very large number. At 745 p.m. a public meeting was held, pre- sided over by Bro. A. E. Eccles, , P.CT., treasurer of Chorley, who gave an excellent address. Ernest addresses were also given by Bro. Morris Jones, D.0.T., of Liverpool, and Bro. R. Skaife, C.S.J.T., of St. Helens: Songs, recitations, itc., were well rendered by varin"_ members and friends, to whose efforts a large aulol testified their appreciation. The meeting closed a 19-30 p.m.

div.head: INFLUENZA.
div.p: INFLUENZA.

ITS SYMPTOMS AND TREATMENT. (Family Doctor, Nov. 14th, 1891.) Influenza, that insidious and dread malady, which within two years has visited and devastated so many families in the kingdom, the high and the low, the rich and the poor, has again made its appearance, and it is impossible to say what the result will be before balmy summer is again with us. It is not so much Influenza as its after effects that are to be dreaded. The danger lies in the low tone to which the system is reduced. It becomes so run down that the patient is an easy victim to lurking diseases,and,, as has been only too deafly evidenced, the hale and strong are no better able to combat them than the old and frail. The symptoms are quite marked although the malady does not affect all alike. Severe headaches, pains in the chest and tinder the shoulders, making breathing diffi- cult; rheumatic pains in the shoulders and general stiff- ness and soreness of the muscles; loss of appetite ; and a gloomy, depressed, nervous feeling, are usually ex- perienced. It is for the public good that we earnestly call attenl• tion to the necessity of preparing in time for the dan- gerous visitant. A malignant and most powerful foe is approaching. What folly to wait until his clutches are on your near and dear ones before you put your defences in order. What agony of mind to realise,when it is too late, that it might have been avoided and a„pgecious life spared.. What is to be done? Simple as the answer may be, it is the "Secret of Health.' If the Blood be pure per- fect health is the result, and you can defy diseases. Is your,Blood pure? Who can say? When an enemy is expected the defences receive first attention, the ram- parts and batteries are critically examined, and every- thing put in thorough repair in erder to withstand the attack. In like manner your system should now be proved, and made invulnerable to the approach of Influenza. Make Warner's " Safe " Cure, the greatest Blood Purifier of the Age, your CHIEF or sTAFF. It will ferret out any weak spot in your defences, rouse the Kidneys and the Liver, those great Blood Purifying Organs, to proper action, make them eliminate from the Blood all poisonous matter, rendering it pure and health- ful, and then Influenza, or any other disease, may be defied. Flannels•should be worn and every care taken to avoid •colds. Take cold sponge baths, rubbing briskly after- wards, and heedfully avoid draughts. If it attacks you, or any member of your househohl, do not allow it to be regarded as a trifling matter, but have the patient lay up. Careful nursing is indispensable, and every precau- tion should be taken. The patient should be given, in fact forced to take as much light nourishing food as pos- sible, but solid and indigestible food must be carefully • avoided, as it would but increase the feverish condition. A thorough course of Warner's "Safe" Cure will tone the system, promote healthy action of each organ, purify the blood, and restore the invalid to robust health and -strength. 107, St. Anne-st., Liverpool, April 10th, 1890. During the latter part of February I' nad a most severe attack of that peculiar ailment known as Russian Influenza. Dreadful headaches, acute pains in the joints, sttffness in the muscular system, loss of appetite, followed by extreme exhaustion, and several other dis- agreeable symptoms, compelled me to consult one of our best physicians. However, his daily visits and pres- criptions were quite unsuccessful, and I still grew worse. A couple of weeks passed by without the least change for the better. I was compelled to keep my bed from weakness and exhaustion. One night I had suffered ,more than usually. Breathing was most difficult and painful, caused by inflammation of the lungs and pressure on the chest. The following morning an old friend called on me. In his hand- he held an almanack, which was given to him by a man who was distributing them from house to house. It was Warner's Altnanack for 1890. Handing it to me, he exclaimed, I wonder whether "Safe" Cure would ,do you any good?' A drowning -man catches at a straw. I there -and then resolved to try a bottle, and sent for ODD. I discarded the other medicine, as no good had resulted from it. Two days I took the several doses, as required, without feeling the least relief; the third day, however, I felt a little easier; dur- ing the night I coughed less, breathed easier, and had a few hours' sleep, a luxury which I had not enjoyed for many a night. From that moment slowly but surely I commenced to improve. Pains diminished, breathing was easier and less painful, the cough gradually dis- appeared, the rigidity of the muscles ceased, the pains in the Joints vanished, sleep was more regular, and the .different functions of the system became quite regular, while I entirely recovered a healthy appetite for food. Gradually my usual strength returned, and after using a few mere bottles of Warner's "Safe" Cure I had recovered my usual good spirits and health, and was enabled to follow my usual occupation. Thinking it would interest you to know how beneficial "Safe" Cure proved in a genuine case of Russian Influenza, and also that other sufferers of this disease may profit by my experience, I thought it my duty to make the above statement.
SOL. A. ARONDSON.
