A NEW WELSH CHURCH FOR WARRINGTON. LAYING OF THE MEMORIAL STONE.

On Saturday afternoon, the memorial slones were laid for a new Welsh Church in Crosfield-st., Warrington. The church will be under the control •of the Manchester Welsh Presbytery, and the build- ing is of an exceedingly plain character, and will have a frontage of 33 feet towards the park, while its inside dimensions will be 43 feet, 6 inches in length, by 30 feet in breadth. There will be a cen- tral entrance door, leading into a porch, and on each side of this will be a door, opening into aisles. he pulpit and seating will be of pitch pine, and accommodation will be provided for 210 persons. A room will be erected at the rear of the chapel, which will be used as a vestry, also as a school- room, and for tea parties and entertainments. The premises will he heated with hot water appliances, and lighted by three pendants. The front of Op chapel will be finished with Ruo.bon red bricks and with Yorkshire stone dressings, and the building will be enclosed within i low brick wall coped with sane which will be surmounted with iron railings. At the ceremony on Saturday there were present the Rev. J. R. Evans (late of Warrington) and 3. Davies (of the Cockhedge Mission) and Messrs. J. Edwards (moderator of the Manchester Presby- tery), W. J. Jones (Manchester), J. Evans, John Humphreys, and H. Williams. The proceedings com- menced with the singing of a Welsh hymn,

The Rev. J. R. EVA.NS then addressed those pre- sent. He said the Welsh people came to Warring- ton many many years ago, but not in sufficient numbers to justify them in meeting together to worship God in their own tongue, therefore they identified themselves with the various English , churches in the town. About ten years ago an I attempt was made to start a Welsh cause in Warrington, and nearly all the Welsh people living in the town at the time banded themselves together into societies, and the great Wesleyan body recognised them as one of their churches. For some time they met in a schoolroom belonging to the Wesleyins, but many of them left, and the faith of those who remained was not strong enough, and the society became extinct. Had they kept to- gether a little while longer, there would have been no gap between that church and the present one, for very soon the Manchester Ship Canal was com- menced, and there was a large influx of Welsh people to the neighbourhood. The number had ever since gone on steadily increasing. Two years last March since the initial step in the present move- ment was taken, and at that time their faith was not stronger than to aim higher than get- ting £4OO to 1:500. The chapel now commenced was to cost between £BOO and £9OO, but their faith had become stronger, and that notwithstanding many difficulties, one of which ought never to exist in connec- tion with any chapel,that was,as to securing a site. They appealed with thb view of a purchase to a company who ;owned land in the town and some in the neighbourhood As to oneillot their reply was that they wanted it for people to dry their clothes op, and as to another he gathered from their answer that they wanted to make a present of it at some future time to the Corporation,in order the, they might open a street ; and they refused to sell any land for a chapel site. They appealed to a gentleman for some land sthich was for sale, but he would not sell them it. He was ready and willing to sell it or part of it in order to build residences for men, but he refused to sell iand in order to erect upon it a temple in which God might dwell amongst men. But notwithstanding all I this they had secured a site; and a splendid site it was. They would require from £4OO to £5OO more than they bad now in hand to defray the cost of the building and many kind friends had promised to do their share ; and in the course 'of a few days they would call upon these friends to contribute. Mr. HUMPHREYS said it was much pleasure to him to be present on this occasion, which he had been looking forward to for some years. It had come sooner than he expected; and it was a bettenbuilding than he expected. Mr. Humphreys then called upon Mr. J. Edwards to lay the first stone, handing him a silver trowel with which to perform the ceremony,and which bore theinscription —" Presented to J. Edwards, Esq. Pendleton, on the occasion of his laying a memorial ;tone of the Welsh Chapel, Warrington, 14 Nov., 1891.1, Mr. EDWARDS then laid the stone saying on the com- pletion of the work : " The memorial stone has been duly laid, and I trust that the chapel when it is erected
4l

and finished, will become the religious home of the Welsh people residing in Warrington." Mr. W. H. PRITCHARD, a co-originator, with Mr. J. Evans, of the Welsh cause in Warrington, made some observations referring to the vicissitudes of the Welsh religious movement in the town. He congratulated the Welsh inhabitants on its ultimate success, as manifested by the proceedings that day, and hoped the new chapel would very soon require enlarging. Mr. J. EVANS then, haring been handed by Mr. Pritch- ard, a silver trowel similarly inscribed to that presented to Mr. Edwards, proceeded to lay the other stone. He said he was sorry that in doing so he was only taking the place of Mr. E. Jones, J.P., Mayor of Pwllheli, who had been announced to do so. He (Mr. Evans) felt very warm towards their Welsh Church, and he hoped that the chapel would be a religious home for the Welsh people in Warrington, and that they would appreciate and support it. The Rev. J. R. EVANS then announced that Mr. Edwards had .laid £lO and Mrs. Edwards £5 on the stone, Mr. Edwards having previously given £5, so that the contri- butions from himself and hikwife were £2O. Mr. J. Evans had placed £5O on the stone, haring previously contributed £4 10s. The Rev. J. DAVIES said he had very much pleasurein being there that afternoon especially on such an occasion as that. Whilst himself a thorough Welsh -nan, yet he could not speak to them in the old language, though he should much like to do so. He was very glad that his Welsh friends in Warrington were banded together and had determined to erect a chapel in order to worship God in their own tongue. There were a good many of those present who knew the inspiration that came to Welshmen when they were worshipping together in the beloved tongue of their fatherland. he native tongue of every man was that which appealed to him most. There were men who might go down into the depths of degradation and to whom a word spoken in their mother tongue might have a mighty power in their salvation. A number of Welsh people who had from time to time come to Warrington had in the colder atmosphere of English churches drifted away altogether from Christ, and he was very pleased that their brethren had determined that this should not be the case in the future, and that Welshmen coming to Warrington should lor lble to worship God if, -11 ti • - ,th -,nd with all

Je able to worship God in a le warm.. the inspiration, of their own tongue. He hoped that those Welshmen in the town who did not worship with their Welsh brethren would contribute largely to the success of the chapel, and give them suhstantial help. Sometimes it was said by their English friends "Why cannot the Welsh people come to our English churches? If they are good enough for us they are good enough for them. What matters it ?" Oh what delightful liberty and freedom.. Of course it did not matter practically in what tongue we praised our God, but it did matter to the man himself. Did the Welsh people ask the English residents in Wales, "Why cannot you worship with us in the Welsh tongue ?" No,they built for them churches and chapels in order that they might worship God in their own mother tongue; and they simply that day asked the English to return the compliment, and enable the Welsh people of Warrington to worship God in their own tongue. A number of children then deposited on one of the memorial stones the proceeds of collections they had made, which -amounted £6 is. 11d. A collection was made among those present, which realised £9 18s. 6d. Mr. EVAN WILLIAMS read a list of• subscriptions amounting to £324 18s. 6d., and which included £lOO from Mr. R. Davies, of Bangor, and the £54 10s. from Mr. John Evans, of Warrington. Another Welsh hymn was sung, and prayer was offered by the Rev. J. Davies, and the proceedings then ended. Tea was subsequently provided for friends in the Bold-st. rooms of the congregation, after which a miscel- aneous meeting was held.

div.head: OPENING OF WARRINGTON , GYMNASIUM.
div.p: OPENING OF WARRINGTON , GYMNASIUM.

The formal opening of the new Warrington Gymnasium and reading room took place on Tues- day afternoon. It is, as our readers well know, a comparatively short time since the Warrington gymnasium was started. The fiest "local habita- tion" of the institution was the. old Workmen's Club in the Market-place, but owing to the great interest which was taken in the classes, which were under the management of Mr. Alexander, of the Liverpool Gymnasium, and the rapid increase in the number of members, it cvas decided to erect a larger and more commodious building in Palmyra- Square, which was the most central position that could be obtaiued. The plans were prepared by , Mr. J. Wright, architect, Sankey-st., who has been from the first one of the most active promoters. The totaf cost of the building (including the site) is about £1,600, and the furnishing and fitting has entailed an additional expenditure of about £l2O. Lord Winma.r- lei,gh's subscription and the sale of the site at a reduced price amounts to about £2OO, and the other generous donors are Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P., £lOO, Mr. Parr, £5O, the Committee of the Warrington Football Club £4O, and Sir A. B. Walker and Messrs. Thomas Morris, Daniel Jones, F. Monks, John Crosfield, W. D. Houghton, and Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co. £25 each. The Charity Commissioners subscribed £630 to the building fund, which sum was raised by the sale of the old Workmen's Club. The main entrance to the building,which ie of an unpretentious character, is from Palmyra-square. The front is finished with Ruabo n bricks and terracotta, and the work generally has been well and substantially done by Mr. Wm. Taylor,builder. Near the front door is a vestibule, and on the left hand a reading-room 18ft. by 16ft., and a dressing-roem 12ft. by llft. From the vestibule a staircase leads to the ladies' dressing-room and a supper room, 26ft. by 16ft., on the first floor. The gallery is also entered from the smile landing, and it will accommodate from 90 to 100 spectators. In the basement, kitchen accommodation is provided, with a good range and other conveniences. The length oft the principal room is 841 t. and the width 43ft., and the distance from floor to ceiling is 25ft. The interior of the building contains all the newest gymnas- tic appliances. The classes are under the directorship of Mr. E. Alexander, of the tMyrtle-st. Gymnasium, Liverpool. The floor of the central room is to be utilized for the purpose of teaching lawn tennis. The building is to be let for bazaars, concerts, and entertainments, but not for political or religious purposes, and the Com- mittee wish it to be distinctly understood that the prim- ary object for which the premises were erected, namely, the teaching of gymnastics, will not be disregarded. ' The president of the Gymnasium is Mr. Thomas Morris; the treasurer, Mr. D. Jones; the secretary, Mr. W. W. Dimmelow, of Bewsey-road ; and the trustees, Messrs. Thomas Morris, J. E. Wright, Thomas Sutton, Joseph Harrison, William Pierpoint, John Evans, and D. Jones. The Committee is composed of the following gentlemen: —Mr. Thomas Morris, chairman ; Messrs. J. E. Wright, Henry Roberts and W. Pierpoint (appointed by the Cor- poration of Warrington), T. H. Sutton, John Evans, J. Lyon Whittle, W. Tinsley, J. Podmore' jun., Daniel Jones, William L. Gorse, Hugh Ferguson, John Hesketh, J. A. McGregor, J. E. Warren, H. H. Evans, and George Vernon. With regard to the opening ceremony, some hopes had been en:ertained that Lord Cross and Mr. Herbert Glad- stone, or at all events one of them, would have been present as representing the National Recreation Society, but unfortunately neither of those gentlemen appeared to have been able to attend. The building was formally opened by Mr. T. Morris,the president of the gymnasium. At the time appointed for the commencement of the ceremony a considerable number of gentlemen had gath- ered at the front entrance, and Alderman\ WRIGHT, speaking on behalf of the Com- mittee and trustees, asked Mr. Morris to formally open the gymnasium for the use and benefit of the public of Warrington. Mr. W. TAYLOR, the builder, then presented Mr. Morn with a handsome silver key bearing the inscriptions "Presented to Thomas Mbrris, Esq., C.F.G.S., on the occasion of the opening of the Warrington Gymnasium and Reading Room, 7th November, 1891." Mr. Taylor expressed the hope that the efforts of Mr. Morris and his co-promoters for the establishment of that institution would meet with the appreciation and success it so well deeerved. (Hear, hear.) 'Mr. MORRIS, having unlocked the door, said that, on behalf of the Committee of the young people of Warring- ton, he declared the gymnasium open. The party then entered the building, in which a tem- porary ptatform had been erected. Mr. Morris presided, and amongst those present were the Mayor (Alderman Greenall) and the Mayoress; Aldermen Francomb and Wright; Councillors J. H. Fleming, James Hepherd, Henry Roberts, James Fairclough, R. T. Fairelough,Geo. Blackhurst,and James Smethurst; Adviral Jones-Parry, the Rev. Father Feeny, the Rev. John Yonge, the Rev. J. W. Varley ; Drs. Smith, Fox, and Bowden; Major and Mrs. Pickmere, Mr. and Mrs. J. Lyon Whittle, Mr. Robert Davies, Mr. and Mrs. F. Monks, Mrs. Morris, Mrs. Venn, Mrs. Smethurst, Mr. A. Alexander (director of the Liverpool Gymnasium), Mr. E. Alexander (director of the Warrington Gymnasium), Mr. W. Welsby Dimmelow (bon. sec.), and Messrs. GeorgeF. F. White, Julian Win- ser, Percival Pearse, Whittle, C. H. Kerry, Geo. Pilling, Harry Toft, G. Riley, C. Jackson Holmes, Wm. Taylor (the builder of the Gymasium), W. H. J. Jenkins, Wm. Roberts, J. E. Warren, S. E. Johnson, J. S. Garland,F.J. Dell, and others. The Hotr. SECRETARY, (Mr. Brimmelow), said he had to read several letters of apology for non-attendance. First of all, he wished to make a few remarks with refer- ence to the absence of Lord Cross and Mr. Herbert Gladstone, as representing the National Physical Retrea- tion Society. On behalf of the committee of the Gymnasium, he wrote to these gentlemen twelve days ago, but as he had received no reply, he could only assume that his letters had either miscarried or that Lord Cross and Mr. Gladstone were from home. Mr. Alexander, the director of the Liverpool Gymnasium, was present, however, as a member of the National Physical Recreation Society, and he would address the audience on behalf of the Soeiety. This explanation would he hoped, be sufficient. Letters of apology kad been received from Lord Winmarleigh, the Rector of Warrington, Mr. J. C. Parr, Mr. Robert Pierpoint, Mr.

div.head: TTTE EXAMINER, SAT URDA Y, NOVEMBER 21, 1891
div.p: TTTE EXAMINER, SAT URDA Y, NOVEMBER 21, 1891

I Gilbert Greenall, (who wrote on behalf of Sir Gilbert land Lady Greenall), Mr. Joseph Davies, Mr. John White Mr. Hartnood Banner (Liverpool), Mr. Win. Pierpoint, Mr. Wm. Long, and Mr. George Woods. The CUAIRMAN, in his address, said their history did not date back far. After an assault-at-arms, held in the autumn of 1888, at the Drill Hall, under the direction of Mr. Alexander, of the Liverpool Gymnasium, a Commit- tee of several gentlemen .was formed for the purpose of furthering the study of gymnastic exercises in Warring- ton. Able advice and assistance were given that Com- mittee by Mr. Alexander, which enabled them to decide at once upon the necessity of opening a Gymnasium. The Committee decided to engage the room lately occupied by the,Workmen's Club; in the MaAet-place. Mr. Smith was appointed, from the Liverpool Gymnasium, as in- structor, and early in the following year, they became affiliated with the National Physical Recreation Society, whose object was to encourage physical development,by the yearly distribution of valuable prizes. In the session of 1888-9, they vere drawn in the first round to compete against Leicester Gymnasium, and although only a few months had elapsed since the formation,their men proved victorious. They, however,had to retire after the second round, being defeated by Dublin Gymnastic Club. After that they lost the services of Mr. Smith. They appealed to Mr. Alexander, who appointed as instructor his brother, Mr. E. Alexander, who was now the director of that institution. (Applause.) Through his careful training the members made rapid strides, and the spring of 1890 found their eight defeating the famous Exeter Hall Gym- nasium, London, Bournemouth, and Sefton Hall (Liver- pool). thus finding themselves in the semi-final competi- tion, against Liverpool and Dundee Gymnasiums, in April. They all knew the result, Warrington being de- feated by a narrow majority of three points. Not dis- heartened by that failure, they still went on until the early part of the present year, when in the first round they defeated the St. Helens Gymnasium,but fell a victim to the renowned Liverpool champions in the second round, and so were thrown out of the competition. During the whole of the intervening period the Com- mittee were anything but idle. Efarrassed by heavy expenditure, they decided to make application-to several of the late trustees of the Workmen's Club (including Alderman Harrison and Mr. George Blackhurst), to assist them in obtaining a sum of money then lying in the hands of the Charity Commissioners. After much de- lay they got a good promise of some £630, and on the strength of this they arranged to approach Lord Win- marleigh, through Mr. John White, for the purchase of the present site. Their special thanks were due to his lordship, and on behalf of the Committee he took that opportunity ef publicly bestowing them. (Ap- plause.) They were bound by the Charity Commission- ers to put their building on freehold land, and although it was 'very much against his lordship's rule to sell land rmtright, he not only broke through the rule,but charged them very reasonably,and gave them a handsome dona- tion into the bargain. He had to express the pleasure lof himself and Corn snittee in having an opportunity of publicly thanking Mrs. F. Pendlebury (late Miss Toft) and Mr. Payton for their kind assistance in supplying the necessary music for the drill exercises. (Applause.). Mrs. McGregor and Mr. White were at the present time ably assisting them by a similar service to the junior classes, and he hoped they might be able to continue. He must chant a hymn of praise to their members. Their former rooms were not at all fitted for gymnastic. exercises, so much so that ladies' classes could not be formed, hut although they were thus handicapped the competitive teams gave a good account of themselves in every competition they entered,and their faith is strong that, now their members had all they could desire in the shape of good rooms, good apparatus, and a most excellent conductor,- they would,. when the next international contest was decided, be found the victors, and the champion shield be I brought to Warrington. ( Apnlause.) Alderman WRIGHT said the Chairman had afforded him Igreat encouragement in another matter, by handing him a slip of paper, on which he read the words, "Thomas Morris and Mrs. Morris have pleasure in contributing £5O towards paying off the debt on the building and the furnishing of _it." (Applause) He was very grateful

Alderman WRIGHT said it would be interesting for• the audience to know that 75. young men were connected with the afternoon an d evening classes, chiefly evening classes ; 60 ladies and young girls had also joined the Gymnasium, as well as 50 boys, so that he thought their progress was highly satisfactory. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) Mr. Wright concluded by praising the manner in which the builder had carried out his work. EVENING PROCEEDINGS.

In the evening, there was a grand assault at arms, by the senior members of the Gymnasium, at which there was a good attendance of spectators. Mr. Morris pre- sided, and in the course of the evening a short address was given by Councillor H. Roberts. He said he con- sidered that that institution was a credit to the Commit- tee who had been instrumental in bringing it about. (Applause.) It was a credit to the town of Warrington; it was a boon to the young men of Warrington, such as few of them could as yet fully appreciate. He hoped and believed that the young men of Warrington, and the boys also, wonld join the institution in such numbers that it would be necessary before long to enlarge their borders. (Applause.) A great deal had been said, on that and previous days. about the necessity for healthy bodies and sound minds going together. As far as the healthy bodies were concerned, the Committee of the Gymnasium would meet all requirements, and they who were connected with the Technical Institute had done some little to provide sound minds. He considered that the young men of the present day had opportunities. such as those who had gone before never dreamt of, and it would be to their everlasting disgrace if they did not make the best of these opportunities. (Applause.) He hoped they would have an opportunity as a Cerporation of lending the Gymnasium some substantial help in a way that some time or other might be desirable. He hoped the time would come when Institutions like these would not be left to the benevolence of a few individuals, but would be a proper and a legitimate charge upon the rates of a town like Warrington. (Hear, hear, and applause.) At the conclusion of the performance Alderman WRIGHT, on behalf of the Committee, thanked the audience for their presence that evening. He wished to say that in seven or eight days.they would have the room heated with hot water, which would prevent the discomfort which had been experienced' that evening.—The meeting con- cluded with the singing of "God save the Queen."

, . for the help which-had been given by the Committee, all the members of which had worked , together most har- moniously, and were doing so still. He believed that they would stand by them until every penny owing on the building was cleared off. He thanked Mr. Alexander for the great help he gave them in starting the Gymnasium. When they started the scheme the first encouragement they received was from Mr. John White. who recommended the present site. Lord Winmarleigh gave them fully one-half the value of the site. indeed they got a freehold site worth £5OO at a cost of £265, and that £65 his lordship generously gave them as a contri- bution to the building fund. t Applause.) The next encouragement received was from Sir Gilbert Greenail, who promised £lOO through Mr. White. and thus the subscriptions went on. They had already received in subscriptions a sum of £1,516, but before theycould pay for the furnishing. &c.. they w,ould have to raise a further sum of £4OO. He hoped that those who were generously disposed would help them. If they could not raise the money they required by subscriptions, it was intended to hold a bazaar early in the spring, in that room and it was important they should have a strong Committee of Ladies to make the affair a success. (Applause.) Mr. ROBERT DATIIS, who was received with applause, said that to have a sound mind in a Round body it was necessary to exercise the muscles of the body and the powers of the mind. He was exceedingly pleased to observe the fine room, which had been erected. In con- clusion, the speaker urged that calisthenics should form part of the curriculum of all young people. Mr. ALRICANDTSR, director of the Liverpool Gymnasium, in the course of an interesting speech, said there was very little doubt that the Gymnasium would be heard of, not only in Warrington, but all over the country. He hoped the Committee would not confine themselves too much to providing contests, but he hoped that they would endeavour to make the building a rendezvous—a health temple, as it were, for the inhabitants of War- rington. (Applause.) Speaking in reference to the ladies of Warrington, he thought that many of them already were tall, supple, and graceful, but there were others who could not lay claim to those advantages. He ad- vised those who were wanti,,g in these qualities to take an old teacher's advice and get them as soon as they could. He had been a teacher for over 30 rears, and his experience showed him that the greatest improvements in the physique were gained by ladies, after a course of gymastics. They had not the same opportunities of "knocking about" as little boys and kittens. They were obliged to assume a certain deportment necessary to the requirements of fashion and Mrs. Grundy—(laughter)—and, therefore, they lost very much of the freedom of exercise which gave the better health amongst the boys. He stated that out of the 50,000 pupils who had passed through his hands, not more than three per cent. suffered from curvature of the spine, whilst a great number of girls were troubled with this affection. Curvature of the spine often happened to girls and boys between the ages of six and 15, when they, could very well afford to spend an hour at the gymnasinm. He was well aware that the requirements of modern education made it difficult to spare time for a course of gymnastics, but lie hoped that the sensible principals of schools, and parents of the children would see that it was no use the children havin; brilliant minds without healthy bodies. (Applause.) A number of the junior members, under the superin- tendence of Mr. E. Alexander, then went through various exercises in a very interesting style.

div.head: TWO CHILDREN BURNED TO DEA.TH.
div.p: TWO CHILDREN BURNED TO DEA.TH.
Aire broke out at midnight on Monday, at a lodging- house in Hastings-A., London; and two children named Edith Farrier, and Charles Faster, were burned to death.
SHOCKING TRAGEDY AT GREENOCK.

A shocking murder was committed on Saturday night at Greenock, when a circus artiste was stabbed to death in the public street. At Greenock,on Monday, Frederick Thomas Storey, circus manager, was remitted to the sheriff on the charge of murdering Lizzie Paston, circus peeformer, by stabbing her on Saturday.

div.head: FREE EDUCATION IN MANXLAND.
div.p: FREE EDUCATION IN MANXLAND.

The Legislative Council of the Isle of Man on Tuesday discussed the Free Education Bill, the second reading of which was moved by the Attorney-General, and seconded by the Bishop. The motion for the second reading was lost by the casting vote of the Governor, who gave as his reasoti for taking this course the desirability of prolong- ing discussion.

div.head: RENUNCIATION OF KING MILAN.
div.p: RENUNCIATION OF KING MILAN.

BELORADV, WEDNIISDAY.—A Cabinet Council was held to-day, which was attended by M. Dakintch, President of the Council of State, who has brought with him from Paris a written statement from the ex-King Milan,in which his Majesty renounces all his legal and constitutional rights, and declares that he will never return to Servia. The Ministers decided to submit this declaration to the Skuptschina.

div.head: LABOUR COMMISSION.
div.p: THE LABOUR COMMISSION.

At the Labour Commission, on Tuesday, Mr. I. Evans- agent to the Neath, Swansea, and Llanelly Miners' Asso, ciation, spoke in favour of legislation for an eight hours day from bank to bank. The sliding scale arrangement could be improved by the appointment of anumpire. He held it important that more inspection should be made. Putting in force of "black lists ' should be forbidden by law, as unions were not strong enough to prevent it. Other witnesses were examined.

On Thursday, Sir George Caldwell, director of Mess- hall Colliery, and ex-president of the South Lancashire and Cheshire Coalowners' Assosiation, gave evidence be- fore the Labour Commission. He said that a legal eight hours' day would materially increase the cost of pro- duction, and in times of depression would mean the clos- ing of many collieries. At present owners were entirely the servants of the men, and practically had to do as they were told.

div.head: MURDER IN GLASGOW.
div.p: MURDER IN GLASGOW.

On Wednesday morning a married woman was mur- dered in the east end of Glasgow. The deceased, who was named Catherine Brown or Marshall, was 43 years of age, and was the wife of John Marshall, coach painter 28, Auburn-st., Parkhead. She was standing at mid- night talking to a man at the close mouth there, and began to sing" Who will hold the horse's head, wo, wo, wo," when a railway fireman named Joseph Kitchen, 23 years of age, came forward, and, after joining in the chorus for a minute, drew a revolver from his pocket, and remarking" That's wo for you," fired at Mrs. Mar- shall. The shot entered below her left eye, and she dropped dead. Kitchen ran off, but was arrested at his lodgings at 11 Auburn-st. It is alleged that both the prisoner and the woman were slightly intoxicated. No reason is assigned for the dreadful deed. Kitchen was taken before the magistrates and remanded.

div.head: IT RECALLS THE BLIZZARD.
div.p: IT RECALLS THE BLIZZARD.

In March, 1888, the great blizzard in America almost extinguished the city of New York. The like of it was never before seen. The snow completely stopped all local traffic. Not a horse or a wheel could move. All the telegraph lines Lading into the city were prostrated, and for two or three days the people of Boston and New York communicated with each other by way of London by means of the Atlantic cables. Thus messages intended for persons three hundred miles distant were sent six thousand miles, crossing the ocean twice. An incident which recalls this experience to the writer's mind happened a short time ago here in Eng- land. Suppose we let the gentleman interested tell his own story. He says: "I have suffered more or less from indigestion and dyspepsia all my life. I had a bad taste in my mouth, pain after eating, a poor appe- tite, and sour stomach. My tongue was coated, and my mouth constantly filled with a watery fluid. No matter what I ate, however light, it disagreed with me and gave me pain. I had fulness of the chest, and pain at my side, with a miserable low, dull feeling. From time to time I consulted a doctor who gave me medicines, but they did very little good. The doctor said that the coating of my stomach was disordered, and the mucous membrane was inflamed. In 1877 I received a pamphlet , from New York telling of , a medicine called Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and of the extraordinary cures it. had effected, so I procured a supply, and after taking the first I felt better, and by the time I had taken four bottles more, I was completely cured, and have been in good health, as re- gards the indigestion, ever since. Having studied the practice of herbs* for many years, I was in the habit of treating people for erysipelas and other complaints, and was frequently consulted by people in the district, so after my remarkable cure, I was so impressed with the merits of Seigel's Syrup, that I procured a large supp ly of the medicine, and recommended it to all who were suffering, and people came from far and near for it. I h may mention that on a Sunday my house was besieged by miners from Coal Pit flqath, and others from a dis- tance. On every hand I heard nothing but the loudest praise and of the cures it effected, and the fame of this medicine was spread throughout the West of England with no other advertising than one party telling another of the benefit they had derived from this' wonderful medicine. I wish everyone to know of this, and if by publishing this statement it will help others Who may be suffering as I was, it will afford me pleasure." The letter from which the foregoing is an extract is signed Moses Goodwin, Old Sodbury (Sodbury), Glos, and is dated April 9th, 1891. He is a farmer. The reader will iaotice that while the headquarters for the sale of Mother Seigel's Syrup is universally known to be in London, by a strange chance Mr. Goodwin's first information concerning it came from America, three thousand miles away, which recalls the incident of the American blizzard above narrated, and also shows that the fame and usPfulness of this medicine extends to all civilized countries.

Mr. Benjamin Egerton, grocer and provision dealer, Plat-lane, Whisall, Whitchurch, Salop, says :—" While livi g with Mr. Roberts, Fens Viro9d Farm, I first began to feel a dull heavy weight at my side, and noticed a bad taste in the mouth with foul stomach and uncom- fortable feeling after eating. I had no appetite, and when I sat down to the table I could not touch the food. I had a good deal of pain and noise in the head, and could not sleep for it. I was not fit for heavy work,and could only do light jobs about the farm. After cutting I. hedge I would go quite faint, and had to sit down, and felt so much depressed I could hays cried. Having al- ways been such a strong man I took it badly to be re- duced to such a weak state I took all kinds of physic and saw a doctor, but his medicine only eased me for a bit, and then I was worse than before. I went on in this way for over a year, when a servant that cams to live at Mr. Roberts' told me of a medicine called Mother Seigel's Syrup. She had heard a gentleman talking about it in a railway carriage, and he praised it so much that I thought I weuld try it. After I had taken two bottles my food did me good, and I gained strength, and by persevering with the syrup I soon got as strong as ever, and have never ailed anything since."

div.head: WOMAN FOUND DROWNED IN THE CANAL. SUPPOSED SUICIDE.
div.p: A WOMAN FOUND DROWNED IN THE CANAL. SUPPOSED SUICIDE.
When the Pie was opened The Birds bean to Sing" The Praises of BIRD'S CUST,tIRD

On Tuesday afternoon an inques!-, was held by Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, at the Black Bear, Inn, Latchford, concerning the death of a woman un- known, whose body was found in the Old Quay Canal under the circumstances detailed as follows: C. Shakesh aft, of 17, Gaskell-st., warehouseman,said on Monday morning he was in the warehouse where he worked, and which overlooked the Canal. He saw something in the water, and got a rake and turned it over, and found it was a woman. He got it to the bank with the help of a man named Ash- worth, and informed the police. She was fully dressed, except that she had no hat on. She was in a decomposing condition. The canal was not public there. People could walk through the gateway and jump in. He had seen nobody about the warehouse. —lnspector Cox: On the other side of the canal there is a towing path.—Witness: Not public.— Inspector Cox: They are never prevented from go- ing there.—Witness: There is a board there.—ln- Spector Cox deposed to bringing the body away, and finding that the deceased had pulled her clothing over her bead and folded her arms in it. The body appeared to be that of a woman of from 30 to 35 years of age. In her dress pocket he found a bottle (produced) which had contained whisky, in another pocket threepenny pieces,an American 5 cent piece, a garter—she had the other on—and a brooch. She was about 5 feet 4 inches high, and had dark brown hair. He had circulated a description of her. —The Coroner read the description,and said the evi- dence suggested yery strongly that the poor woman had determined to take her life, from the fact of her arms being fol&d inside her dress, but he did not think the evidence would justify the jury in coming to the conclusion that she had committed suicide.—The jury returned a verdict that the deceased was found drowned in the canal.

MR. DIGGLE AGAIN ON THE WARPATH. Mr. Diggle, in accordance with a notice of motion he had given at a previous meeting, proceeded to comment upon certain matters at the Workhouse which he consi- dered might be improved. First of all he referred to the rule that the inmates could only be allowed out on& in three months.—Mr. RATCLIFFE, who is chairman of the House Committee, here rose to a point of order ann some little altercatioq tdok place between him and Mr. Diggle. Mr. Ratcliffe said that a fortnight ago Mr. Diggle broaght the same questions forward and a resolution was passed referring the whole matter to the House Committee. There had been three meetings of the House Committee, but Mr. Diggle had not attended one of them. He brought it forward skt the Board meeting merely to get it into the papers. (Hear, hear and laughter.)—Mr. Disioul said he did not attend ~the House Commit- tee because the chairman of the Committee was at fault.—Mr. HIBBERT thought Mr. Diggle was out of order.—Mr. DIGGLE : I think you should mind your own beef. (Laughter.) Continuing, he said that at one time the inmates were allowed out once a month, and it was a sore point with them that they were now only allowed out once in three months. They could only see their friends when they were in the hospital. He should like a reason to be given why the privilege was with- held from the unfortunate people in the workhouse. He then referred to.the want of accommodation and venti- lation in the apartment in which the chips were chopped. Although there had been as many as 25 people employed at one time in this room there was no outlet or inlet to it except a door from another rocm. This he thought, was a terrible state ibf affairs for a lot of people of the age he had seen there, and he thought the least they could do was to provide a gas stove.—Mr. Aukland : It would smother thom.—Mr. Diggle retorted that it would be better if some people were smothered and a graitestone on them . Mr.. Ratcliffe : Have you brought that before the House Committee P—Mr. Diggle: I would not bring it before you. (Laughter.)— The Clerk suggested that it would be better to hear what Mr. Diggle had to say.—Mr. Diggle said that when he ;visited the "chip place" he saw a big preserve can, to bold about a dozen pounds, contaieing water, and when he was asked what that was he was told that they had no other vessel for the supply of water, but that "con- founded big can." (Laughter.) He next referred to the state of the parade ground for the itimates, which he considered was in a disgraceful condition as there were pools of water upon it, and he had seen two:old men walking with a stick each, plodding through the water. —Mr. Hibbert was of opinion that Mr. Diggle should sit down. Perhaps they might have a nice greenhouse.— The Chairman thought they were very much indebted to Mr. Diggle.—Mr, Diggle said he was not going to raise their rates, but if he could put the inmates of the Workhouse in a better position he thought he was right in doing it.—Mr. Flibbert We had better have a water- proof for each of them.—Mr. Diggle was proceeding with further remarks when there was considerable in- terruption, several of the members expressing the opin- ion that the whole matter should be brought before the House Committee.—Mr. DIGNUM suggested that if the House Committee did not take any notice of Mr. Diggle's complaints he could bring them before the Board.—Mr. DIGGLE said he had brought them before the House Committee,and while some had been attended to ethr had not. He would reserve what more he had to say till another day.—Mr. RaTcLiFee, in replying, said that everything that had been brought under the notice of the Committee by the Medical Officer and the Local Government Board Inspector had been remedied. With regard to the state of the yard he argued that it would make matters worse to break it up this weather. He had no doubt that when the proper time of the year came the yard would be attended to. They could not expect roads and yards to be in a good condition this weather; he had no doubt that Mr. Balharry's farmyard was not in a very good condition just now. He thought Mr. Diggle had said a good deal that was imaginary.—Mr. N. Houghton said that Mr. Diggle seemed to have forgotten that that workhouse was under the close surveillance of the Local Govern- ment Board inspector.—Mr. Dignum moved a resolutima to the effect that, after hearing the explanation of the Chairman of the House Committee, the Board was satis- fied with it.—Mr. Aukland seconded the proposal.—The Clerk, in dealing with Mr. Di,ggle's statement, said, with regard to the leave of absence from the workhouse, that if Mr. Diggle only saw some of those people before they came there and the sort of homes they had, if they wore worthy of the name of homes, and the people with whom they associated when at home, he would say the less they were permitted to get into those associations the better for tem. (Hear,hqar.) As to the room in which the wood-cutting took place it was the most convenient place they had for the purpose, and he did not think it was any very great punishment for 25 people te be put into a dry room of that character. As to the state of the yard lie said it was most difficult to Imp everything inapple-pie order in a place like that, land unfortunately the ashphalting of the yard would give way in process of time, but he thought it was not a matter of dipute that something should be done. Tne ' motion proposed by Mr. Dignum was then passed by the Board, and the discussion terminated. This concluded the business. •
THE SHIP CANAL. PROGRESS OF BRIDGE-MAKING

A writer in a contemporary says :—To begin with, take the Acton Grange Bridge. over which will run the London and North-Western trains on the deviated line. In point of height it will not be much inferior to the Forth Bridge. Although the wcrk was only commenced last April, under the superintendence of Mr. Duncan, late of the Tay and. Forth Bridge undertakings, over 2,000 tons of iron had, on the occasinn of a recent visit, been used in the erection of the girders, of which there are five, and which are sft. high from the masonry of the bridge. The structure is divided into four sections —one set of rails on each—and is on the verge of being finished. A little nearer Warrington a second bridge, itself an enormous structure, carries the deviated line mentioned over the Mersey, just alongside the existing bridge known as Walton Arches. The arch over the river has a span of 160 ft. Passing Warrington, and going a little further to Latchford, there is another great bridge, so high that the workmen on the top look like pigmies, and little ones at that. It is the cynosure of all eyes, and a favourite point of the works much affected by visitors. It also will carry a railway bridge over the canal at a wide part. The piers which support it are, up to water level, composed of large blocks of Manley sandstone. Above water level they are composed Of red bricks, faced with blue bricks, and it will be of interest to learn that a single layer of one pier absorbs from 4,000 to 6,000 bricks, while each pier requires .atsout one and a half million bricks to complete it. Most of these bricks have been manufactured by fhe company them- selves at Statham, a short distance away.

THE LUNATIC ATTENDANT.-CHRISTMAS DINNER.

The House Committee recommended that Joseph Duck worth, aged 47, be appointed lunatic attendant at the Workhouse at a salary of £25 per annum with uniform, rations, bed, &c. at the Workhouse. The Committee also recommended the usual Christmas dinner be given to the inmates of the Worichouse.—The minutes were confirmed. Duckworth attended before the Board and, in answer to a question, said that he had been in the army and was far a time a prison warder. • GIFTS.
The Workhouse Master reported that parcels of papers for the inmates had been received from Messrs. Buckton, Houghton and Kean.
A VACANCY.

A short discussion took place as to whether it was worth while having an election to fill the vacancy on the Board caused by the death of Mr. T. Jones, or leave the matter over till the triennial election of guardians next April. It was decided that the vaca,ny should be filled at once.

div.head: SOUTH MOLTON ELV.CTION.
div.p: SOUTH MOLTON ELV.CTION.
GREAT LIBERAL VICTORY.

The result of the polling in this division through the vacancy caused by the succession of Lord Lymington to the peerage on the death of his father, the Earl of Ports- mouth, was declared on Saturpay. The zandidates were Mr.. Charles Buller (L U) and Mr. George Lambert (G). There are 8,612 votes on the register. The result was declared shortly before three o'clock to be is follows G. Lambert (L) 4,222 C. W. Buller (L U)

Majority The result of the election was a supprise..even to the most sanguine Gladstonians, and there was great excite- ment on its declaration. Mr. Lambert, in thanking the electors said it was not for him they had recorded their votes but for the great party to which he and they belonged, and especially for the great leader whom he was proud to follow. Mr. Buller also thanked hit supporters, and added that he hoped to win at the next election.
At the last general election Viscount Lymington (L U) was returning by a majority of 1,689, the figures being as under : Viscount Lymington (L U) W. B. Walker (G L) 2,352 -- 1,689

div.head: MURDER BY A MOTHER.
div.p: MURDER BY A MOTHER.

At Huddersfield, on Wednesday evening, the coroner's jury returned a verdict of wilful murder against Mary An Fowler, wife of a coachman, living at Edgerton. On the sth inst, the woman murdered her baby by cut- ting its throat, and her husband arrived home just in time to prevent her committing suicide. The woman was confined of the child about three months ago, and had been low-spirited from that time. She had told neighbours that when she had these moods on she felt she must do something desperate. The coroner committed her for trial.

div.head: BURGLARS AND THEIR BOOTY
div.p: BURGLARS AND THEIR BOOTY

IMPORTANT DISCOVERIES. After the arrest of the nine prisoners accused of burglary effected by Inspector Beach at the Queen's in spector and Wharf-road, City-road, London, the and his officers took possession of the beerhouse used as the" fenee," where, in various cupboards, they found the proceeds of numerous robberies. Continuing their search, they preceeded to take up the boards, and underneath they discovered pro- perty which justifies the statement that alniost every floor was a mine of wealth. On the property being taken to the Clerkenwell Police Court in various conveyances, it was found to comprise an infinite variety of things. The property recovered in respect of one burglary alone,at Chelsea,was valued at no less than a sum of .£5OO. Among one lot of valuables was property identified as belonging to Mr. Oscar Wilde. Ever since ti.e publication of the fact of the property being on view persons who have suffered from burglars have been calling at the station. Though the property identified relates to 61 different burglaries, this does not form one-tenth part of that still awaiting identification. The police think a great deal may be the proceeds of provincial , robberies.

The custom of wearing black for the dead dates back to the time of the Romans, since when it has always been popular amongst Western nations. The great mortality of this coun- try, considering its sanitary arrangements, has given birth to a number of shops exclusively for the SALE OF MOURN- ING. These shops, subsisting entirely on one department, are compelled to charge exorbitant prices, as many a be- reaved one is able to testify, haviiag found to her cost when the funeral was over, that she had made a bad bargain. Whilst making these statements we wish to draw the attention of Ladies to two facts :-1. That we are Manufacturers of Mantles, Costumes. and Millinery, doing a large WHOLE- SALE TRADE in these departments, and that we supply our customers at the WHOLESALE PRICES. 2. Ours being a GENERAL TRADE, with a number of departments, we are not dependent on our Mourning Trade for the profits, and can consequently afford to sell at Lower Prices than our competitors. Our designs are copied from the latest Paris and Berlin models, modified to suit the tastes of our venous customers. Every garment is thoroughly examined before being sent out, and for fit, finish, and style, we cannot be surpassed, whilst our prices will be found nearly half of those charged elsewhere. During the sale SPECIAL PRICES will prevail in this department. Ladies requiring deep or complimentary mourning will receive every attention, and they will doubtless be astonished at the value which they receive.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 21. 1891.

Pulpit THE Rev. J. Li. W. Stafford, Wes- and ieyan minister, of St. Helens, Playi2eume. seems to have brought a hornet's nest about his ears through a sermon, which he preached the other week, in which he denounced the theatre and theatre-going. Mr. Henry Irving had a word on the subject to say, last week, by way of reply; and this week, as will be seen from another column, Mr. Wilson Barrett, and other well-known actors, repel the attack which has been made upon their profession. The morality or immorality of the stage is by no means a new subject of debate ; but opponents are less ready to attack than they were some years ago; and Mr. Stafford must at least be credited with having the ' courage to speak his mind. It happens that min- isters are at a great disadvantage in speaking of the stage and its influence, from the fact that they are not in the habit of attending theatres. Some of them do take advantage of the solitude of the large crowds of London to visit the theatres when they visit the metropolis,but we do not suppose that it is from this section that denunciation of the theatre proceeds. It comes rather from those who know least about it ; and in whose eyes one u pit" is a sure way to the other "pit." The most bitter opponent of the stage we remember to have heard was a Dissenting Minister, who boasted that he never had and never would set foot in a theatre. This was very effective as a piece of pulpit rhetoric; but it looked weak in print, for the public who might have paid attention to what he had to say concluded that his zeal must, under the circum- stances, be in inverse ratio to his knowledge. That the theatre, like many another institution, r has its weak and its dark side may well be ad- mitted without its being thereby conceded that society would be improved by the stage being swept entirely out of existence. It is as natural to seek enjoyment as it is to seek meat and drink; and it is a step upward,at any rate,when the enjoy- ment sought is of an intellectual kind. There was a time when Englishmen found pleasure in bull- baiting and cock-fighting; it is an advance upon that to take an interest in the poorest of stage plays. But stage plays are not, as a rule, poor, nor are they immoral in tendency. They are the products in many cases of the finest intellects of the age; and the playwright understands his business too well to make vice attractive and virtue repellent. Vicious men there are—men who know they are far from being as good as they should be; but if a theatre were filled with this class it would be found that they would sympathise with suffer-
ing virtue, and detest,villainy, however high-placed or however clever. • Probe Nature to her inmost core, There's more of good than evil; And man, down-trodden man, bath more Of angel than of devil.

And it is because this is so, and because stage plays do "probe Nature to her inmost core," that they are for the most part wholesome, and a stimu- lant of the right kind. Let those who would condemn the theatre reflect for a moment how it helps to brighten and beautify the dull and sordid lives of thousands of toilers who have no better means of enjoyment. What would become of. them if the stage were no more? Would they flock to the churches? Not a bit of it; they would spend more and more of their time over the coarser stimulant of the alehouse, and their last state would in every respect be, worse than it is at present. The theatre is an, evolution ;it is a necessary part of social life; and can be no more dispensed with than sermons or Sunday schools. That its aims are not the highest is not to the point. It is here ;it cannot, and ought not to be got rid of, and as it cannot be ended it must, if possible, be mended. The nomadic life of actors and actresses is not con- ducive to the development of family virtues ; but their status is improving, and if they are given a helping hand, it will still further improve. The churches have no monopoly of morality, for there are sinners even amongst the saints of the communion. There are ser- mons that are bad, and there are plays that are good. The Rev. F. K. Freeston, of Warrington, gave a series of addresses recently, on " The Reli- gion of Shakespeare's Plays," and from all we hear they were in the highest degree instructive and, edifying. It is true all plays are not equal to "Hamlet," and it is also true that all discourses. are not equal to the Sermon on the Mount. What is needed is to keep these great examples before us, with the reasonable hope that pulpit and play- house will in the future be less apart than they are at present.

WHERE is the Liberal who is not as Another surprised as he is pleased at the Victory. result of the election for South Mol- ton? It is "something like a, victory" to convert a Tory majority of 1,689 into a minority of 1,212 The Tories are staggered by it; they cannot tell what to make of it, and there is confusion of ton- gues amongst them. The " Times " admits that it is a serious blow to the Unionist party; and the Standard" falls foul of the Government for giv- ing so much more time to Ireland than to England.. It says "the Government seem smitten with a kind of blindness, almost resembling the blindness of the Stuarts, to facts so patent that any child could understand them." The "Dublin Express"—an- other Tory organ—" freely admits the gravity of the reverse in South Melton, but says it is not a victory for Home Rule. It urges Liberals to drop Home Rule and return to their former Liberalism." "Not a victory for Homo Rule," with Mr. T. D. StaadvAN and other members of Parliament on the spot to keep that question to the front,and explain what other reforms would follow! The Liberals are not going to change their plan of battle in order to please the enemy, especially after such a magnifi- cent victory. We grant that it is rather hard on the Tories that the agricultural labourers have not been influenced by "assisted education"; but they have themselves to blame even as to this, for have they not, within the past half-a-dozen years, denounced Free Education as a plank in the Liberal platform? What if they were to-day to.set about converting their Irish Local Government Bill into something which they could declare was in the direction of Home Rule? Is it not likely that the Irish would see through the trick, and still give their votes to the Liberals? The fact is, the electors are getting sufficiently wide-awake to know on which side their bread is buttered. The Tories have been in office for five years, and when Hodge asks what they have done for him, he is - constrained to answer that they have done nothing. So far as the Allotments Act is concerned, he • might as well try to fly to the moon as endeavour to pass all the barriers that block his way to an acre of land under its provisions. As to County Councils, they have been of no service to him. He wants Parish Councils, through which he can exercise a real control over matters that immedi- ately affect him ; but this is just what the Govern— ment don't want him to do; and so it happens. that, while County Councils are in f all swing,. Parish Councils are as yet merely in the Land of Promise. Besides, our land laws require reforming right through; they stand in the way of agricul- tural development, and that means that labourers who should be at work on the laud are left to- swell the ranks of toilers in towns, who are tramp- ling each other down in the struggle for existence.. Hodge may not as yet see far ahead; but he can see a little beyond his nose; and that is the mean- ing of the Liberal victory at South Molton.
FOR a lone/ time the Commissioners- A Vexed Question. of Newton paid little heed to the-

ratepayers demand for the erection of a Town Hall at Earlestown; and now that the matter has been decided upon the difficulty is that they are going in for too much of a good thing. It was considered settled that the building contract should not exceed £5,000 ; and many inhabitants, anxious to avoid a serious increase in the rates,, voted for the scheme at a ratepayers' meeting, on the understanding that that figure would not be exceeded. The Local Government Board gave their sanction to the requisite money being bor- rowed; and all seemed to be going "merry as a marriage bell" when it was made known that the Commissioners had taken a fresh thought and were committing themselves to a scheme which involved, to begin with, an aduition to the building contract of £2,700, with the prospect of a proportionate in- crease in the furnishing, &c. The result is that Newton and Earlestown are again ift a state of ferment, and protests are being made on all sides. It appears that the Commissioners have come to the conclusion that the Surveyor requires more room; but what has not yet been made clear is that, to provide this extra accommodation, there is need for an extra expenditure of £3,000. If the Commisioners have a good case, let them lay it before the public. At present the rate- payers who have agitated for a Public Hall, believing that one could be en‘cted with- out being a burden on the rates, have a feel- ing that they are being tricked. AA •fe GO not say this is so ; but that is the view they a r 3 disposed to take of the matter, in the absence of any arrange- ment to take them into consultation at a public meeting. The situation is aggravated, too, by con- flicting interests as between Newton and Earles- town. The Newton ratepayers certainly do not see why the seat of authority should he removed at a cost which they regard as extravagant on the face of it. On the other hand, Earlestown ratepayers do not wish to pay more for their whistle than they think it is really worth. It would be a 'misfortune -

Mr. William Morris, speaking as an authority on art, says Mr. John Ruskin's works are "about the worst printed and ugliest looking books in the language." What will Ruskin have to say of this? It is hard upon him, or his printer, or both.

The had weather of Sunday was a special dis- appointment to many who were thus prevented from seeing Mr John Crosfield's brilliant display of chrysanthemums. Still, over 400 persons made their way to Walton Lea, while the number of visitors on the Monday was about 1,500. It is evident that Mr. Crosfield's kindness in this mat- ter is highly appreciated ; and it is to be hoped that nothing worse than bad weather will ever disturb what is now regarded as "a hardy annual."

Prince Bismarck has not been forgotten in his retirement. He had occasion to pass through Berlin,on Saturday evening, and received a magni- ficent ovation. As was the case with Mr. Parnell after his fall, people prefer to remember his high achievements. The ex-Chancellor is not in touch with the Germans of to-day; but the masses do not forget how much he had to do with making Germany a nation. It is pleasant to hear that the man of blood and iron was much moved," emotion choking his words." He has a heart in him after all.

There is a small congregation of Mahommadans in Liverpool; and there are heathens who call themselves Christians who seek to convert them by storming their place of worship, and showering stones and filth upon the worshippers. A nice oc- cupation truly for Sunday evening "Tie a mad world my masters." The world is yet in its in- fancy; I ut these vicious howling, ston,e-throwing infants should be Finished severely for All that. That is the way to convert them.

Typhoid, or enteric fever, from whleli Prince George of Wales is suffering has. a tendency to attack the young from 20 to 25. Mr. C. B. Cor- lett, of Earlestown, a promising young man of 21, died of this scourge on Saturday last, It would seem from the fact that both the Prince of Wales and the Prince Concert suffered from typhoid that there is in the family a susceptibility to this dis- ease. prim§ George is having the fever, it is reported, in a mild form ; and, as he has a vigorous constitution, there seems to be little doubt of his recovery.

Typhoid is essentially a sewer-gas fever, which is to say that it is nature's protest against bad sanitation. The great thing is to look to the drains, though it should be nnderstood that fouled milk, or bad drinking water, may be the source of infection. Considering the insanitary condition of many of our courts, narrow streets, and back passages, the wonder is not that so many people suffer from fever, bat that so many escape.

Mr. Diggle is happy in a capacity for being thankful for :mull mercies. He received 14 votes at the municipal elections in Warrington, and is as " proud as Punch" of the fact that his election expenses amounted to 12s. only. He boasts of having shown people "how to work things cheaply ;" but it would have been cheaper still if he had not "come out ;" and the result would have been about the same, wouldn't it William?

Sunday last was "Mayor's Sunday," and there was a good muster of the Warrington CorpoPation at the Parish Church, despite the wet without, for were they not assured that, at the finish, there would be something in the shape of wet within? Ten bottles of champagne were, it is stated, knocked on the head after leaving church and returning to the Town Hall. This was a very effectual way of course of knocking the sermon on the head.
The Rector showed the sin of drunkenness, Until the Corporation pulse went quicker; But, such is life I the searching sermon o'er, They drowned their good resolves in" fizzing"i liquor.

The Bishop of London in reply to a suggestion, at an Bast End meeting, that "the Church should pay more immediate attention to practical social politics, such as the eight hours question and labour interests in general, said that he thought it was at present too early for the Church to take up such matters officially.' What does this mean? That the Church will step in when all the hard work is done, and take credit for the victory? If these things are 'tight, the Church should help now, victory or no victory.

Elizabeth Tither, of St. Helens, has been in pri- son times innumerable for being drunk and dis- orderly. She came out of gaol on Saturday morn- ing, and has since been before the Bench for hav- ing, as usual, taken a drop too much. Oddly enough, she pleaded, this time, that going to pri- son had" so ruined her constitution that she could not stand any drink." The drink of course has not injured her. How would it be to give her "another month" in a brewery by way of restoring her con- stitution ?

The "Manchester Examiner and Times," after having had the misfortune to fall into the hands of Liberal Unionists has had the further misfortune to be turned into a Tory paper. The" Weekly Times" and new" Evening Times," are part of the same property, and pass into the hands of the same Company. Liberals wit have had their faith nursed by the " Examiner " in the brave days of old, and they are to be numbered, by thousands, cannot but feel a twinge to think of the change. To what base uses may we return "Horatio !"

It is obvious from the evidence on the bodies of the four men who were drowned near Formby, during the gale last week, that they were lured to destruction. There was at one time a lifeboat at the point ; the boat is gone, but the house remains with the words " Lifeboat house " conspicuously painted on it ta be seen at sea. The poor fellows would, it is . said, in all probability have saved their lives if they had not trusted to this braken reed. The boat should be replaced, and if the Lifeboat Institutioh, is as reported, short of funds, provision ought to be made for Government aid. It is anything but creditable to the greatest mara- time nation of the world that lives should be lost for want of a boat at an important station.

Something is still seen of the "dropping fire" of the Municipal Elections. There is an end pre- sumably of the threat of proceedings against Mr. Julian Winser for placing a bus on "sacred ground" in St. Austin's Ward ; but an action is threatened in connection with the Whitecross con- test. Mr. W. Bellian, the Tory candidate, is aggrieved at something alleged to have been uttered by Mr. Isaac Hayward at a Liberal meet- proceedings are threatened in this ing, and legal case. But there are two sides to contests of this kind,in which nobody but the lawyers have an ad- vantage, and Mr. Bellian will do well to consider whether the game is worth the candle. Both Judge and jury are averse as a rule to a fuss being made about things said in the heat of an election.

div.head: ACCIDENT TO A FOOTBALL PLAYER.
div.p: ACCIDENT TO A FOOTBALL PLAYER.

On Saturday afternoon, during the progress of a football match between Earlestown St. Johns, and Golborne, one of the St. John's players, named Geo. Pickup,was charged by one of the Golborne players, and had to be conveyed off tte field and taken home. Dr. Valentine was called in, and on examination found the lad had received some internal injury, and was suffering from hemorrhage of the kidneys. It will b 3 some time before he will be able to leave his bed. _ _

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

SIMMS CROSS PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, WIDNES. The evangelistic services in connection with this chapel were concluded on Sunday, when the services were well attended. The preachers were Mr. J. Jones and Mr. C. Sage.

div.head: VICTORIA-ROAD CHAPEL, WIDNES.
div.p: VICTORIA-ROAD CHAPEL, WIDNES.

During the past week a mission has been conducted In connection with this chapel, by Mr. William Sampson, who has delivered stirring addresses to large audiences, and it is hoped much good will ensue.
WIDNES VICTORIA CRIbIEBT CLUB.

In aid of the funds of this club a concert was held in the Baths Assembly room,under the presidency of Mr. D. Brookes. There was a crowded audience, who were provided with a first class entertainment of songs, comic sketches, and legerdemain. BETHESDA BA.ND OF HOPE, RUNCORN.

The members gave an entertainment in the school- room on Wednesday evening under the presidency of the Rev. John Simpson. An admirable programme of music was gone through. Mr. R. Bowen was the conductor and Mr. A. Price the accompanist.
WIDNES IRISH NATIONAL LIAGUR.

At the usual weekly meeting on Sunday, held under the presidency of Mr. P. Whelan, a resolution of condo- lence with the family of Mr. P. W. Nally was unani- mously passed. Final arrangements were made for • Canvassin to in cnection with the O'Keeffe g the - town . gn. - testimonial.
TER ASSISTANT LIBRARIAN AT WIDNEA.

rot. thd position of assistant librarian at Widnes Free Library, 30 applications were received, and the Commit- tee at a special meeting on Monday, interviewed nine of them. Eventually their choice fell upon Miss E. J. Jones, formerly assistant mistress at Farnworth National School who was appointed at a salary of 153. a week. GREENWAY-ROAD PRIMITIVE CHAPEL RUNCORN.

The annual sermons in aid of the home and foreign missions were preached on Sunday by the Rev. E. A. Davies, of Rochdale. There a good congregation at each service. On Wednesday the annual missionary meeting was held and suitable addresses were delivered by the Rev. E. A. Davies, J. Martin, J. P. Williams, H. Daven- port, and C. Finch. Mr. Upton presided.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH AT MINCOHN.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH AT MINCOHN.

The wife of Frederick Ditehfield; of 9, tgerton-st., died suddenly on Sunday morning. Tilt deceased, who was 21 years of age, had been confinedlra fortnight be- fore, but appeared to have recovered, although she was still under the care of Dr. Robinson. On Saturday night she retired to rest apparently all right, and at 5 o'clock next morning she awoke and asked her husband to rub her arm. He did so and inquired what was the matter, and receiving no reply, found that she was dead. Dr. Robinson stated death was due to natural causes, pro- bably from a clot lodging in one of the arteries of the brain. The Coroner deemed an inquest unnecessary.

GRIENWAY-ROAD BOARD SCHOOL.—EVENING CLAMS. After the close of the lessons on Tuesday evening, the students of these classes were entertained by means of the magic lantern. The entertainment which had been arranged by the teachers with the worthy object Ot increasing the interest of the pupil in thdir work, con- sisted first, of a number of geographical views of Eng- land, Scotland and Ireland, and concluded With views of the principal local objects of interest, together with portraits of notable men of the present day. There was a large number of students present, and Mr. Epps des- cribed the various pictures in an interesting man.ier. The lantern was manipulated by Mr. T. Boroyer and the entertainment closed with the singing of the National Anthem.
RUNCORN FRIE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood. The Librarian (Mr. J. D. Jones) presented his report which showed that 2,042 books had been borrowed during the month, an increase of 303 on the same period last year. 37 books had been issued from the Reference Department, an increase of 21.—The Book Selection Committee recom- mended the purchase of 161 new volumes including 60 educational books in French. The recommendation was passod on the motion of Mr. W. Handley seconded by Mr. H. G. Grice. The Librarian reported that a number of books had been presented. On the motion of Mr. Humphreys seonded by Mr. Grice it was decided that the lending library should be open on Christmas Day and closed on the following day Bank Holiday and that the caretaker be alloweß ss. for extra services.—Mr. C. E. Dawson wrote asking for an alteration of the rule which compelled non-residents to pay a fee for the benefit of the library. He argued that woi king in Runcorn entitled him to the use of the library without the payment of a fee. —The Committee held a different opinion and it was resolved that they could not accede to Mr. Dawson's wishes.
RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

The employes of this society held a social gathering in the Co-operative Hall, on Wednesday, and together with their wives and sweethearts, spent a most enjoyable evening. The proceedings commenced with a bountiful tea, the ladies presiding at the tables being Mrs.liughes, Mrs. Rushton, Mrs. Price, Mrs. Leach, Mrs. Davenport, Mrs. Baiter, and Mrs. Ashbrook. Afterwards a concert was given, under the presidency of Mr. D. Worthington, who delivered an appropriate address. The pr6gramme was as follows :—Trio, "Ihe little farm," Messrs. Brown, Shaw, and Shingler ; song," Robin Adair," Miss Morris; song, "The hero of the war," Mr. Shingler; song, "Another colour," Mr.Withington •, recitation, "A night at the pantomime," Mr. Davies ; selection. " Rule Brit- tania," Miss Cartwright (aged seven) ; song, "A soldier and a man," Mr. A. Shingler; song, "The anchor's weighed," Mr. Lacey ; song, "The white squall," Mr. Brown ; recitation, "Mr. Simpkins' adventures at Mar- gate," Mr. Saunders ; duet, "Larboard watch," Messrs. Brown and Shingler : song, " Only to see her face again,".Mrs. Price. . The accompanist was Miss Palmer. In the course of the evening Messrs. Brocklebank and Blinston gave a magic lantern entertainment. The usual votes of thanks were passed. HOLY TRINITY CRTIRCH, RUNCORN. A social tea meeting and entertainment was held in the schoolroom, on Wednesday evening. It was mainly due to the efforts of three or four of the young men in connection with the church that the aforesaid meeting was brought about. After tea had been partaken °Lever which the following ladies presided, viz., Miss Smith, Miss Turner, Mrs. Oliver, Miss Cooper, Miss Massey, and Miss Watson, the- following programme was gone through :—Song. " Anchor'd," Mr. J. Leathwood ; song, "Ask a policeman," Mr. Kenyon ; song, " McGee's back yard," Mr. Risley ; reading (Lancashire), Mr. Rhodes; song. "The wolf," Mr. Norris; song, "Do, Ra, Mi, Fa," Mr. Scott; song,"Madoline," Mr. Pilgrim ; song,"What a fool I must have been to Mary Jane," Mr. Kenyon; song, "Yo, ho, my lads," Mr. Norris; reading (Lanca- shire), Mr. Rhldes : song, "Serenade," Mr. Scott. Each item was rendered in a most excellent fashion, being very well received by the audience. Mr. Norris gave "The diver" as an encore to "The wolf." The Rev. Dr. Preston was unavoidably absent, owing to a sudden at- tack of bronchitis. A vote ef thanks, proposed by Mr. Manning, and seconded by Mr. Kilcross, to the ladies and performers for their services, brought a very plea- sent evening to a close.
ROBBERIES AT RUNCORN.

Yesterday before Mr. Henry Reynolds and Mr. James Handley, William Worrall of Five Crosses, was charged with stealing a pair of boots from the shop of Messrs. Tyler and Co.,Bridge-st. The prisoner who was caught in the act was sentenced to 14 days hard labour.— Frederick Cross, a youth 15 years of age, whose home is in Alccck-st., was charged with having on the pre- vious day stolen a purse containing £2 the uroperty of Geo. Fife, a seaman on board a vessel at Weston Point. The prisoner said he went on board to get a bucket from the forecastle, and seeing the purse on the bed he , yielded to the sudden temptation and took it.—The Bench accepted this view of the case and fined the pri- soner in the lenient penalty of 103.—John Brown was charged with stealing a railway automatic vacuum break gage value £4, and also a number of joiners tools, the property of some person unknown. On Thursday afternoon P.C. Bullock was walking down Water-st., and saw the prisoner attempting to avoid him. He therefore followed him and searched him, finding him in possession of the articles named. As he could not give a clear account of how he obtained them he was arrested and he was remanded for inquiries to be made.
