This was the title of the third lecture, at Runcorn, by the Rev. J. Yonge, on the subject of Histori- cal Nonconformity. Bethesda Lecture Hall was fil'ed by an attentive audience and the Rev. J. P. Williams presided. The illustrations were ably shown by Mr. W. H. Handley by means of a tri- unial oxyhydrogen lantern. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and .W. DUTTON, Sankey-A., Ward ngton.—Advt.

iof the existing sewers in the township of Helsby, and prepare and carry out a proper drainage system for effectually draining the district for the purposes of the Public Health Acts. The system of draining in Helsby was totally inadequate for the requirements of the place and was in a disgraceful condition. The sewers were mostly open ditches contaminated with filthy matter. The present method of dealing with the sewage in the village was just the same as that which existed thirty or even fifty years ago, although there had been an im- mense increase in the number of inhabitants. The stenches arising from the open sewers were a grave dan- ger to the public health of the district. If there was any delay in dealing with this matter he should take such steps as he might be advised to enforce the rights of his clients.—Mr. Farrington said there was no doubt that the sewage got into the ditches. The Railway Company had cut off the natural outfal: into the river, and it was their duty to abate the nuisance.—Mr. Brandreth said the matter wanted attending ts, and he moved that a parochial committee consisting of Messrs. W. Collin, J. Ella,m, J. Brandreth, Croston, Taylor, J. Jeff, and W. Thornley,deal with the subject.—Mr. Aaron seconded.— Carried.—The Medical Officer of Health (Dr. Adams), re- ported that two cases cf typhoid fever had occurred at Helsby,and the .owners of the property had promised to make good several minor defects.

div.head: CONCERT AT CADISHEAD.
div.p: CONCERT AT CADISHEAD.

The annual concert of the Cadishead and Irlam Cricket Club was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, on Monday evening. The concert was a great suc- cess, the room being filled with the elite of the neighbourhood and the cricketing fraternity. The programme was a good one,.and the artistes nume- rous. Mr. N. F. Clegg accompanied the vocalists. The Cadishead Old Brasil Band played selections during the evening. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—L and W. Durrox, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adv. DEATH THROUGH DRINK AT WIDNES.

The Widnes police on Wednesday, received infor- mation of the sudden death of Joseph Noon' a chemical labourer, who lodged in North-street. On Saturday night Noon was drunk, and went out about eleven o'clock, telling his landlady that she need not wait up for him. Re did not return until nine o'clock on Sunday morning when he was bleed- ing from a wound in the forehead. He complained of pains in his head and went to bed, and on Mon- day afternoon Dr. Richards was called in and pre- scribed for him. He died at six o'clock in the evening. The deceased stated that he had fallen down and so received his injuries. Mr. Husband held an inquest on the body on Thursday afternoon. Dr. Richards said deceased had had an auremetic fit and death was due to auremic poisoning induced by alcoholism.—A verdict to the effect that death was due to auremic poisoning brought on by exces- sive drinking.
UMBRELLASItECOYEBED.—L and W. Durrox, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. MR. J. VERDI& AND THE COMPENSATION FUND.

Mr. Joseph Terdin, of Northwich, has decided how to dispose of the £26,000 originally intended for the compensation for subsidence fund, when the compensation bill was passed. The money was found unnecessary for that purpose, and Mr. Verdin will give £6,000 to the Victoria Infirmary, Northwich, the other twenty thousand to be divided between Northwich and Winsford for the foundation of technical schools, &c. Tle " Star " says :—" Mr. Joseph Verdin, who has just given £26,000 to public institutions in Northwich, was, until recently, 4. director of the Salt Union. Like Mr. Corbett and Mr. Brunner, he his credited with having amassed enormous wealth out of natural deposits in Cheshire. Recently he became tenant of Roseneith Castle, the Duke of Argyll's famous seat in Dumbartonshire. He is also a large landowner in Mid-Cheshire. His tenants at Wim- beldsley are loud in his praises, for he has built new farmhouses right and left, 'constructed roads, spent large sums in drainage and water supply, and promised his tenants that he will not look for a penny of the outlay back again in increased rents. The Verdins will try hard to oust Mr. Brunner from the representation of the division." InsißmlTlTike 411(.1 W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warringteq•=4M, COLLT)/1111 FATALITY : A MINEII. CENSURED.

On Monday afternoon, Mr. W. T. Husband,deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Boar's Head Inn, Sutton Meath, touching the death of Danial Brown- bill, 38 years of age, a waggoner, of 720, Mill-lane, ,Sutton Heath, who was killed in Sutton Heath 'Colliery on Friday morning. Mr. IL Hall, Govern- ment inspector of mines, attended, and Mr. Pennington, certificated manager, represented the proprietors, the Sutton Heath and Lea Green Collieries Companies. John Smith,. of ' Marshall's Cross, and William Cutts, of Rainhill, waggoners, gave evidence that they and the deceased were removing several boxes of coal from one of the "shunts," when by some means two of the waggons got disconnected and ran down an incline. They collided with some waggons, of which Brownbill was in charge and Brownbill was crushed to death. —Mr. Hall, the Government inspector, said the rules of the mine required all waggons to be coupled when descending an incline, and there had been a breach of the rules on the part of the man Cutts, who had attempted to take three waggons, two of which were uncoupled. If the rule had not been broken the accident would not have happened. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," but considered that Cutts ought to be censured for his carelessnesA in moving the waggons uncoupled. —The Deputy-coroner called Cutts into the room, and reprimanced him for his neglect.
GAS Fall/035.—J. S. Garland, Gas Fitter, Bridge-st., Warringtou.—Advt. Tint LATE MR. WHITELBGG OF GRAPPINHALL.

Mr. William Long, J.P., writing in reference to the death of this old inhabitant at the age of 88, says :—I thought it might interest some of your local readers if I supplemented the information there given. It was early in 1846 that he entered the service of my father's firm, and except during a severe attack of smallpox about 25 years ago, he was rarely absent from his post, as& so strong was the force of habit, that he was about the tanyard as usual on the Friday before his death. Few men were better known in the neighbourhood or mere loved or respected,:with his stalwart form and plea- sant greeting. He was descended from a long line of yeoman ancesters, which I have traced back over two centuries. His grandfather, on retiring from the tanning trade in the beginning of this century, bought an estate in Stretton, where he ultimately died. He used from there to drive down each Sun- day with his large family and servants to the old Presbyterian chapel, now known as the Cairo-street Chapel, Warrington, putting up his horses and re- maining for the morning and afternoon services. He left a large family. One of them the Rev. William Whitelegg, was for about 50 years the minister of the Unitarian Chapel at Plitt, near Manchester; another the father of the subject of this notice, car- ried on the business of tanning until his death.
UMBRELLAS HECOVERED.--J. and W. DUTTON. Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.
RIVAL CHEMICAL AND COPPER WORKERS.

The Chemical and Copper Workers' Union, which was started some two years ago by Mr. P. J. Krng, had not been in existence long before another society under the name of the St. Helena Labourers' Union was formed, having for its secretary and general manager a Mr. James Chadwick, a former member of the Union, but the success of the venture hardly came up to expectations. From the announcement of a proposed meeting on Saturday, it appears that the name has been revised, the title reading thus—" The United Alkali and Capper Workers' and General Labour Union." Mr. Ben Tillett, of the London Dockers' Union, was ad- vertised to speak, but within the last few days he has written to Mr. Chadwick, asking why he had been invited to come to a Union which he under- stood was under the 'dominant influence of the employers.' This Mr. Chadwick indignantly denies, and says that the representations that have been made to Mr. Tillett are untrue. It is stated that Mr. p. j. King had written to Mr. Tillett with reference to his proposed visit, and Mr. Tillett in his reply to Mr. Sing, says that he was under the impression, when he promised to come to St. Helens, that the society was a branch of the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union, and that Mr. James Chadwick was one of his members, and that nnder the circum- stances be will not come to the meeting. KITCHEN R ANGERS.—Garland Builders Ironmonger, War rington.-- Advt. FARE FIRE NEAR ST. ITELENS.—SUPPOSED INCENDIARISM.

Early on Tuesday, information was received at the St. Helens Town Hall, that a fire had broken out on the premises of Mr. James Hayes, Royal Oak Farm, Eccleston. Supt. Birchall and a staff of men with steamer and horse reel proceeded at once to the spot, which is about four miles distant. There they found the barn, shippon, cart shed, and other out-buildings on fire. As it was useless to "try and save these the firemen directed their efforts to pro- tect the stables and the twelve stacks of hay in the yard. In this they succeeded, having a good supply' of water f-om a pit in a field as well as from the St. Helens Corporation mains. The barn, shippon, cart- shed, and other outbuildings were completely gut- ted, and about twenty tons of straw in the barn , were destroyed. The fire was not completely ex- tinguished until half-past four in the morning. Considerable damage ws,s done, but the loss is covered by insurance.—At Prescot Petty Sessions, ofi. Tuesday, Martin Foy, fern labourer, was charged with setting fire to the farm buildings of Mr. James Heyes. Prisoner was in prosecutor's employ, and about midnight the shippon and barn were found on fire, when prisoner was seen running away shout- ing, "My Ged, shall I ever be forgiven for this?" The entire building was destroyed, and it was stated that the damage was roughly estimated at £l5O. Prisoner was remanded as the prosecutor was un- able to proceed with the case that day.—Martin Foy, the farm labourer who on Tuesday was remanded on a charge of setting fire to the shippon and outbuildings at the farm belonging to James 4 Heyes, in Gregson's-lane, Eccleston, was again Ibrought up on Thursday. Superintendent Barker informed the bench that he was satisfied that the fire was purely accidental, prisoner having no con- nection with it. Ife would therefore offer no evid- ence.—Prisoner was discharged.

div.head: FINANCES OF RUNCORN UNION.
div.p: THE FINANCES OF RUNCORN UNION.

• At the meeting of Runcorn Board of Guardians, on Tuesday. the clerk (Hr. J. Ashton) submitted the financial statement of the Union accounts for the half year ended Lady Day last. The balance in favour of each parish at the commencement of the half year amounted to £1,859 15s. sd. ; the contribu- tions amounted to £4562; other receipts £3 4s. 3d.; balance against parishes at the end of the half year, £142 is. 9d.; total £6,567 is. 54. The expenditure included common charges £1,889 108. 3d.; separate charges, £25 17s. 4d.; Workhouse loan and interest repaid .ClO9 13s. 4d. ; county rate, £3,126 14s. 9.1.; balance £1,380 10s. 6d.; total .C 6,567 is. od. The particulars of common charges showed that in- maintenance cost £570 14s. 7d.; out-relief, £1,815 Os. 44.; lunatics in asylums Sze., £384 131. 2d.; salar- ies and other remuneration of officers, £542155. 9d.; officers rations, £75 Os. 44.: superannuation allow- ances £4l; vaccination £73 ; registration, .CBO ' 7s. ; legal expenses, .C 9 7s. 71. and other items making a total of £3,883 24. 44. The common fund receipts amounted to, £1,993 12s. 14. and included Cheshire County Council; grant for registrars, £18; grant for lunatics, £376; grant for union officers, £1,416; repayment of relief, £ll9 16s. 7d.; Bankers' interest, £22 13s. 7d.; profit on pig and garden account, £33 19s. 44. The outstand- ing liabilities of the Guardians amounted to £2,964 3s. Bd. The rateable value of the Union was £218,841 being an increase of £844 on the corres- ponding half year. Of the total contributions of £4,562. Runcorn township contributed £1,169, more than one quarter, leaving the remainder to be con- tributed by the other 36 townships.

div.head: ADULTERATED FOOD AT WIDNES.
div.p: ADULTERATED FOOD AT WIDNES.

r Before Mr. J. Brock and Col. Gasket!, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Thomas Wiles,milk dealer,Salisbury- st., was charged with having on the 27th October, sold to P.C. Thompson a pint of milk which was not of the quality demandod.--Superintendent Noblett said the analyist, Dr. Campbell Brown,cortified that 20 parts of water had been added to every 100 parts of the poorei t milk.—Defendant said he bought it for new milk and paid 2s. 9d. per dozen for it. He had been selling milk in Widnes for 21 years, and al- though his milk had been tested many times it had never been found wrong before.—Supt. Noblett said he believed this statement was quite accurate.—Mr. Brock said in consequence of defenndant's good record they would only gne him 203. and costs £1 Os. 6d.—James Gittens, of Moss Bank, was summoned for selling lard which was not of the quality demanded.—P.C. Thomp- son deposed to purchasing a pound of lard, and after he had told Mrs. Gittens that it was for analysis, she told him it was beef dripping.—Supt. Noblett said it was plain the stuff was beef dripping, and the analyst certi- fied that it contained 96 per cent, of beef fat.—Mrs. Gittens said the business was hers, but there was not three pounds of goods in the shop and she did not do much trade.—P.C. Thompson said , the bueinesi YMS a small one and the woman was very poor.—Mr. Brock warned defendant that when people asked for lard, she must not sell beef fat. In conse- quence of her circumstances she would be mulcted in the small penalty of 2i. 61. and co3ts 20s. 6.l.—John Francis Kelly, grocer, Ann-st., was summoned for ex- posing for sale margarine without havino, attached there to a. label printed in capital letters of not less than one and a half inches square. P.C. Thompson proved the case.—The defendant said he did not know that he was required to have such labels. Mr. Brook told him it was part of his business to know the law on the subject, and he must pay a fine of 20s. and costs 20s. ed.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held at the Work- house on Tuesday, Mr. Mclntyre presided and there were present. Rev. J. W. Tanner, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. J. Weir, Aaron, Lewis, P. Hall, T. A letter was read from the Clerk to the County Council who stated that the following rates had been ordered for the half year ending March 31st., general 2idy in the £, police id., local police Runcorn Union 7-8 of a penny. The precept would be made in due course and made returnable at the end of January.—The Clerk Said the amount required was £3,292 103., exactly the same amount as last half year.—ln the corresponding half last year, the amount was £3,126 us. 9d.

div.p: FINANCE.
On the recommendation of the Finance Committee accounts amounting to £l5l were passed for payment.— The balance in the treasurer's hands was £3,003 is. 7d.
TIM RELINF DISTRICTS.

Mr. Brandreth moved that the relief districts be re- arranged by the transfer of the townships of Aston, As- ton Grange, Stockham, and Sutton from Frodsham Re- lief District to Runcorn, and the township of Norton from Budwerth district to Runcorn, so as to bring each relief district contemperaneon4 with each vaccination and registration district.—Mr. Lightburn seconded, and said it would be a great improvement in every way.—ln answer to Mr. Danes', the Clerk said the populations of the nropo;ed districts were as follows: Runcorn 24,886, Frodsham 8,763, Budworth 8.332. The area was—Run- corn 10,213 acres, Frodsham 15,723 acres, and Bud worth 21,168 acres.—Mr. Da.nsey said he did not think there would be any objection to the change, but he should like to know the number of cases in each district.—The Clerk could not supply the infortuation.—Mr. Brandreth said Runcorn had the greatest number of paupers: it was tho place where all the pauners came from. (Laughter.)— Mr. Lightburn : And it is the plaae where the money comes from. (Laughter.)—The motion was carried.
ALTERATION AT THE ROUSE

Mr. Dansey said the Boaici 1W(i'f;;;;;;;ded to the Local Government Board, a plan, showing an outside staircase to the children's dormitories as a meansof escape in case of fire. He suggested that the same end might be gained at less cost hr fixing several smoke-proof doors on the landings. With regard to the plan for building cells to accommodate seven more vagrants,he suggested that the Board would do well in the present changeable state of law to have an association ward. It was not. improbable that they would have to treat vagrants as inmates, and in that case cells would not be available, whereas an as- sociation ward would.—The Visiting Committee after- wards considered the question on the spot, and it was resolved, on the motion of Mr. Aaron, to write to the Local Government Board fototheir rules as to construct- ing vagrant wards.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held, at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Mr. Mclntyre presided, and there were present Messrs. Brandretb, W. Turner, Wilkinson, A. Bretherton, P. Hall, Lewis, Heywood, Aaron, J. Weir, J. Ashton (clork), G. Ashton (assistant clerk), and Mr. Dansey (Local Government Board Inspector).

div.head: TUE POLLUTION OF RIVERS.
div.p: TUE POLLUTION OF RIVERS.

Mr. F. C. Hulton, County Offices, Preston, wrote as follows, under date 2nd Nov.—" Dear sir,—Mersev and Irwell Watershed: The joint Committee for carrying into effect the provisions of the Rivers Pollution (Preven- tion) Act, 1876, within the watersheds of the -rivers Mersey and Irwell as constituted under the Act passed in the last session of Parliament, have mat, and have come to the conclusion that the time has now arrived when in the interests of the health and comfort of the community, steps should be taken without delay to purify the rivers within their district and if compelled to do so, to put in force the provisions of that Act. The Committee, are however, most anxious to enlist in their endeavour to improve the state and condition of the rivers the support and aid, of all the local authorities within the district without which it is felt that the duties imposed upon them will be not only most arduous and most disagreeable to perform. With the object of ac- curately ascertaining what has been done, I am desired by the Committee to request you to be kind enough to inform me what steps have been taken by your Authority with regard to the disposal of the sewage within your district, and it would also be of much assistance to the Committee if you would also state what effect the steps you have taken have had upon the health of your dis- trict. In the event of your not having adopted any scheme of sewerage the Committee would be glad to learn what steps are being taken by your Authority to provide such a scheme, and the stage at which it has arrived."—The Clerk was instructed to reply.

div.head: SEWAGE AND DISEASE AT EEL BY.
div.p: SEWAGE AND DISEASE AT EEL BY.

Mr. S. Thornley, solicitor, Chelsea, London, S.W., wrote with reference to the Helsby Sewers and Sewage, complaining that a Committee appointed to deal with the matter, had failed to keel) an appointment with Mr. Thornley and his representative. He was instructed to ask that the Authority would place the sewers round Mr. Thornley's property in a thoroughly healthy and sanit- ary condition and render them suitably adapted to the requirements of the immediate neighbourhood ,and would also see that the ditches in his meadows were not con- taminated with sewage. He was also in.tructed to ask that the Authority would thoroughly inspect the whole

div.head: POLLUTION or KECKWICK BROOK.
div.p: THE POLLUTION or KECKWICK BROOK.

The Clerk said with reference to this matter Mr. Long- ton had supplied him with evidence to the effect that the brook was a public sewer, but this was not exactly what was wanted and he wrote to Mr. Longton asking him if he could furnish him with a copy of the evidence which was given before Colonsl Ducat at the Government Inquiry. Mr. Longton replied that he could not do so, and added that Mr. Earp explained the large proportion. of solids in the analysis by the fact that he tanned prin- cipally foreign hides, which each contained several pounds of salt, which was washed into this brook.—The Clerk said he had written to the Local Government Board for the information, and he wanted the matter adjourn- ing fora fortnight.—Mr. Aaron said they had all along been blaming Mr. Earp for this brook, but refuse from that tannery had been carted into pits on the Aston estate. (Mr. Wilkinson: Only one). Well in one pit, and the sulphuretted hydrogen, which was deadly poison to both man and beast, drained from that pit into the brook. Mr. Earp was not to blame for that, if he had had permission to place the refuse there.—Mr. Wilkinson said he did not see that either the estate, Mr. Earp, or the tenants were to blame.—Mr. Weir said something stronger than salt was going down the brook. It was turned out from the works as black as ink sometimes. The subject was deferred for a fortnight.
PRESTON-'6TE-RILL WATER- SUPPLY.

Mr. Aaron said for many months past there had been complaints of want of water at Preston-o'th-Hill and yet nothing was done. How was this.—The Inspector said the place was very badly off for water and he had been in communication with the agents of Sir Gilbert Greenall, whe kept promising but never performed anything.—Mr. Aaron proposed that the Clerk communicate with Messrs. White and Co., of Warring- ton, the agents.—This matter was carried.
NUISANCE AT HALTON BROOK.
Letters ware read from Messrs. Pritchard, Cunning- ham, and Baguley of Preston Brook, complaining of the nuisance caused by an open dtain. A Committee was appointed to deal with the matter.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday afternoon, there were present Mr. James Burehall (chair- man), Rev. S. A. K. SyJester, Rev. Dean Finegan,Messrs. Tyrer. Johnson, Middlehurst, Wareing, Ranson, Kan- wright, Whalley, Huhne, Davies, Syder, Jos. Birehall, E. Birchall. Kenwright, P. Longton, Borrows, and A. F. Mann (clerk). .

workhthise thaster reported that there were 551. inmates this week, 551 last week and 555 in corresponding week last year. During the present week outdoor relief had been granted to 2,881, persons, at a cost of £237 us. 9d., against 2,896 persons, and a cost of £2OB is. 11d. last week.

AGED MARRIED COUPLES.-Mr. Middlehurst moved the adoption of the minutes of the Building Committee, which included a recommendation that the sum of £2OO be spent on the erection of two cottages on the Work- house premises, for the provision of accommodation for aged married couples.—The motion was carried. THE LOCAL GOVRRNMENT BOARD AND EMIGRATION.— The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board acknowledging receipt of a letter from the Guar- dians relating to a proposal to incur on expediture not exceeding £lO in assisting the emigration to the United States of America, of three children named Forsyth. The Board in consequence of objections by the United States Government,for many years declined to assent to any ex- penditure out of the poor rates in the emigration of per- sons to the United States, except so far aS, was necessary to convey persons in certain cases to the port of embarka- tion. Having had the subject under further consideration the Board some time time since arrived at the conclusion that it was inexpedient that, even to the limited extent referred to, the public rates should be applied in aid of emigration to the United States, and they therefore, felt precluded from assenting to the proposal of the Guar- dians in the present instance.—Mr. Wareing said the Local Government Board appeared to be under the im- pression that the Guardians wished to send paupers to the United States. Such was not the fact.—The Clerk explained that the children were deserted by their parents and were at present chargeable to the Union. A relative had written from New York offer- ing to accept the children and take charge of them and had forwarded part payment of the passage money.—The Chairman said the children ' would not be paupers after being placed on board.—Mr. Wareing said if the children were removed it would mean a saving of £2O per year to the rates of the Prescot Union.—The Clerk was instructed toNain communicate with the Local Government Board upon the subject.

WIDNES VACCINATION OFFICERS.—The Local- Govern- ment Board wrote assenting to the vaccination contracts with Dr. Creighton Hutchinson for the Farnworth and Lower Widnes districts. The Board also approved of the admission of Dr. Hudson to act as occasional deputy to Dr. Hutchinson, but only on'the distinct understanding that his services would only be employed in the unavoid- able absence of the public vaccinator, who was respon- sible, and who ought to habitually perform the opera- tion. This was UK, principal business.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The usual monthly meeting of the Widnes School Board was held in the Widnes Town Hall, on Tues- day afternoon, Mr. T. S. Timmis presiding. The School Management Committee recommended an alteration in the schedule of salaries of head teachers—namely, that head masters of schools where the average attendance was 200 or more should receive £195 for the sixteenth year's service, and £2OO for the seventeenth. Pre- viously, it had been £l9O for the fifteenth year, which was the maximum salary. IT:. recom- mendation was opposed by the Rev. Dean Finegan (chairman of the committee), who said he thought their teachers were well paid at pre- sent, and this recommendation was simply to in- crease their salaries under cover. He was in favour of the board adopting a regular scale of salaries for their teachers. .The Chairman said be would rather they had a scale of salaries for their 'teachers than the present system. A long discussion ensued, and eventually the recommendation was passed by 5 votes to 3.—The Clerk read her Majesty's inspector's report on the schools, which was in each case satis- factory. The Government grants earned by the schools were as follows :--Simm's ..C1,353 6s. (less £77 17s. 4d., the amount of the Government grant under the Free Education Act, which has not been spent by the board) ; West Bank, £932 48.; and Warrington road, £553 2s. 6d.

Ti Mmrrieci.—The scholars attending the Wesleyan Sunday school, numbering about 40, were last evening week entertained to tea by Mr. John Frodsham. After the children had done ample justice to the good things provided, Mr. Frodsham informed those present that he Intended to establish a Band of Hope Union in the dis- trict. A very interesting magic lantern exhibition was given by the Rev. J. Hanby. of Holton, to which friends and parents of the children were admitted free. MISSIONARY SIRMONS, ice.—The.. annual missionary services in aid of foreign missions were held in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, on Sunday, when two ser- mons were preached by Mr. Charles Finch and Mr. tea- cock, of Runcorn, to good congregations. After each of the services a collection was made on behalf of the society. On Tuesday evening, the annual missionary meeting was held in the same place, under the presid- ency of Captain Roger, of Newton :Bank. A collection was made at the close of the meeting, which, together with Sunday's amounted to about £3. - .

OPENING OF AN ORGAN.—On Sunday evening, a special service was conducted in the Wesleyan Chapel, by Mr. B. Kniveton, of Runcorn, being the occasion of the opening of a new American organ. "The Methodist Hymn Book: Its History and Associations" formed the subject ot Mr. Kniveton's address, which included inter- esting accounts of the lives of Charles Wesley, John Wesley, and others. A special selection of old Methodist hymns was given by the choir, and in several instances the circumstances under which the hymns were written were told by the preacher. The anthem "Make a joyful noise," by Simper, was rendered by the choir, and a col- lection was made at the close on behalf of of the organ fund. Mr. Albert Webb was at the organ.

It apnea,rs from the o' facial return of railway accidents in the United Kingdom during the six months en ling in June last that 547 persons were killcd and 2,378 in- jured, being an increase of 70 fatalities and 380 minor casualties.
IA RUNCORN LICENSING PRO-

div.head: SEC lITION.
div.p: SEC lITION.
A CONVICTION RECORDED.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. C. Reynolds, and Mr. A. Thomas, James Ditch- field licensed victualler of the Royal HoteloMersey- st., was aummoned under two informations for having on the 10th inst. supplied intoxicating liquor to a drunken person named Thomas Haddock and with permitting drunkenness on his premises. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys prosecuted on behalf of the police and Mr. Brown, barrister-at-law, (instructed by Mr. F. A. Lake) defended.—ln opening the case Mr. Humphreys said no attempt was made at the time of the oecurence to deny that the man was drunk. The barman admitted it, and the manager admitted it. Such being the case, it was a matter as to how far those facts presented themselves for a conviction. It was almost necessary that separate summonses should be issued with respect to the charges, in order to secure a conviction on one of them, for in a case heard at the Surrey Sessions, it was held that supplying liquor to a person on licensed premises in a state of drunkenness did not mean permitting drunkenness.but in a case decided by the Court of Queen's ll:nich on the 27th of last month, it was clearly laid down that selling intox- icating liquors to drunken men did undoubtedly mean permitting drunkenness. D2fendant was charged with both offences. and he asked for a con- viction in each case. He did not know what the defence of his learned friend would be, but anticip- ating that it would be the ignorance of the licensee as to Haddock's condition, he wioted a section of the Liceneing Act, which stated that a publican might be convicted, although the fact that the man was drunk was unknown to him, or his ser- vant at the time when he was supplied. That meant. , the public must take the risk with regard to what those in his employ did. Mr. Humphreys proceeded ' to say that two months before the licensing session, the defendant came to reside on the premises, and took actual Control of the licensed premises, and assured the police that if the license was renewed he would continue to reside on the premises, Mr. Ross Brown contended that such remarks Avere irrelevant, and the Bench concurred, Mr. Reynolds re- markinz that the only question was "was this man drunk?"

Inspector Cooper said about half-past four on the after- noon in question, he was in the police office, when he saw Haddock enter the Commercial Hotel. In about two minutes the man left the hotel and staggered down the street. Witness and P.C. Bullock went to the door, but lost sight of the man at the end of Mersey-st. Ten minutes later witness visited the Royal Hotel, and in the bar he saw Haddock standing at the counter. He was very drunk, and had before him a pint pot three- parts full of beer. He was the only customer in the place. Witness drew the attention of Brown, the bar- man, to the drunken condition of the man, and he re- plied, "He (meaning Haddock) was leaning against the counter." The manager, Edward Hankinson, was then called, and after looking at Haddock, he said, "I am very sorry ; I was out in the back yard. I hope you will look over it." Hankinson then rstnoved the pint pot, and Haddock, who staggered outside, was after- wards locked up and remanded until that morning.—By Mr. Brown: He had only been in Runcorn three months, and could not speak of the general conduct ef the housQ,_ He would have gone to the Commercial Hotel if Haddock had not come out. He could not say whether he was served there or not. The reason he lost sight of Haddock was because a man and two women came into the office respecting a prisoner, and whilst talking to them he lost sight of Haddock. When he saw Haddock going along th• street, it was his intention to have him arrested, because he was not in a fit state to be in the street. There was no one in the hotel besides Haddock and the barman.

P.C. Bullock gave corroborative evidence, and gave his op;nion that Haddock was thoroughly drunk. Cross- examined by Mr. Ross Brown, witness said that he did not see Haddock go in to the Royal Hotel. He thought that the barman meant by saying that Haddock was leaning against the counter when heserved him that he had been thus deceived as to his condition.

Superintendent Large deposed that aboat tbreeo'clock on Tuesday afternoon, the 10th inst., he saw Haddock in Bridge-st., staggering about, and scarcely able to keep upon the footpath. He had no doubt as to him being drunk. The same evening he met the defendant's manager in Greenway-road, when he said, "The inspec- tor found a man drunk in our house, and he is going to report me. I was in the yard getting some coke in at the time, but had I been in the bar I would not have served him." In cress-examination, witness said he only knew from the office books that Mr. Ditchfield had kept the Royal Hotel for 16 years, and had not been convicted. He was not awarethat Mr. Ditchfield had been a licensed victualler for 42years. Re-examined by Mr. Humphreys witness said Mr. Ditchfield did not now reside upon the premiss. _ _

William Huhue, licensee of the Commercial Hotel, said on the afternoon in question Haddock came to his house and asked for a pint of beer. He did not serve him, as he thought he had had as much as was good for him. He staggered a little as he left the house. Cross-examined, witness said be had been summoned to attend as a wit- ness that day. 10 he on the safe side, he thought it better not to serve him.

Mr. Ross Brown, for the defence, said his client had been a licensed victualler for 42 years, and during the whole of that period he had only been convicted once, which was 22 years ago, the fine on that occasion being only 2s. 61. and costs. He had been the licensee of the Royal Hotel for 16 years, and while in that house there had been no conviction recorded against him. Mr. Ditchfield had evidently discharged his arduous duties both to the satisfaction of the community and to the Bench, and the jealous watch kept upon a licensed vic- tualler:and the fact that the license might be endangered by merely one offence made it clear to them that it was to his interest that he should take care that his business was very carefully conducted. The question seemed to be whether the man was drunk or not, but he submitted with great confidence that that was not the only question. There were two more questions, first as to whether the barman who served the man was acting in direct contra- vention of the orders of the licensee, and furthermore whether the man was intoxicated to the knowledge of the defendant's servant. Whether he was drunk or not, he might not be drunk at that moment when he was be- ing served, for it was no difficult matter for a man to brace himself up and appear quite sober when demanding to be served with drink at a bar. He would point out to their worships that the defend- ant's servant who served the man with beer, was not in so advantageous a position to see whether the man was drunk or not as the police. The barman had not had the opportunity of watching him for 80 yards, and the man could brace himself up for a few yards when entering the bar. If he established to the satisfaction of their worships that the barman did not think the man was drunk, then they were entitled to a dismissal of the sum- mons.

William Brown, barman at the Royal Hotel, said he remembered Haddock be4ng in the Royal Hotel on the afternoon in question. Re was at the bottom of the bar when he entered, and was leaning against the counter. About two or three minutes after he had served him, the Inspector came in and said" Who has served this man ? I have been watching him." Witness told him that he had served Haddock, and then sent for the manager. Haddock did not stagger as he left the house. He threw out his feet and walked a little awkward. There was a man named Compton in the bar at the time. He could not see that the man was drunk.

Zachariah Compton, 14, Stanley-st.. Runcorn, said he was in the Royal Hotel on Tuesday afternoon when Had- dock was being served. He then appeared to be sober. Had he been in the position of the barman he would have served him. He heard the Inspector say that he had been watching Haddock. Edward Hankinson, manager of the Reiyal Hotel, said he was called into the bar by the barman on Tuesday, afternoon. When he entered, the Inspector said he would report him for serving drink to Haddock, who he said was drunk and had been refused at a hcalse or two. Wit- ness replie I " lain very sorry if such a thing has hap- pened, but the man does not appear to me to be drunk as he stands there." Haddock then left the house, and he (witness) being upset followed him. He then heard the Inspector say "13mlock, we haven't got his name?'— P.C. Bullock then went out, and Haddock was taken into the police station. Cross-examined: He had never been employed in a public-house before three months ago, when he undertook lee management of the hotel. The man could not be drunk when he walked straight out of the house. It was not true that he had said had he been there he would not have served him. He said he should not have cared to have served him. He had never admitted to the, Inspector nor the Superintendent that Haddock was drunk. —Re-examined, witness said he told the Inspector that he would have been better satisfied had he served the man himself. The Inspector told witness that Haddock was a disreputable fellew, and would get anyone into trouble. It was not a fact that he was cautioned by Ser- geant Woolley a short time since. Mr. Ditchfield, the defendant, said he had been a licensed victualler for 42 years. There was a conviction made against him 22 years ago, but them had been none since. His instructions to his men had alcftys been "Do less business and do it right." Cross-examined he said he lived on the premises about two months before the last licensing sessions. He did not tell Superintendent Large at the licensing sessions that it was his intention to continue to live there. He ceased to reside at the hotel because of ill-health, a fortnight after the licensing sessions.

After a few minutes' deliberation, the Chairman said the Bench believed that the case was proved, and they would convict. Mr. Ditchfield would have to suffer for the action of his servant, but they would not endorse the license. For selling drink to a drunken person he would he fined 20s. and 10s. 6d. costs. The second ',information would be dismissed.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

Another step has been made towards the erection of a Technical Institute for Runcorn. A meeting of the Technical Instruction Committee was held the other night, and the organising secretary to the Council was present, and gave the members the benefit of his knowledge and experience. Mr. P. Speakman, C.C., I bear, announced that he would give a donation of £5O towards the proposed insti- tute. As Mr:Brunner's offer to give £5OO or any por- tion of it if a similar amount were subscribed by the townspeople, still bolds good, Mr. Brunner 'A ill Of course add £5O to that of Mr. Speakman's. This is a capital commencement of a subscription list, and it is to be hoped that Mr. Speakman's generosity will be imitated by other gentlemen in the town, and so capture the whole of the amount offered by Mr. Brunner.

The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi yesterday departed for a trip to the Mediterranean and Palestine, and will be absent from Runcorn for several months. I hope he will have a pleasant holiday and that his health which has not been very good of late, will be much benefited. The Rev. Father H. Geron, S.Y,, will officiate at St. Edwards during his absence.

The speeches delivered at the ivaugural meeting of the \Vidues Educational Association have created quite a sensation amongst the followers of the church and the believers in the Catholic faith. And it is v'ery probable that an attempt will be made to reply to Mr. liolliwell's impeachment of denomina- tional education. The increased interest in the educational question which the Association will aim to foster, gives promise of a lively contest at the approaching School Board election, and the denominationalists will scarcely be able to maintain their present absolute supremacy on the Board if the independents are united and vote straight.

It will be pleasing news to the people of Widnes, that the construction of a new copper works has commenced in Ditton-road. The works are being erected for a company of St. Helens gentlemen. It will be a grand day for the town, when it is not so dependent upon the chemical trade as it is at the present ti me

Sir Richard Brooke Bart., has this week enter- tained a shooting party at Norton Priory, and I un- derstand there hare been some distinguished people there: There was game in abundance, specially pheasants,.and the " bags" have been very large. _ _ _

Mr. Brundries. ill-luck with his grey-hounds still pursues him. At the Altcar Club Coursing meeting this week he has run about six dogs and with one exception they all succumbed in the first round. Boss Jones did wimone course but went down next round.:liowever,it's a long lane that has no turning, and Mr. Bruudrit has proved himself a plucky sportsman.

PLEASANTETENINGS.—The first of a series of Saturday evening entertainiwnts- was held on Saturday, in the schoolroom. Chapel-lane, when an excellent programme was gone through, including pianoforte solos, vocal duets, songs, quartettes, and readings. During an in- terval, coffee and buns were handed round at a small charge. It is intended to hold these meetings fortnightly. PAROCHIAL COMMITTEES.—At an adjourned meeting of these Committees held yesterday week, Mr., A. Thomas, J.P., presiding, die Chairman reported that the deputa- don, consisting of himself, tne Clerk (Colonel Ashton), and Mr. H. E. Haywood, had conferred that afternoon with the Chairman, solicitors, and engineer of the West Cheshire Company, with reference to a supply of water to the townships of Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship. —lt was found that the Company had not been able to arrange terms with the Liverpool Corporation for a sup. ply of water from the Vyrnwy mains, and they, there: fore, could not include the two townships within the limits of their supply. After some consideration, the re- port of the Sub-Committee was adopted, on the motion of Dr. Robinson, seconded by Mr. H. Tiley.
AILWAY ACCIDENT AT WARRINGTON.
AN ENGINE TIIROWN OVER AN EMBANK-
MENT.
An accident occurred at the London and North-

Western Railway Co.'s Bank Quay Station, Warring- ton, about seven on Wednesdav night. A large , goods engine (1,376), which had lately been ordered to do light work at the station, was proceeding in charge of William Whalley, the driver, of 44 Walker- st., and John Shaw, the stoker, of Eustance-st., out ,of the Bank Quay station (high level) to go to Arpley to take on some waggons. To do so they had to run on the main line up to Walton Arches, and the accident occurred at the home signal- box points. The engine had no waggons attached, but full steam was up, and from some, as yet, unexplained reason, the 'engine failed to go on to the main line, but ran against the scotch-block at the end of the siding which leads from the station. The consequence of the collision was that the scotch-block was dislodged and thrown some fifteen feet over the end of the bridge into Slutchers-lane. The engine iLself, being a light one, with no load on. must have rebounded a yard or two for instead of going sheer over the end of the bridge it has toppled down the railway enbankment. The draw bar of the engine 'became imbedded in the soil as the engine roiled down the bank, and this prevented the locomotive landing entirely on the footway. Whalley and Shaw state that se sudden was the overthrow, and so dense was the steam, smoke, and fire, that they had no idea where they were. The- points which caused the acci- dent are not more than fifteen yards from the scotch-block, against which the engine ran. It seems marvellous that the two men were not killed on the spot, but they managed to crawl through a hole either in the engine or tender. They were drenched from head to foot, and it was found that Whalley was badly hurt. Both were able to walk home. Dr. Adams was immediately sent for in Whalley's case, and after an examination found that no bones had been broken. The injured man com- plained of severe pain in the back, and was unable to move. Shaw, was able.3resterda.y to move about as usual. The officials at the station think that Whalley must have mistaken one of the signals, but this the injurel man says is not the case. The engine, almost a wreck, remains in a perilous posi- tion half-way up the embankment. With the almost contintious stream of railway traffic that passes within a few feet of where it lies the draw- bar might easily become dislodged or be snapped, and the engine would roll on to Slutchers-lane. It is turned completely upside down, and the funnel and buffers smashed. The parapet of the bridge has also been overturned.

div.head: EXTENSIVE AND DISTRESSINCi• FRAUDS.
div.p: EXTENSIVE AND DISTRESSINCi• FRAUDS.

Further revelations as to the business transactions of the late Mr. H. S. Whalley, a solicitor carrying on business in Blackburn and Southport, are of a peculiarly distressing character. Clients who invested their money through the medium of Mr. Whalley are turning up from different parts of Lancashire and Yorkshire, only to learn that their property has been mortgaged over and over again, and that in many casesthey are practically ruined. it is alleged that the defalcations will amount to nearly £lOO,OOO. He had an .extensive monetary connection with builders, prominent tradesmen, and workpeople, and it is stated that widespread distress has been caused amongst his numerous clients.

div.head: THREE CHILDREN MURDERED.
div.p: THREE CHILDREN MURDERED.

A shocking tragedy was committed on Monday morn- ing at Titchfield, a village about ten miles from Portsmouth, Alice Hinton, a married woman, killing three children by cutting their throats and attempting to take her OWR life in a similar way. The children we:e known as Freddy, aged ten, Willie seven, and Augusta, between five and six. The boys were children of the husband by a former wife, and the girl was Mrs. Hinton's own daughter, born before her marriage with Hinton. The woman's wound was not very serious, but she struggled violently, and it was difficult to dress it. When it was stitched up, she was removed to Fareham by the police, and then taken before the magistrates, being subsequently removed to the county lunatic asylum on a certificate that she was insane. She talked incoherently, but admitted that she had killed the children.

div.head: BEFORE TET IVEAGISTRATEI3.
div.p: BEFORE TET IVEAGISTRATEI3.
A GUARDIANS' OFFICIAL'S STRANOS CONDUCT,

At the Borough Magistrates court, on Monday, John Jefferson was charged with leaving his wife chargeable to the Union. Mr. H. Shearer, prosecuted, on behalf of the Guardians, and said the defendant had been appointed lunatic attendant, under the Guardians at a Aalary of £lO a year, uniform, and rations. He went on very well until the 3rd of October, when he went out, it waasunposed to draw a pension, which he had, amounting to £3 163., per quarter. He did not com- back. having probably gone on the spree, and left un- paid £3 ss. for the maintenance of his wife in the union —The defendant said he had had his head split open and when he took whisky he did not know what he was doing.—He was sentenced to 2 months' hard labour. A TMIEVISH YOUNG WOMAN. At the Borough Police Court on Monday, Sarah Ann Hoyles, a young woman, apprentice to a fustian cutter, and lodging at 55 Oliver-st., was charged with stealing on Saturday from the stall of Thomas Richardson in the Markit Place two boots, value ss. 11d., his property, ° also with stealing on August 15th from the stall of Ellen Brookbank in the same place, a man's coat and vest. She pleaded guilty in both oases. She having stated that she could only get 2.3. 6d. a week at fustian cutting, Alder- man Francomb advised her to try to obtain a respectable situation. The girl's father was present and was repri- manded for not having her at home and looking after her. The Bench contented themselves with recording a conviction against the prisoner. A HEARTLISS FATHER.

At the borough magistrates' court, on Monday, Henry Bennett, paviour, was charged under a warrant by Mr. Basil Shearer, on behalf of the Board of Guar- dians, with leaving his two children ehargable to the Union since April 1889. Mr. Shearer said the man had married a well-to-do woman, with plenty of money and doing a good business. The children had cost the Union £59 18s., independent of the cost of that proir:cution lie., lid. The Chairman, after the evidence, said it was the worst case of the kind he had ever had before him in that court.—The Chief Constable sail a man convicted twice of this offence could be punished with the lash.—The Prisoner: That would'nt do for me. I have got the rheumatics very bad.—The Chairman : It would cure that.—The prisoner was sent to jail for three months with hard labour. CHARGE OF FURIOUS DRIVING.—AN OLD MAN SERIOUSLY INJURED. At the borough magistrates' court, on Monday, William Thomas, printing machinst, 18, Fennell-st., VW charged with furiously driving to the danger of pa i ssengers, a pony and trap, n Buttermarket-street, on the Bth inst.—Mr. Browne appeared for the defence.— P.C. Corbett said he was taking a drunken woman to the station when he saw the defendant driving the trap at the foot of Buttermarket-st. at the rate of 10 miles an hour. Witness shouted to him. There was a crowd, and an old man in it was knocked down and one of the trap whells passed over his body. The defendant then drew up, and it was found that the man's ribs were fractured. They removed him to the Infirmary. Wit- noes was assisted by some one,he believed the defendant, to remove him from the footpath.—Mr. Browne : Don't you know the horse cannot possibly go 10 miles an hour? —P.C. Corbett: It could.—Mr. Holt, a coachman, said the pony was going 8 to 10 mile i s an hour.—lnspector Cox said the injured man was still n the Infirmary, and was likely to be there for some weeks. He had two ribs fractured and a bad scalp wound. He was a man aged about 60 years. His case was serions.—Mr. 13rowne said if the case was so serious he would ask the Bench to adjourn it and not by convicting his client pre- judice the decision in any civil action that might be brought against him.—Alderman Sutton could not see the object of an adjournment.—The Chief Constable said in cases like this in which there was an inquest the Coroner was always anxious that the matter shpuld be thrashed out before the magistrates.—Mr. Browne said. people were liable to be injured in the streets without furious driving.—For the defence Arthur Dowd was! called. He said he was in company with the defendant in the trap. They had been having a drive round the Ship Canal. Near Orford-st. when they were coming back there was a crowd. The defendant shouted to them to get out of the way, but they did not all do so. The policeman did not shout to the defendant. Thomas was perfectly sober. The pony was hardly going four ailea an hour. He could have walked as quickly. He got out to help the man up who was knocked down.— A young lady of Runcorn, who had also been in the trap, corroborated.—Thomas Holbrook, debt and rent collector, Fennell-et., the owner of the pony said that he could never get six miles an hour out of it. It was only At for light work.—Mr. Hunt: Why don't you sell it ? Witness: I will sell you it if you want it. (Laughter.) —ln reply to Alderman Sutton, witness said the price of the pony with the harness was £s.—Mr. Browne: A. 25 horse going ten miles an hour !—Mr. Lowe said he had &lip the pony in the roads many a time, but never going more than five miles an hour. With his machine he had left it miles behind. He had seen those in the trap when it was drawing it get out on a level road to ease the animal.—By Mr. Hunt: It was not winded then.—The defendant said he would take three gentlemen iri the trap with him and if they could make the pony go six miles an hour he would give it. away.—The Mayor said the charge of furious driving had not been proved, and the case would be dismissed.

div.head: AUDACIOUS ROBBERY OF WHISKY.
div.p: AUDACIOUS ROBBERY OF WHISKY.

John Owen and John Troy were charged before the magistrates, at the borough Police Court, on NVf;dnesday morning, with stealing about half-past twelve the pre- vious day, a quantity of whisky, value Bs., the property of Mr. Shilcock, of the Bay Horse Inn. Mr. Browne appeared for the prosecution. He stated that about the time in question the prisoners were in the home having some beer, and the barmaid being out for a Short time returned and found them there with pint jugs of raw whisky, for which they had not paid,before them. Mrs. Shilcock went for her husband, who was out, and he came back with a constable. Troy had drunk himself insensible, and Owen was under the influenoe of liquor. They had to be taken to the Police Station in a hand- cart.—Miss Reynolds, the barmaid deposed to finding the whisky tap running and the defendants with four pint jugs before them containing whisky.—Mr. and Mrs. Shilcock were sworn, the former stating that one jug was about a third full of whisky and the other three each were half full. Troy was lying insensible and Owen leaning on the counter, apparently not much the worse for drink.—The prisoners cleaded not guilty. They admitted that "liquor " got into their beer,but how they did not know. The whisky before them was half beer.—Mr. Browne: What's the use of saying that ? There (pointing to a bottle containing unmixed whisky on the desk) are the remnants of the Avhisky from the jugs.—The prisoners were each fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days.

Wm. Farrell, son ti-t-A-n-n Farrell, """"""""" a lodging- house keeper in Higher Bank-st., was charged with stealing in the Crown and Sceptre yard, from James Doyle, an old man, a labourer in King-st. brewery, and lodging at 33, Dolman's-lane, a quart bottle of beer.—The .complainant deposed that the prisoner snatched the beer from him`and ran away with it, leaving the cork with him.—The prisoner pressed the complainant hard with questions, enjoining on him, amidst laughter,to " tell the truth and shame the divil."—James Walsh, landlord of the" Crown and Sceptre," and P.C. Hardy, gave evi-

dence, thelatter having witnessed the snatching, and apprehended the prisoner.—The prisOner denied the charge, and said Hardy thought it was a good opportu- nity to "put him in for his Christmas dinner." He was sent to gaol for 14 days' hard labour.
TIIIIFT FROM A LODGING-ROUSH

At the Borough Folice Court, on Wednesday morning, Peter Burns, navvy, was charged with stealing at Plins- ton's lodging-house, Rose and Crown-st., the previous afternoon, 31bs of bacon, 'value is. 7d., the property of William Cickley, a navvy, from Runcorn. 10s. or-seven days. _ _
MR. DIGOLE AND His ELECTION EXPENSES

At the clo:e of the police busin,ess at the Borough Court, on Monday. Mr. Wm. Diggle, one of the defeated candidates for the Hawley Ward at the recent municipal elections, handed the deputy magistrates clerk a printed form, headed" Declaration of candidate to expenses." In answer to one of the Bench as to the amount of his expenses, Mr. Diggle replied " 12." (Laughter.)—The Clerk: What about your agents ?—Mr. Diggle : lam agents and all, I will Show you how to work •things cheaply.—Mr. James Fairclough : That was not quite a shilling a vote. • (Laughter.)—Mr. Diggle: However, it is what it is. It shows you people how to manage these matters to save expenses. Mr. Diggle signed tho decla- ration and then left the court.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SATURDAY.—Betore Alderman Burgess and Mr. John
Geddes%

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Martin Higgins. a Corpora- tion labourer, drunk and disorderly the previous night, in Manchestenroad, was fined ss. and costs. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Aid. Greenall) in the chair, Aldermen Francomb, Sutt,m, Wright, and Harrison, and Councillor James Fairclouv,h. DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A HonsE.=-Patrltk Gillick, charged with being drunk in charge of a horse and cart, in the Market Place, on Saturday afternoon, was dis- missed.

Damix.—Gideon Park, charged with being drunk, in Horsemarket-St., on Sunday night, was dismissed. PITCII AND ross.—William Griffin, charged under a warrant with playing at pitch and toss, in Jones's build- ings, on the 30th of March, 1890, wasfined 10s. and costs. DRUNK AND DISORDIRLY.—Goorga Carter, drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st., on Saturday night, 5s.— Thomas Kenyon, in Bridge-st.; on Saturday night, ss. Oscar Durand and Patrick Gleeson, were .charged with being drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road, on Sunday night. The men were fighting, and P.S. Chantler said Gleeson was shouting that he had caught Jack the Ripper. Gleeson said what he told the Sergeant was that the latter could catch a drunken man but not Jack the Ripper. The defendants were discharged on promis- ing better behavieur.—Matilda Weston, of Oswestry, in Buttermarket-st., on Sunday night, discharged.— Bridget Toole, in Pye's Yard, on Saturday night, ss. and costs.—John Murphy and Annie Shepherd were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bank-st., on the 7th inst. Shepherd did not appear.—Mr. Browne said there was another charge against Shepherd, that of assaulting the landlady of the Royal Arms, in Buttermarket-st. She had been celebrating thero the elevation of his worship the Chairman to the Mayoralty, and severely thrashed the landlady (Mrs. Thomas), and had to be tumbled out, then she began to be disorderly in the street. He applied Tor a warrant on the charge of assault. The application was acceded to.—P.S. Rowbotham deposed to being called into the house to eject Shepherd. The landlady was leeding. , Witness and another officer put Shepherd out; Murphy -challenged the landlord to fight and he and an- other man were ejected also.—Murphy and Shepherd were then disorderly in the street, Murphy, saying he was a respectable ratepayer and would go when he liked. P.C.'s Marsh and Turner corroborated as to the defend- ant being drunk and disorderly, Turner saying than Murphy said he was a respectable ratepayer and such as he kept such swine as witness.—Mrs. Thomas denied that Murphy was drunk, and Mr. Thomas that the.defendant challenged him to fight.—Murphy was fined 105. includ- ing costs —Joseph Whittaker, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st., on the 7th , inst.—P.S. Cox said he was taking some prisoners to the station when the defendant, who was drunk, and others I shouted at him, and this made the prisoners worse, so that he had great difficulty in getting them tothe station. ' Witmsss had to threaten him with his stick to get him away.—The defendant wanted to know why he was singled out.—The Chief Constable said it was a practice to shout at the police when they had prisoners, and the only way to stop it would be to take 20 policemen and apprehend some of the delinquents.-ss. and costs, or seven days.

FlGHTliG.—Richard Welsby and David Cornfield, for fighting in Sankey-st., on the 7th inst., were bound over in the sum of £lO each to keep the peace for six months. Cattmgvs ON Film—John Evans and William Wood, for having their chimneys on fire were fined is. each. Alarinda Clark, similarly charred, was dismissed, the Bench considering from the evidence that the constable in the case P.C. Cooper, had confounded another chimney with the defendant's. Alderman Chandley for having his office chimney on fire was fined is. CIIARGREI BY THU SANITARY INSPECTOR.—Robert Lowe, 23, Catherine-street, Bewsey-road, was charged by Mr. Norman with having a defective drain on his premises, a nuisance caused by which he had had notice on the 23rd ult., to remedy in two days.—The defendant said be was only agent for the premises. The deputy magis- trates' clerk said the defendant was the owner within the meaning of the Act.—The dbfendant said Mr. Church, the assistant inspector, had informed him that the drain had cleared irself, but he had it put right on Saturday afternoon.—The Bench made an order that the nuisance be abated within three, days, if it had not already been remedied; and for payment of costs.—The defendant said these cases ought not to be tried by a Bench con- sisting, merely of members of the Corporation. Alder- men Francomb and Wright told the defendant that he could have the case adjourned if he objected to the Bench.—Mr. Norman: The magistrates have had no hand in bringing these proceedings one—The defendant: There are several members of the Sanitary Committee on the Bench.—Alderman Wright: There is not one.—The defendant said in that case he was mistaken.—The order made therefore stood, the Bench fixing the time for compliance with it at 7 days.—Geo. Weaver, 22, 26 and 28, Pierpoint-street, was charged with having insanitary premises. His dase was adjourned 7 days.—Elizabeth Winstanley, 10, Catherine-street, for having insanitary out premises, was ordered to remedy their condition in 7 days and pay costs. TUBSDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett and E. J. Guess

AN INSANITARY SLADOHTERHOUSE.—John Marsh wao charged that on .the 24th ult, he unlawfully failed to purify and cleanse his slaughterhouse, also that he, on the same date, deposited a quantity of garbage in the middenstead instead of in the proper receptacles pro- vided. Mr. Norman, Inspector of Nuisances, and his assistant, Mr. Church, proved the case; the defendant and his foreman, whom v` he called, denied t..ie truth of the charge. On the latter saving he saw no garbage put on the middenstead—The Chairman asked : There was not an eclipse on that day that you could not see it ?—Witnes6 : I was not aware of it.—The defendant was fined 103. BREAKERS OF THE SANITAR2 LAWS.—Bridget Kimblin,g, 17, Dial-st., was charged by Mr. Norman, Sanitary In- spector, with neglecting to whitewash the walls of her lodging-house. he was fined 2s. 6d.—John Kay and John Bate, 7, and 9, Heath-lane, were fined is. each for having their out-premises in an offensive condition. ABSENCE FROM SCHOOL.—The following persons were dealt with on the prosecution of Mr. Riley. School Attendance Officer :—William Crank,labourer, 32, Aiken- st., who was charged as to a boy, whose excuse was that the master was always peevish with him. The Chief Constable talked about birching the boy. The fine in this case was ss.—William 'Quinn, labourer, Fennell-st., 52.—Henry Howe, joiner, 87, Hoyle-at., ss. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Councillor James Fairclough and Alderman Wright. CHILD DESERTION.—Geerge Wyatt, from Winsford, was charged under a warrant with leaving, an the 21st ult. his child chargeable to the Union.—A month's hard labour. - -

A WILD INcsminear.—Wm. Patten was charged with as- saulting Wm. Hall,his father-m-law,on the 31st ult.—The complainant said he had kept the defendant and his wife four years now without a halfpenny return. On 'the evening of the date mentioned witness was having a pint of ale in a public-house, when a woman rushed to him and said "Are you tieing to see your }louse on fire ? ' He ran across and found the place all in smoke, the chimney blazing, and the lamp broken and burning on the floor, the mantelshelf knocked down. The defendant was standing behind the door, and as soon as witness got in he " up with his fist and landed him right into the stair- case." He had burned a basket, with which he had set the chimney on fire.—The defenc4nt's wife corroborated, and said the defendant seized her father by the throat and threw him against the stairs.—The defendant said when he got situations his wife came and "disgraced him out of the shop."—He was committed for a month with hard labour.—The defendant: Thanks. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—EIizabeth Smith, drunk and disorderly in Fennell-st., on Tuesday afternoon, 53., in- cluding costs.

ASSENCR FROM Scuoon.—James Moseley, employed at the Whitecross Works charged under a warrant with not sending his regularly to school, was fined ss. and costs. FRlDAlL—Before Mr. John White (chairman), and Dr.
Gornall.

THREATENING A MFR.—Patrick Hoaty, 8 James's-st., was charged with assaulting Emma Floaty, his wife on the-14th inst.—The complainant said he threatened to kick her stomach in, hecause she remonstrated with him for using bad language.—Rose McNally corroborated.— The defendant said his wife had been away and left him without food, fire, or bedclothes, and had refused to come back.—P.S. Chantler partly corroborated this state- ment.—The defendant was bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay ss. WAS. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Thomas Walsh, 11th appear- ance, was charged with not appearing to a summons for being drunk and disorderly in Bank-st., on June 23rd, 1890. It was stated that the defendant's father, who was formerly a recruiting sergeant in Warrington, was

div.head: 1 11.. E 1-4:.X A..M.IN tilt, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 21, 1891.
div.p: 1 11.. E 1-4:.X A..M.IN tilt, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 21, 1891.

dying and in consideration of this fact and of the defend- ant promising to reform, he was dismissed.—Patrick , McCabe, of Widnes, and James Murphy, Fennell-st., ' were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Mersey- st. on Thursday night, and Murphy was charged with assaulting P.C. Harrington. The constable said about 11.50 p.m. on Thursday, he heard the defendants cursing and swearing at the top of their voices, and he asked them to go away. McCabe struck him a violent blow and he atruck him back and knocked him down. Murphy then struck witness in the neck, and rushed at , him again when P.C. Newey took him into custody.— Newey corroborated the latter statement.—McCabe charged Harrington with knocking him down, which he denied.—P.C. Baxendale said when Murphy was brought to the Police Station he was bleeding from the head, and complained of being struck there, by Harrington, who was present.—The Chairman expressed the opinion that a constable ought not to knock a man down except as a last resource, and said Harrington was near• the Police Station, and it was hardly necessary to knock a man down who was druuk.—Harrington said as he was alone with two men, he struck in self-defence as they might have been rough.—Tlie defendants were fined ss. and costs each for being drunk and disorderly, and the charge of assault was dismissed. THE DELINQUENT LODGING-HOUSE KEEPER.—Michae Joyse was again brought up by Mr. Norman to show cause why he should not be committed to prison for non- payment of £1 53. 6d. due as line and costs for not keep- ing his lodging-house in proper condition. His case was adjourned a week. CRUELTY TO HORSES.—Peter Bigharn, Bank-street, was charged with cruelly treating a horse on the 7th inst., by working it while in an unfit state, and Samuel Stokes, Chorley-street, Thomas Pilkington, jun., contractor, were charged with causing it to be so worked.—lnspector Dowty proved the case, and said the horse was drawing one of the Corporation carts, and suffering from a large deep suppurated wound, from which matter was exuding. They were fined ss. and costs. —James Hiokey, Lovely- lane was charged by Dr. Dowty, with cruelly treating a horse on the 14th inst.—Mr. Dowty said the horse was attached to a furniture van, and as it was unable to draw its heavy load, the defendant beat it violently with the whip, using both the lash and the stick. He was fined 103. and costs, 183. in all. Asset:um. —Wini f red Noon, Bth appearance, for assault- ing Martha Barker, was bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for 6 months.
WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. J: Rylands (chairman) and
G. Comber-.

CRUELTY TO ANIMALS .—Robert Rushton, farmer, of Cuerdley, was charged by Inspector Do wty, R.S.P.C.A., with cruelly using a cow at Cuordley, on the 3rd inst. —The Inspector said he found the animal in a field, and in a wretched condition and very lame on the near hind stiple from dislocation of the off " elbow." An abscess had formed in each joint, and putrid matter was exud- ing from the animal. The cow was unable to walk about to get its food. The defendant admitted that the cow was his, and had been in the field for two months, and no one had been to it during that time to look after or feed it.—Mr. Hill, veterinary surgeon, of Altrincham, gave corroborative evidence,and said tile cow was in the last stage of COl2St3 neption ,and was suffering from disease of the kidneys. This was the worst case of cruelty that had come under his notice for 35 years.—The defendant Was fined 103. and £1 us. costs.—Wnt. Bibby, of Pen- keth, who was absent through illness, was charged by Inspector Dowty with working a horse while in an un- fit state, on the 27th ult. The Inspector said it was attached to a carrier's van, and was very lame in the off far leg, aud suffering from contraction of the tendons.— The defendant said its shoe was not put on right, and it had suffered in consequence, just as a human being would do in such a case.—He was fined 23. 6d. and costs.
Dnuigx AND Drsorinnarx.l—John Daniels, drunk and disorderly on the 31st ult., at Sankey Bridges, was fined 6s. and costs.

DRUNK ON LICENSED PREMISES. —Jam es Cu nli ffe, drun k on the licensed premises of James Berry, Newmarket Common, on the 31st ult., was fined 10s. and Costs. BRIACH OF THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACT.—Henry Webber was charged with committing a breach of the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act by driving, on the 4th ult., without a license, three pigs from Warrington to Rixton, and fined 10s., including costs.

BREACH OF THE COUNTY COUNCIL REGULATIONS.—Peter Gleave was charged with driving a steam thrashing maching along the highway at Southwick, on the 7th inst., at other than the time provided by the County Council regulations. Me was fined ss. and costs.

Hood ultimately having an open field, Potts checking his career when dangerous, and it was left to Daniels to effect a good clearance. It was again Bfoughton's turn to be pressed severely, but the visiting three-quarters were very safe, and subsequently sent the leather to the home quarters. Loose scrimmages were then the order, in which the visitors had the advantage, but Warrington resumed the attack, bad passing spoiling the chance. Success came at last, when Mather secured a good try, Lomas again converting. The first to show up on the Broughton side were Sa.wers and Hollings- worth, who made a pretty combined run, and the movement being well taken up by the visiting for- wards, Warrington territory was invaded, only to see a huge kick by Webster regain the ground, and half-time arrived with Warrington 2-1-2 to nil. On the resump- tion of hostilities, the visitors were pressed, the penalty kick by Lomax almost causing the downfall of the goal. Hollingsworth shone by a fine bit of work, which was , however, nullified by Lomax. Broughton, who were now playing better, created quite a surprise at this point. Getting a clear field, they outwitted the home custodian, and by pretty dribbling, carried the ball over the line, scoring between the posts. Race converting the point, a hearty round of applause greeted the performance. Tall kicking between the backs was then witnessed to the advantage of Warrington, but several sharp visits by the Broughton men to their opponents' ground matte mattertlively. Race improved the position, and a lot of loose scrambling packs occupied the time, the passing also exhibited by the home backs being very poor. Webster, who was receiving most of the back work, was too closely watched to get far, the visiting backs tackl- ing well. The style of play adopted by the home for- wards was but moderate, and nothing further was scored on either side, a very pleasant game ending— Warrington, 2-1-2 to 1 goal. •
Widnes made a plucky attempt to equalize. The home defence proved too good for them, and they were com- pelled to retire defeated by two points to nil.
ASSOCIATION.

FRIENDS SCHOOL, PENSIETH V. WARRINGrIfON, Gnmr- Mau SCHOOL.—Played at Warrington. Penketh were weakened by the absence of Robinson.who was not playing. The Grammar School at once pressed but Pen- keth soon had a turn,the ball going wide. After twenty minutes play,the ball was rushed through Penketh goal, the keeper being too slow in clearing. Score at half- time, Grammar School, 2 ; Penketh, 0. After cha,nging over, Penketh had hard lines, the ball twice hitting the cross-bar. Results :—Grammar School, 5; Penketh, O. Waine and T. H. Robinson played a splendid game for Penketh at half, and the Warrington right wing played magnificently. WARRINGTON V. EARLESTOWN ALMON.—Played at War- rington on Saturday, before a good attendance of specta- tors. Atkins kicked off at 3.30 for the home team, Norman nearly effecting the downfall of the visitors' citadel, their backs clearing. splendidly. Atkins then sent in a scorcher, the goalkeeper saving at the expense of a corner, which was fruitless. The visitors paid a visit to the other end, and through some misunderstand- ing between the home backs, Worstley scored, the goal- keeper never attempting to stop the ball. After the kick oft the home team still kept up the pressure, but were unable to score, the goalkeeper playing a marvellous game. Atkins, in centre, for the home time was playing a splendid game, having hard lines on several occasions. Half time arrived with thO score Albion 1, Warrington nil. After the resumption of hostilities, the home team at etie,e took up the aggressive, Atkins sending in a splendid shot, followed a minute later by one from Norman, but Phillips, the visitors' goalkeeper, was safe as a house, repelling shot after shot. The home team were playing splendidly at this point, Clayton at half back fairly excelling hlmself, pulling the visitors' right up continually. Phillips and Kincare, full back, were also playing well, checking the visitors' forwards time after time. Powell then had a shy at the home goal, the goolkeeper saving splendidly. Careswell was then fouled in the goal mouth, the free kick coming to nothing. The homestere continued to keep up the pressure Ball on the right wing missing several easy chances, and the whistle sounded for time with the homateam swarming round the visitors' goal. Result : Albion 1,. Warrington nil. Kincare, Phillips, Clayton and Mather at back were in champion form, and Atkins and Powell were the best of the forwards. Warrington team : Goal, Jones; backs, Kincare and Phillips; half backs, Searle, Mather, and Clayton ; right wing, Ball and Norman ; centre, Atkins ; left wing, Powell and Careswell.

MONDAY.—Before Mr. C. Reynolds and Mr. A. Thomas. MISCHLLANEOUS.—George Hignett, labourer, Sutton, was fined 6d., and costs 83. 6d., fin- allowing two dogs to be at large without collar or muzzle.—A similar penalty was imposed upon George Cowap for allowing a dog to be at large at Halton.—Richard Brown was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for being drunk. . .

THunsniY.Before Mr. J. Brock and Lieutenant-Colonel Gaskell.

DRUNK AND DISORDEItLY.—John McCahe, Midwood- street, made his 16th appearance and pleaded guilty to having caused a breach of the peace. He was bound over to be of good behaviour for three months.—For being drunk and disorderly a fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon Rose Ann Carney, Moon-street; Michael Mullen, Midwood-street ; Richard Kelley, Pleasant- street; Patrick Walsh, Fisher-street ; James Green, Midwood-street.—Grace McGoffer and Annie Lock, respectably dressed women from Wright-street, were bound over to keep the peace for two months for fighting together. DOG WITHOUT LICENSIL—Richard Almond, Norlands- lane, was summoned for having a dog without a license and also with allowing the animal to be at large unmuz- zled. He was fined 7s. 6d. and costs 12s. 6d., for not having a license ; the other case was dismissed. _

Sci-oor. BOARD CASES.—On behalf of the School Board Mr. G. Danby prosecuted a number, ef parents for not sending their children regularly to school and the usual fine of 6d. and costs in each case was imposed. _
PITCH AND Toss.—John and Michael Fitzsimons, Duke- street, were each fined Is. and costs for playing pitch and toss.
WIDNES POLICE COURT. MON DAY .—Before Mr. T. S. Timmis.

DRUNK. —John Saxe and Joseph Jones, of Sutton, were each fined ss. and costs for being drunk. Thomas Boardman, landlord of the George Hotel, St. Helens, applied for a license to sell intoxicating liquor at a public ball, which was to take place at Widnes Drill flail, in aid of a St.- Helens Band.—Superintendent Noblett, objected on the ground that the license was not necessary. The charge would otily be a shilling,and it would be a means of getting a lot of young men and girls together, which was not a desirable object .—Mr. Timmis said applicant would have to try his ball at St. Helens first. He should not grant a license. WEDNESDIY.—Beforo, Mr, H. Gaskell.
THI CLOCK RoBBERY.—WITI. Newman, of Carlisle, was brought up, and again remanded on a charge of stealing a clock from the house of James Jennings, 24 Church-st., on the 9th.inst.
