div.p: FOOTBALL.

* * Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning. RUGBY.
Sr.' HELENS v. RONCORV ("A" TeAms).—This match was played at St. Helens, on Saturday. The final re- sult was—Runcorn, 1 goal; St. Helens, 1 tly.

WIDNES ST. MARY'S V. STANDISH SOUTH END.—This West Lancashire League match was played at Widnes, on Saturday, before a moderate attendance. In the first minute Gould scored for Standish, but no goal resulted. Immediately after Clarkson scored a grand try. Subse- quently Drury and Connor scored for the Saints. Final result—St. Mary's 3 tries; Standish 1 try. ST. RBLENS v. TUMORS (A Teams).—Played at Stf Helens, on Saturday. Cross, the Lancashire county hal back, assisted the Saints. Play throughout was of a very fast nature. Hopley scored an unimproved try for St. Helens, and May for Runcorn dropped a goal in the .first half. Nothing was done in the second half, and the final result was Runcorn 1 goal, St. Helens 1 try. WARRINGTON ST. MART'S V. WIDNES RANGERS.—At Widnes. The home team started, and the game at once assumed a scrambling nature.the visitors missing several chances of scoring, through the ground being very slip- pery, hut after some loose play, Woods dodged over the line, the point not being improved. After the drop out, the home team played in better form, Bate scoring a good try, the same player failing at goal, and at half- time the score was, equal. The Saints kicked off, and. were soon on the Rangers' line, Peckham scoring between the posts. After this the visitors were over the line several times, only for the referee to disallow the points, the game ending in a win for th 3 Saints by 2 tries to 1 try. • --

WARRINGTON A v. Booroirrox A.—There was a consi- derable crowd of spectators to witness this match on Saturday. Broughton kicked off, the play being forced to the home quarters, where Lawless, picking up, smartly threw to Mather, who transferred to Webster, and all efforts to check his career were futile, a try in an easy position resulti nfx. The kick at goal failed. Directly after this, some loose play ensued, the result being that Knowles secured a second try, Lomax on this occasion proving successful. . Re-starting at mid-field, Broughton showed up better after these early reverses, but the home defence, Daniels in particular, repelled their advance. Packed scrimmages were then the order. and Daniels passing to Webster, the latter punted towards the visitor's goal. -A fine kick by Potts followed, Webster supple- menting this by a long run. Broughton defended well,

div.head: WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON.

• This fixture, one of the most popular on the Warring- ton card, was played at Broughton on Saturday, in dull weather. rhe recollection that it was the Broughton club which first instructed Vie Warrington in the art of passing, combined with the fact that our local team had never gained a victory over the Manchester Club on their native heath, accounted for the large sprinkling of Warrington enthusiasts present. There was a fair at- tendance when the game was started, the visitors com- mencing with one short, Jolley failing to put in an appearance at the last minute, whilst John T. Bate was missing from half hack owing to indisposition. Skidmore kicked off, and Barnes's return found the first scrimmage at half way. A cross dribbling move- ment, in which Berry and Holmes were the leaders, was followed by Smack Bate passing to Evans, the lat- ter's kick being brilliantly responded to by Hassell. Bate kicked finely to the home lines, but this time the Man- chester men were penalized for paying a too early atten- tion towards Evans. A minor point was all that came of the advantage, and then some exchanges between the backs settled slightly in favour of the homesters. Nevins was floored at half way, but some beautiful pas- sing between Bate, Antrobus, and Heesom saw the latter being surely tackled by Craven. In fact, the Brough- ton men tackled in no "kid glove" description, and rarely did they fail to bring an opponent to grass, and not in a gentle way either. However, Warrington were having slightly the best of it, and Bate, Ashton, and Holmes dribbling well down the open. Warrington then attacked. Thornley now joined his comrades, and from a pack which he immediately • joined Bate was pulled up on the line. Roberts got the oval out of danger, and Boscow in response sent it dead.: An excellent dis- play by the half-backs and three-quarters of Warrington was loudly cheered, but again the tackling was severe, and the home forwards, playing a determined game, rushed the leather to the quarter flag,Turner saving well. A long kick by Bate was taken upby Ashton. Warrington now had a rare chance, but they failed to utilize it, and instead of taking advantage of it, the affair ended in disaster. Hassan cleared his lines when Warrington had failed, and Hadwin, snapping up an opportunity when the visitors' custodian had missed returning, a long dribble sent the oval over the line,a try being the result, from which Shepherd placed a goal. This success seemed to inspire the Broughton forwards, for en the restart, despite some fine individual play by Bate, the homesters again assumed the aggressive. The game I fluctuated considerably, and each goal in turn was assailed. Bandies on one occasion was held under the posts, whilst on behalf of Broughton, Roberts made his mark in a, favourable position, but both had a futila ending. The last-named's kick was met by Bandies, who responded to touch at half-way. Bate now put in a good run, and on another occasion passed to Evans, but Broughton defended admirably. Exchanges between Hassall and losc,ow were in favour of the first-named, but again Broughton were pOnalised. Fair. Turner's kick reVized half-way, and from another cross dribbling movement, the oval was passed across to Evans, who had a shot at goal, a third minor being recorded. Suc- cess rewarded a movement the next minute, for Bate led Warrington to the line, and Donohue scored far out, the difficult place being failed at by Nevins. This latter item brought half-time, the score reading as Warrington, 0-1-3, Broughton, 1-0-0. Fair. Turner's re-start was followed by exchanges on the part of Evans and Hassan, the game opening in favour of Warrington. Bate ran finely to Shepherd, being pulled up a yard from the line. From a pass by Bate, Evans had another futile shot at goal, but Piercy this time ran the oval out. and from this movement the home forwards rushed down the field, heedless of .the Warrington backs, and Boscow was compelled to concede a minor. Buckley be- catne prominent directly after the drop out, but his pass was forward, and then turner.Ashton,and Bate dribbled past Craven, the Broughton quarter flag being reached. The defence hadnot weakened, but from a pass by Bate, Barnes should have got in. The game now settled to a forward display, and, if a.nything, Broughton had a trifle the best of it. Boscow was seen at his best on one occa- sion, but Roberts the next minute was nearly in. A series of rushes and scrimmaees was followed by Whiteley scoring and Hassell placing a second goal, and although Bandies raced to the line in the last minute, Warrington failed to augment their score, and in the end had to re- tire defeated by two goals and a minor to a try and three minors, or ten points to two. Teams :—Warrington: Boscow, hack.; Barnes, Hee- som, and Evans, three-quarters ;J. T. Bate and Antro- bus, half-hacks; Ashton. Turner, Nevins, Randles,Berry, Donohue, Holmes, Buckley, and Thornley, forwards. Broughten : Shepherd, back; Piercy, Craven, and Hassall,three-quarters ; Roberts and Whiteley.half-back ; Broadbent, Derbyshire, Glendinning, Hadwin, Munro, Skidmore, Squires, G. and R. Tomlinson, forwards. RUNCORN v. WIDNRS.—This match between local rivals created immense interest on Saturday, about two thou- sand crossing Runcorn Bridge from Widnes, and there were six thousand spectators on the Runcorn enclosure when the game started. As showing the posi- tion of the two teams it may be stated that Runcorn have won all their engagements, and scored 9 goals, 11 tries (86 points) to their opponents' I. goal, 3 tries, (11 points) ; whereas out of eight matches played, Widnes have won 5, drawn 2, lost one, and have scored 4 goals, 15 tries, (50 points) to their opponents' 3 goals, 5 tries (24 points.) The following were the teams :—Runcorn: Houghton, back ; Davies, Crompton, and Pendlebury, three-quarter backs ; Evans and Abrams, half backs; Faulkner, Riley, Dolan, Hughes' Shaw, Hamnson, Williams, Massey, and Reece, forwards. Widnes: Barber, back; Peters, Bren- nan,and Plumpton, three-quarter backs. Drummond and Wright, half backs; Hewitt. Gordon, Johnson, Lyons, Farmer, Emery, Whelan, Holmes, and Hardman, for- wards. Dolan kicked off for Runcomand Widnes failed to return. From a scrimmage, in the Widnes quarter, Plumpton, however,relieved with a kick tocentro, where Houghton made his mark. Plumpton again returned to centre, and a few minutes later received a pass from Peters, and transferred play beyond the centre line into the home territory. From the line-out the home forwards carried the ball by means of loose play and dribbling again into the visitors' quarter, and narrowly escaped scoring. Barber kicking dead just in the nick of time. From the drop out. Runcorn continued the pressure, Bar- ber and Peters relieving at times with good kicks. Drumat9nd put in a smart run, but Houghton returned to the visitors' territory, when some neat passing between Abrams, Crompton, and Davies resulted in the latter getting over, but the ball was called back on the I ground that it had been thrown forward. Directly after- wards' Barber brought Crompton down on the line. A I rush by the Widnes forwards,headed by Holmes,relieved, I and some fine play between Brennan and Plumpton I carried the ball again into the home quarter,but Houghton I again returned. Play for a few minutes then settled in midfield, and the game was several times interrupted by the players getting injured. Plumpton put Widnes on the aggressive, and Brennan further improved the position, Plimpton being brought down almost in the act of crossing the line. Some very exciting play now followed near the home line, Widnes giving their oppon- ents some trouble in defending their line. The Runcorn defence, however, proved too good, and eventually the home team breathed more freely, after Hughes,Abrams, and Riley relieved. Crompton shied at goal, but his _kick mai charged down. Davies failing to take a pass, Peters did the needful, but lie was eventually brought down, and Crompton carried the ball again to the visitors' quarter after a good run. Pluinpton and Drum- mond bringing him down. Barber again relieved and Drommond put in a smart run and kick. At this point the whistle sounded for half-time when neither side had scered. On changing ends, Widnes was the first to attack, and appeared very mach like scoring. They kept up the pressure for some minutes, when Houghton touched down to save disaster. Pendlebury was brought down smartly by Plumpton, after some good passing between Davies and Crompton. Play continued even for a few minutes, and then Widnes were repulsed into their own territory by Plumpton not playing the ball. Drummond brought temporary relief, but Peters, in trying to get through, was attacked, and failing to hold the ball, Runcorn took the opportunity which had not hitherto presented itself of seering. Abrams passed to Crompton, and then to Davies, the latter scoring. Houghton, however, failed to convert the point. It now became evident that Runcorn would retire victors, but notwithstanding this,

div.head: CHARITIES OF FRODKIAM
div.p: THE CHARITIES OF FRODKIAM
IMPORTANT INFORMATION.

In Frodsham Liberal Club on Saturday evening, Mr. W. Handley, of Runcorn, read a paper entitled "The Charities of the Parish of Frodshami". before a large company of the members, who gave their most earnest attention, and appeared deeply inter- ested. Mr. Moseley Williams presided and intro- duced Mr. Handley, who, after some preliminary observations, said the charities of Frodsliam as shown in Lord Broughan's report in 183 G, were mainly connected with and for the benefit of

TUB PURR GRAMMAR SCHOOL. The origin of the school seemed to be involved in a con- siderable amount of obscurity but from the fact that in the earliest accounts, coupled with its undoubted anti- quity, it is styled the free grammar school it would appear to•be a relic of that forgotten period when the parochial cure had to undertake as a part of his duties and work the free education of his allotted district. The old school was situated in the churchyard,but in the early part of the present century it had become so dilapidated and inconvriently situated that its removal was consi- dered necessary, and in the year 1824 the present school was built on a portion of the charity lands, the necessary funds being provided out of the parish rates. The earliest bequest dates from the reign of Charles the first and is or was known as

div.head: TRAFIY)RD'S CHARITY.
div.p: TRAFIY)RD'S CHARITY.

By an indenture of the 15th April, 1641, William Trafford left two sums of £lOO each to certain trustees to buy lands, the net income to be bestowed for pious uses, one half in the city of Chester, and theiother half within the parish of Frodsham. The trustees not being able to exactly fit in a purchase of land with the even sum of SlOO each, £l4 of the Frodsham bounty was added to the Chester £lOO and laid out in the purchase of land in the township of Huntington, with the condi.• Lion that £1 of the income should be paid over to the Parish of Frodsham. £BO of the remainder was spent in the purchase of land (3 closes or crofts) in the zo,,vnship of Christleton, aad the balance of £6 was expended in legal coats of the conveyance. The land.; in Christleton were purchased on the condition that they were to yield a fixed rent or payment of £4 yearly, and not to be an improvable rent. The Chester portion of the beques was paid over to the Presbyterian Chapel, Chester. and the authorities of that place had always paid: over the £1 stipulated., At the time of the inquiry Mr. Daniel • Ashley, whom tlae Charity Commissioners stated eon- ducted the legal business of the parish, produced the deed relating to the ChriAleton lands, stating that the £4 was paid bya Mr. Barker, of Chester, as the agent of Mr. John Brockwood, but as no subsequent trust deed could be found, and it not appearing that the executors had appointed trustees to secure the performance of the intentions of the testator, Mr. Barker was written to and the following information was 'elicited. In August 1772 the late Mr. Brock (from whom Mr. Brockwood derived his property) purchased a house and cottage in Christleton and the above charity land from a person of the name of Mr. Jos. Trichett, and his mortgagee for £6OO and the premises were conveyed as a freehold free from all incumbrances, except a certain clear yearly chief rent of £4 pavablethereont at the feast day of All Saints for ever to the trustees for the time being of the Gram- mar School in Frodshato. By the recitals in the convey- ance it appeared that the property had been in the possession of the Trichett family prior to the year 1738: Mr. Brockwood and his trustees, in the year 1823, sold the greater part of the premises free from all encum- brances, but gave an indemnity to the purchaser against the chief rent of £4. This sum of £4 was paid to the Master of the Grammar School and the £1 was distri- buted in eight half crowns to eight Po a persons of Frodsham.

div.head: THI NEXT CHARITY
div.p: THI NEXT CHARITY

in order of date originated as fnllows. A Mr. Samuel Davies conveyed certain lands in Overton and Frodsham to his executors and trustees, John Davies and Samuel Hughson, subject to the payment of two mortgages and interest thereon for the residue of a term of 2,000 years, to the use and intent that the rents thereof might b. employed by the Rev. John Davies (the than Vicar of the parish), and others for the use and benefit of the Schoolmaster, for the time being, of the Frodsham Free Grammar School, at the discretion of the trustees, their executors and assigns. The deed conveying the land was dated Nov. 15th, 1688, and the land has ever since (so reads the report of 1835), been under the man- agement of trustees not appointed by new deeds or en— dorsement on the old one, but simply by the election of the parishioners in vestry assembied. "The report goes on to say that" The parcels of land at present belonging to the School are most probably the same which were originally purchased by the trustees, but the absence of of deeds and the change of names, render it impossible to exactly identify them. Appended is a table showing the names by which the lands were known at the time of the inquiry (1835), with the names of 'the occupiers, all of whom were tenants from year to year at rents which were considered to be fully equal to their then value. Description. Occupier. Measure. Rent. A. R. p. £B. d. House and Garden W. S. Littler, Master. 225 7 0. 0 House, Croft ditto 2 2 15 J Oakendale Joseph Penkyman 22 38 'l3 0 0 Bridge Croft John Hayes 235 3 0' 0 School Common lot Robert Gorst , 2 033 2 0- 0 Hool Pool Meadow Thomas Miller. 5 321 11 0 0 Lordship Marsh Roger Banks Meadow 5 324 9 0 0

20 231 40 0 0 Mr. William Littler, ttie then master. was appointed by the trustees on the 18th, February, 1823. His income,in addition to house, garden, and two crofts, and the back of the school being the rents of the above lands, 24-from the Christleton estate, and a tourth sum ot £l. 10s. from Bushell's Charity. The next charity or bequest in order of date was given in 1726. by a
MR. TEDOMA.S MOOR.

By his will of July 15th he gave £5 for a stock, the in- terest of which was to be paid yearly to the under master of the free school of Frodsham.if any such officiated,. and if there were not the interest was to accurnulateluntil such time as one was appointed. This sum remained in the hands of Mr. Moor's representatives, and so long as there was an under master, they regularly paid him the interest, but about the year 1822, the estate of Mr. Moor was sold in lots to Mr. Harrison, of Overton, subject to the sum of £5 and another rent charge of £1 as an en- cumbrance on the property. In 1832 the parish agreed to accept £6 55., and arrears of interest amounting to 155., altogether £7, in discharge of all demands for principal and interest, which Mr2Harrison invested in hid own name in the Frodshana Savings Bank, but which the Commissioners instructed should be at once invested either in ths names of the churchwardens or the trustees of the Grammar School. The above-mentioned sum of £1 was also left by Mr. Moor, to be given on every Christ- mas day for ever to some one poor person, an ancient inhabitant of Overton. This, the Commissioners found was distributed, but not to a single individual; t4ey therefoce instructed Mr. Harrison to observe the rule laid down by the donor, and to consult the curate or church- wardens as to the selection or a proper person to receive the benefit of it. In the last complete reported digest of the Cheshire charities issued in 1888, it was stated that so far as could be ascertained all income from the Moor charities had ceased. The average of •
'MR SCHOOL LANDS was also stated as 19 acres, 3 roods, and 39 perches ; pro- ducing an annual rent of £44 53., also an investment of £lOO In Dock liond4roducing annually £4 10s. He (Ur.

Handley) had also a remembrance that same years after the passing of the lindowed Schools Act an inquiry was held-as to the Frodsham Grammar School, presumably with a view to its reconstruction,and that a draft scheme was prepared in 1874, but from some cause or other the scheme was not proceeded with. Legally, therefore, the original constitution of the School was still in force, though whether so carried out was a question of local knowledge and interest. The above sum of £lOO invested in Deck Bonds was supposed to be the proceeds of BIISHPILTIS CITARM, and dates from the year 1104, given under the following eonditions and as, Mr. John Bushell, of Hackney,London, who was born in Fradshatn in the year 1642, gave in his lifetime the sum of £lOO to the School and poor of Frod- sham, to remain as a stock for ever and the interest to ne dispensed of yearly, as follows. One-third to the School- master of the Free School of Frodsham, one-third to a poor decayed householder in Frodsham, and one-third to a poor decayed householder in Frodsham Lordship. At the time of the inquiry in 1835 the care of the Charity was in the bands of Mr. Daniel, Ashley, who paid £5 a year to the Churchwardens,and two-thirds of the amount was distributed each Christmas topoor widows,of whom a list was kept. The remaining third was paid to the master of the Grammar School. There was- no deed found showing any legal title, and the only clue to its origin was a statement on the table of benefactions. In the digest of 1868, no returns were stated as being fur- nished with respect to the Charity, but as it was found that ;2,100 was invested in Dock Bonds it was concluded that Mr. Ashley or some member of the family had paid over that sum, but that the whole income was paid to the Schoolmaster and not only one-third as intended by the donor,Mr.Bushell. The next bequest was in January, 1752, by

div.head: MRS. MARY CITISSHYRR
div.p: MRS. MARY CITISSHYRR

of a piece- of land containing two Cheshire acres called tics Brook Furlong, one half of the rent to be paid to two or more pony widows of Frodsham who received no relief from the township and resorted to public worship according to the ritual of the Church of England and the remaining half to poor persons of the like description of the township of Stockham. This charity was, so managed that in 1828 £154. 10s. was owing to it, and a fresh scheme-for its management was drawn up, thecost of the inquiry and settlement swallowing up nearly the whole of the amount, the solicitors' bill being £130) 18s. 7d. Within the past twelve months a new scheme had been brawn up for the re-arrangement of the portion - belonging to.Stockham, and according to the accounts. submitted to the last vestry meeting at Halton, the. annual rent had been accumulating, and at that date the agent of Sir Richard Brooke stated there was Eso hand. The next charity was a bequest of several pieces of land, in all-some six Cheshire acres, by

div.head: MRS. JANI GASKELL,
div.p: MRS. JANI GASKELL,

widow of the late Rev. F. Gaskell, vicar of Fiodshan4. the' date of the deed being June 17th, 1774. It appeared from the digest' ot 1868 that no account or return was obtainable, so Ilhat at that time it had apparently been ' lost. The land consisted of four fields in the Lurdship, of Frodeham called Helsby Mill Field, Helsbv Upper Mill Field, Brandreth's Lower Mill Field, and Bran-. dreth's Little Mill Field, and was conveyed to Sir R. Brooke and his heirs upon trust that the said Sir R. Brooke and his heirs should out of the rents thereof pay the sum of £lO to the trustees and stewards of the clergy at their meeting held at Warrington for the. relief of the widows and orphans of clergymen ; and also in trust that the said Sir R. Brooke and his heirs should for ever thereafter suffer the Vicar of Frodsham and Ins- surcessors to take the residue of the rents of the land premises in augmentation of the Vicarage. The vicar at the time of the inquiry in 1835 resided in Essex,and a. Mr. Purcell, who occupied a portion or the land, received the rents as his agent,vrhich amounted to £4O a year, and paid £lO thereof tO the treasurer of the clergy meeting at Warrington. As to whether the charity was still 'in existence and the income applied to:the intended uses,he was un able to give any further information. In 18384

ANOTHRIt CHARITY'. was founded by the will of Mr. Harrison consisting of .1.0t345. 10d. invested in consols in the name of the o fficial trustees,the annual income being for distribution in money amongst the poor widows resident in the ham- lets of Overton and Bradley. The Charity was persum- ably in the hands of the churchwardens and the inform 4 atlon could readily be obtained from the vestry minute book. Mr. Handley then dealt with the CHARM rri OF, KINGSLEY, which consistlii of the Free School the building and establishment 43! which dated from short lY before 1788: The master for the time bring was to have the use of land, schoolhouse, and school buildings free from rent, in consideration that he should i rig truct four poor children of Kingsley and two of Newton at the appointment of the Trustees for charity and all other children belonging to the said townships at the rate of is. 6d. per quarter for. reading, 3s. for writing and ss. for arithmetic. He was also to be under agreement to be dismissed for mis- conduct upon the trustees giving six Months' notice to quit possession of the schoolhouse and premises upon pain of forfeiting the sum of £lOO. According to Lord Brougham's report-the land, exclusive of buildings, was worth £lO kt year.—Atclothing charity consisting of a rent charge of £1 a year upon a house called the Horse Shoe, used to be paid to the overseers, who distributed it in clothing every Christmas to poor persons,but a note in the " Digest " stated that the payment had been dis- continued for many years, so that this 'night be classeil' amongst the lost charities. There were

TIVO,OI7IER CHARITIES with the heading "-Lost" Mrs. Hardware's charity founded in 1611 and the Miss Hvde charity of 1786. conclusion Mr. Handley drew attention to an act passed this year having the suggestive title " An act to facilitate the recovery of rent charges and other payments owittg to charities, which provided that the printed reports issued by the CharitrCommissioners, should be admis- sible as prima facie.evidence of the document and facts therein stated, and that where any yearly or other perio- dical "payment has been made—in respect of any land to or for the benefit of any charity or charitable purposo. for twelve consecutive years such payments shall he deemed, subject to any evidence that may be given Co. the contrary, prima fin-le evidence of the perpetual liabi- lity pf such land to such yearly or other periodical pay- ment, and no proof of the origin of such payment shall be necessary. Parliament had thus at last provided; a legal instrument for the

RECOVERY OFID6T On MISMANAGED CHArtITIES and it Row remained' for the inhabitants of any local area affected to take theinitiative in such cases by communi- cating thereon, with the Charity Commissioners., Mr. Handley contended:that the trustees of charities should be elected and not nominative and pointed out that the accounts of all public charities should be submitted' to the annual vestry meetings, and he urged the ratepayers to attend such meetings in order to see to their produc- tion.

An interesting discussion followed.—The Chairman said.tlie money and principles involved in the charities ought to.cause every man to hunt up these things and see how they were carried on at the present time.—A. 'mem- ber asked if the master of Kingsley School was stilt sub- ject to six- months' notice, and Mr. Handley replied no new scheme had ever been established for that school.— The member said the master was partly laying claim to the place.—Mr. Handley said the schwa was under the same old foundation. The school was built with the rates of the parish and the master was appointed on the condition stated.—The Rev. Mr. Trotter said, he was given to understand that Frodsham Grammar School was under the control of the church.—Mr. Handley said the school was built out of the parish rates, and the gover- nors were appointed yearly at the vestry meeting in Frodsham, but he was afraid this had been allowed to lapse: The Grammar School was the old free school of ,Frodsham.—Mr. Rigby asked should the managers of the present school be elected by the ratepayers and Mr. Handley replied in the affirmative.--A, membersaid they had been informed that the Vicar Was chairman of the Committee by right and that the members must be churchmen.-L--Another member said all the benefaction tables had all gone since the church was restored. Where they had gone to was a puzzle.—Another member: They hare raised the burial fees since the tables came down. (Laughter.)—Mr. T. A. Rigby in moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Handley for his interesting and instruc- tive lecture, said he had been a member of the Committee of the Grammer School, but his position was made such that he could not retain it and keep. his self respect. Be' was told that according to the constitution a member must subscribe a guinea a year and mnst be a church- man. But they had allowed him to be there, and he was. not a churchman and had not subscribed a guinea a year. He should net be sati4ied unless something practical came of the meeting that night.—Mr. Gr, Rhodes seconded the motion,, and said it would arouse them to a deeper interest in.the Charities and the.way they were administered.—The motion was carried and a. vote of thanks concluded the proceedings.

A Lens telegram of Wednesday stated that the•adher- ents to the strike movement among coal minars are in, creasing every hour. In the Pas de Calais. coalfield& there are now about 34,5100 men out on striket.very few remaining at work.

The M—anchester School Board elention resulted on Monday in the return, of seven churchmen,. six unsect- arians, and two Catholics. Salford election, resulted in the return of .sevens churchmen, six unsectarians, and two Roman Catholics.

The result of the polling at the Liverpool School Board election was announced at the Town Hall by the. Mayor on Wednesday afternoon. The board as, now consti toted is composed or four Nonconformists (instead pf three), five Churchmen, and six Roman Catholics. I Mrs. Louisa Beppel, hasjust died at 105, Sunderland- read, Forrest-hill, London, in her 102nd year. The death is also announced from Bath of Lieut. Bayley, in his 101st year. He had been through the Peninsular cam- paign, but had been on the retired list forlseverity years. div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATTILETICS.

700TBALL. The meeting of Runcorn with Widnes last Saturday caused a lot of excitement in the chemical district, and the whole rivalry between the clubs brought a fine • crowd together to witness the match. The supporters of the Widnes team were there in great numbers, and were very sanguine as to the result, consequent on the splendid gamed which the " Chemicals " have played this season. It was a hard-fought match from b39.inn- ing to end,and it was only through the cleverness of the Runcorn backs that the narrow victory was g tinal.

There was a lot of ill-feeling exhibited durinm the pro- gress of the game, and as the time wore on it d,>veloneci into personal violence, much to be regretted. The Wid- nes men feel a special grievance, and allege that but for the active interference of the Runccrn touch-line judge there would not have been any unpleasantness. It' is but fair to state that Hughes who was acting in that capacity, strongly disavows any intention or knowledge of striking a man ; in fact,anything hedid was intended te,stop such unfortunate incidents and not to promobe them.

Says the" Athletic News " : The usually serene atmos- - phere of Warrington football life has been greatly dis- turbed owing to the fact that Bate was not selected to play for the Lancashire Cerunty team in the match with Cheshire. The admirers of "Smack " have been greatly exercised as to the reason vrhyland are prepared with all sorts and conditions of arguments to meet any objections that may be made againsl him. Some people evidently have an idea that Bate is only a light weight, hut a youth weighing list 71b cannot by any means be termed a feathery character. I may-add further that the Warring- ten half-back was born in the wire-pulling borough about 21 years ago, and that it has taken him that length or time to rise to the lovely height of sft. 74in.

ha view of the great battle on the 28th int., the pre- liininary cantor of the Yorkshire fifteen, on Saturday last, was eagerly awaited. They were expected to be fully tested in their match at Hull. and to afford an idea as to the probabilities of victory when they meet their Lancashire rivals. There was a doubt about the appear- ance of Lockwood, as, for some reason or other, many people associating it with,the question of the captaincy of the team, the famous thne-quarter cried off. He changed his mind, however, and took his place with Dy- son and A.Goldtherpe. Durham gave the Yorkshiremen an exceedingly good a arne,and although the latter were successful by three goals a:nd a try to one goal and a try, the, winners did not give entire satisfaction. As a rule the Yorkshire forwards are unsurpassable, but their dis- play left much to be desirqd. The combination of the backs was also capable of improvement,a.nd Standen did not shine at all at half back. Durham made a renlly good show, Alderson being in grand form and setting his side a rare example. The passing of the backs was ['ihfirritely superior to that of the Yorkshiremen.

• We shall get a further glimpse of county form to-day, when Lancashire are to visit Cumberland, Yorkshire are to go to Nawcastle-on-Tyne, and Cheshire are to oppose Westmorland. These will make up a busy programme.

For the second time this season the North End finished ' in front of Mackburn Rbvers, but only by one point. It was a grand game from start to finish, and all the five grKils were scored in the first half. Albert Smith, the • Notts Forest half back; who last seaFon helped England ' against ScotZand, joined the Rovers for the first time. He intends playing with them regularly, and should ' prove an adquisition. A close game at Turf Moor ended • in' the overthrow of Accrington, BUrnley winning by two • to one. The forwards,of the first-named club were again belovr par. It was as much as Notts could do to draw- with Wolverhampton Wanderers. The play was very vigorous at times, and Oswald, the Notts captain, was severely bruised. Aston Villa were much too smart for West Bromwich Albiuti, and Sunderland settled Derby County by no fewer than seven goals to one.

As already intimated there was a bid, athering at the • Alliance match, between Ardwick and Notts Forest. The latter have so far not been beaten in the competition, and • they added anotherto their long list of victories. They were hard put to it, however, and only won a magnificent game by two g0a.10.. Higgins, their centre forward, is a splendid Player, and by far the best shot of the many• capital forwards who have b.en at Ardwick this season. Their defence, too is exceedingly strong, and the AM- wick attack cotild do little against it.

There were again some very numerous attendances at the League Matches on Saturday. Fourteen thousand at Preston, 10,009 at West Bromwich, 8,000 at Burnley, and 6,000 at Nottingham testify to the great popularity of the best class of Association football. Then there were • fully 10,000 at Ardwick, and another 10,000 at the FA. cnp tie between Bury and Blackpool, all of which go tz. show how keenthe public are tct see what they know wilt b 3 really interesting contests.

The leaders of the League competition were supposed, to have a light task on with Stoke, especially as the. match was down for Tikes Lane, but they were lucky to escape with a draw. Indeed it was not until their cap— tain, Jones, went from full back to the right wing that they could get a goal, and then he scored it himself. Row-- ley kept goal'magnificently for Stoke. Everton met with. another reverse, this time at Darwen. Few people were. sanguine enough to believe that the Barley Bank team, would win and yet they obtained three .goals to one. Everton had two new backs in Harp, of Notts Forrest,, and Kent,. of Long Eaton Rangers. Earp played finely.

The Committee of the Lancashire Rugby Union .met at the Grand Hotel, Manchester, on Tuesday evening, and selected the following team to represent, Lancashire. against CI-timberland, to be played at Whitehaven, to-day (Saturd'ay), viz. :—T. Coop (Leigh), back*: J. Valentina, (Swinton), 'J. Marsh (Swinton), and .°W. M'Cutcheon (Oldham). threequarter backs ; J. Berry (Tyldesley),and W. Cross (St. Helens), half-hacks; E. Bullough (Wigan), R. P. Wilson (Liverpool Old Boys), J. Pyke (St. Helens Recreation), P. Steelo. (Manchester). T. Rothwell (Swin- ton), Holmes (Widnes), E. W. Bullen (Liverpool Old Boys), S. E. Wilson (Liverpool), and A. Ashworth, (Old- ham), forwards. Reserves: L. Rigo. (Rochdale St. Clem- ent'). back; J. C. Stork (Liverpool Old Boys), and F. Mites (Salford), three-quarter backs ; J. T. Bate (War- rington), half-bacla; J. A. Squires (Broughton), Herbert Basleham (Manchester Rangers), and H. Lomax-(Svrin- ton), forwards. The return match with Cambridae University has been fixed by the Committee for Non', day, the 21st December, at Whalley Range.

CRICKET. County crichet in Cheshire seems. to be doomed. At any rate the Stockport organisation are determined that they will rat loseany more money by beina amalgam ated with the County Club. While this determination is to be regretted, yet the Stockport Members cannot be blamed. For the sevel or eight years during Which the home of Cheshire cricket has been at Stockpot t. the club has lost between LTA anti IMO, in maintaining the fixtures and keeping together the Counts, Players. The interest which was lavished on• the echeme when first it waa tried has gradually but surely diminished, and from a membership of ga affiliated clubs the number has elMined to two.

There seems to be very serious doubts whether the Australians vill visit England next summer. 'The following counties have declined to:meet the Antipodieans —Lancashire, Yorkshire, Sussex, Middlesex, Tient, and Resolved, that the arrangement arrived Notts. The Lancashire committee passed following,* resolution :—" 9,t by the Cricket Council in 1889 with respwe to the future visits of the Australian cricketers to this country not having been carried out, the Lancashire county committee are not prepared to arrange any; ra.,tette,ivrittt the Avetraliam for season 1891"

ANECDOTE OF THE CELEBRATED SIR
RICHARD STEELE.

Few people were greater admirers of prudence and economy than was Sir Richard Steele, and few people practised them less. Expensive habits, and a disposition naturally thoughtless, ieduced him to difficulties, and exposed him to circumstances not a little painful to a man of so refined and elegant a mind. Amongst the number of those who were charmed with his conversation and writings, and aspired to the honour of his acquaintance, was a certain L—e Baronet, who frequented the same tavern with Sir Richard, and took every opportunity of getting into his society. This gentleman pos- sessed a large fortune, and great interest, and once solicited Sir Richard to command his utmost ability—adding that he should feel honoured by his request. These offers though made with apparent sincerity, Sir Richard, with a politeness peculiar to himself, thought proper to decline, as at that time he stood in no need of the gentleman's assistance. Shortly after this, however, some instance of extravagance having reduced him to the necessity of borrowing a sum of money to satisfy an unfortu- nate creditor, he thought this a proper opportunity of calling upon this obliging friend, to request the loan of a hundred pounds for a few days. The baronet received him with increased civility, began to renew his offers of service, and begged Sir Riehard would give him some bccasion of showing his sin- cere friendship and regard. "Why, sir," said Sir Richard, "I am come to you for that very purpose: and if you can lend me a hundred pounds for a few days, I shall consider it as a singular favour." Had Sir Richard put a pistol to his head, and Rade a peremptory demand of his money, the baronet could not have shown more surprise than at this unexpected request. His offers of assistance had been made on supposition that they never would be accepted, and intended only to secure the intimacy of Sir Richard, of which he was particularly proud, so long as it cost him nothing. RecoveritT, however, from his surprise, be stam- mered out: " Why really, Sir Richard, I would serve you to the utmost of my power, but at present I have not twenty guineas in the house.' Sir Richard, who saw through the pitiful evasion, thus addressed him :—" And so, sir," said he, "you have led me to expose the situation of my affairs, by a promise of assistance, which you now meanly refuse —a disappointment I can bear; but never will I put up with an insult; therefore I would have you consider whether it be better to comply with the terms of my request, or to submit to the consequence of my resentment."

Sii Richard spoke in so determined a tone, that the baronet was startled, and seeming to recollect himself, said: "My dear Sir Richard, I beg you a thousand pardons. I quite forgot that I had a hundred pound note in my pocket, which is very much at your service." So saying, he produced the note which Sir Richard put into his pocket, and addressed him in the following words: "Though I despise an obligation from so dirty a fellow as you have proved yourself to be, yet rather than be made a fool of, I shall accept this hundred- pound note, and will return it when it suits my convenience; but that the next favour you confer may be done with a better grace, I must take the liberty of pulling you by the nose, by the way of preserving your recollection." This Sir Richard Immediately did, and then took his leave.
NOW ERRORS SPREAD.

In one of the sittings of the Academy of Dijon, 111,1817, M. Ballot gave, on the authority of M. Her- mann, at Strasburg, the followink; explanation of a fact in nwural history, which, on the credit of that celebrated naturalist, h,d been received for the preceding forty or fifty years in the elementary books of the science:

In the year 1764, the father of the naturalist, Herrn.,nn, visited, for the recovery of his health, the baths uf 'liar. He remarked, upon the surface of the water, a fat substance which resembled melted tal- low; lie sent an account of this observation to his son, who wrote.on the. subject to Pueltard, in Paris. The latter read Hermann s letter in the Academy of Sciences. some. time after Hermann convinced hit.self that this pretended mineral tallow was a mere cheat of the cunning attendant of the baths, who, in order to procure more customers for his baths, threw balls made of clay and tallow into a kettle. The Strasburg naturalist immediately informed his Paris correspondent how he had been deceived, and begged him to destroy his first letter in the academy, and here the matter rested for the time.

Ten years later, Hermann, to his great surprise, found his orginal o o..,,rvation printed under his name in the Journal de Physique for May, 1774; but he was still more surprised to find it also in Kirwan's Elements of Mineralogy, from which it was copied into other works, and mentioned as a newly dis- covered substance under the name of "Bitumen Sevum." In spite of Herm .nn's repeated protesta- tions, this gross error continued to be propagated for years.

div.head: RESISTANCE OF PAIN.
div.p: RESISTANCE OF PAIN.

The Hlowing anecdote b related in the travels of a missionary in South Africa. On one occasion, while the mis,,ionaries were at dinner in their own tent, some of the native chiefs and their wives being present, one of them seeing a missionary help him- self to a little Cayenne pepper, its colour attracted his attention, and be asked for some of it. On get- ting the Cayenne, he instantly threw a quantity of It on his tongue, but, on feeling its pungency, he shut his eyes, clapped his hand upon his mouth, and, holding down his head, endeavoured manfully to conceal the pain. When he was -able to look up, he slyly touched the missionary with his foot, to intimate that he should say nothing, but give the same dose to the others present. Another chief next got some, who also instantly felt its power, but understanding the joke, as soon as he was able to speak, he asked for some for his wife; ana thus it went round, to the great diversion of all at r,rtvards. Though the pungent condiment caused the big tears to roll down their cheeks, they scorned to show that they -felt pain, until it had gone round, and then they smiled at each other with taciturn gravity.

div.head: TIBBY AND TEE MINISTER
div.p: TIBBY AND TEE MINISTER

The late venerated Dr. C., of Cupar, was in the habit of taking his evening walk on the high-road in the immediate neighbourhood of the town. During one of these stated excursions, he had occasion to meet several people returning from Ceres market, whose conversation and step indicated that Ceres and Bacchus had not been separated. Amongst the rest, a well-known, canty little body, of the name of "Tibby Brown" hove in sight, manifestly after having 'made, as was sometimes Tibby's practice, a little too fee with a certain little stoup, which contains a gill. Tibby was a character, and though somewhat additted to a glass at orra times, was a well-doing body upon the whole, kept a clean well-swept house, a soesy cat, and a cheerful tongue in her -head, what time the minister paid her a visit. Tibby, however, had that day disposed of some sale yarn, and had tithed the price to the amount of a cheerful glass with the merchant who purchased it. Tibby was close upon her pastor, ere she perceived him, and finding it impossible to retreat, did what most people would have done in her circumstances; she put the best face on it pos- ,ibie—bronght up her leeway—steadied her pace to a miracle—cocked her head—and, from her very aniiety to disguise her unsteadiness, immediately tripped, stumbled, and all but came in contact with the penon of her pastor. Dr. C. saw Tibby'slitua.- tion, and knew her general character as well as her foible; so coutiuuing that benignity of countenance which was natural to him, he proceeded to rally Tibby in the following terms :—" Hout tout, Tibby, woman, ye're reeling, I see." Tibby heard the assertion, and o.ivg more accustomed to the pro- fessional than to Ma; English sense of the term, in- continently and trolly rejoined, " Weel minister, ye ken a body can,, aye be spihning."

div.head: MR. PEERS AND HIS CONCESSIONS.
div.p: MR. PEERS AND HIS CONCESSIONS.

Sir,—ln my last letter I showed how a concession on the part of Mr. Peers virtually neutralised his agnostic- ism, and rendered it worthless for practical purposes. He now piakes another concession which very seriously affects his boasted statements regarding the immutabi- lity of the laws of nature, and which virtually grants all I have contended for. Mr. Peers distinctly states again that the laws of nature are "inevitable and immutable." Man, in "rolling down, will, in strict obedience to im- mutable law, be inevitably dashed to pieces at the bottom." This is clear enough, but the more clearly it is understood the more clearly does it conflict with another of his statements, viz. : "If man conforms to these laws it is well with him ; if not,he suffers." Now, how can man fail to conform to laws which are "inevi- table and immutable," and which, therefore, cannot be broken? Whether man follows the dictates of conscience or the impulses of his lower nature, in either case he obeys the laws of nature. Such a statement is intelli- gible if man possesses a free will; otherwise, it is utterly unintelligible. Nor does this comprise the whole of his concession. Man's greatest wisdom is exhibited when " he'pits law against law." Indeed! but how can man pit one law against another fn a system of immutable law which cannot be changed? This is all I contended for when I said that one law could be modified by another: and here is Mr. Peers in his dire extremity, coming forward to maintain the same opinion. Moreover, if one law is 'pitted against another, it is bound to give rise to some modification. Why, therefore, should Mr. Peers work himself into such a fury over my statement regarding the modification of the law of gravitation, and desig- nate it a "bit of rant: cant phrases unthinkingly scribbled ?" Such an irrational ebullition of temper is innocuous, so far as I am concerned, through its very excess. But on Mr. Peers it falls with terrible effect, for it applies to both the statements quoted above regarding the immutable laws of nature. Mr. Peers treats prayer as if it was a useless appen- dage of the Christian system, which could be detached without vitally affecting Christianity. Now, this is im- possible. In certain circumstances, it is as natural to man to pray as in other circumstances it is to reason. Both these are essential to human nature. In the words • of one who has long and deeply pondered on ihis subject —" Man in distress instinctively asks for supernatural "help." "There is in man an appetite of thirst, but the Creator has prepared water to slake that thirst. He is hungry, and there is food to satisfy that hunger. So with prayer : man prays because there is a corresponding blessing connected with it."—Yours truly, GNOSTIC.

PROPOSED TOWN HALL FOR EARLESTOWN. Sir,—Excuse the liberty I take in thus addressing you, but you will presently see that it is needful for someone to throw oil on the troubled waters, just now. The public mind is in a ferment over this proposed Town Hall. " Ratepayer " has been followed by "Shareholder," in prose who tilts at certain of the Commissioners,in rhyme, with the object of showing that they are exceeding their commission in spending so much on a Town Hall as is proposed. Whether this is to cost us threepence or four- pence in the pound in perpetuity I do not gather from the correspondence. If so I would rather table down my five Pounds at once and have done with it, for that, roughly speaking, is what it will cost each of the 2,300 ratepayers ultimately whether they pay directly or indi- rectly by compromising. This should give us pause. But if the deed is done we know what to expect and prepare for during the building of this palatial residence. Raising the rates won't induce people to take up their abode in our midst and won't tend to lower house rent. This matter was mooted more than a dozen years ago, but on quite a different basis, when I was an advocate for it, so that it is not my intention to cry it down now. I do,however,demur to the extravagant scale uponwhich it is intended to be erected. You might not suspect—but I have had some experi- ence in building fine buildings. One seems so paralleled that I give it as an illustration. Plans were submitted for a building to cost a few thousands, but the plans looked so nice that it was felt on all hands that it would be a pity to cut them down in any way, so it was almost but not quite unanimously resolved to accept the respon- sibility and proceed with thebuilding, but grievous were the deficiencies in the money, those being most reluct- ant who were at first most forward. • Now to the point ef my remarks. I was, like al- most everyone taking an active interest io public affairs is a humble sort of way, present at the meeting when the Commissioners were chosen with a ' mandate to see to the building of this particular Town Hall, and like those present voted for them with the distinct proviso that they should keep down the rates. I distinctly stated that if they did this they would be doing us a public service,but only on condition that they did it economically. Will this extension of dimensions of this proposed Town Hall tend to keep down or send up the rates? I answer for many who will not speak, and I also answer for those who have not the moral courage to say so,—No! I may also say that I do not expect to see an answer to this question, for I observe that our public men affect not to notice anonymous letters ; but let me tell them that they often express the public mind more truly than letters written with names attached,because they are taken on their merits without any local surroundings of the writer who gives his name. As I state. I was at the said meeting, I give the initials of my name, which I enclose in full, and am yours truly, P. M. C.
THE PUBLIC HALL THAT IS TO BE, AT
EARLESTOW N.

Sir,—There is a crucial question in connection with the above Hall, that I should like to have answered, and it is this: Can a body of Commissioners lead the rate- payers whom they represent to understand, that they spend £5,000 on a Public Hall, and then, without calling the ratepayers together again, increase the cost to £7,700? I should like much to know this; and also, if the said Commissioners have got the consent of the Local Government Board, who, I presume, have the right of veto, when such expenditure is made, and the money borrowed, on the securing of the rates. The ratepayers of Newton and Earlestown would like to know all about it, for this is exactly how they are being treated. Nearly £3,000 extra going because, forsooth, the Surveyor hasn't sufficient room where he is! Why, sir, the Surveyor's only assistant is a boy; and he has two rooms at least that he can claim as his own ; and I have no hesitation in saying that in the larger of the two rooms six clerks could be comfortably placed. The truth is, when the Chairman gave that as the reason for enlarging the new Hall, he was—" not to put too fine a point upon it "—under the impression that the rate- payers would be set aside as nothing andnobody. And when the new building is completed, and the whole of the dicers and offices are removed under the "shadow of the London and North Western Co.s' wings " what is to become of Cu! old Town Hall? Are we to perpetuate the folly and blundering of the Commissioners by keeping up both plabes and pay for both in the bargain? Well may we take the alarm when our affairs are mismanaged in such an egregious manner, and well may we use strong language when we cast our eye over the list of individuals who are our representatives! Why, sir, the capable men have left, or are leaving in disgust ; and others are being pitch- forked into their places who know as much about town's affairs as a bull knows of a total eclipse! And the worst of it all is, these nobodies are all of one mind—the Chairman's mind ! and whatever questionable idea he may get into his head, they say ditto to it with complacency worthy of a sictly lamb! But thank Providence, we have a Court of Ap- peal who wiil probably look strictly into these expensive goings-on, when they find that they are being mulcted in an extra fourpence in the pound by the action of their own upper servants, and that court is the directorate of the London and North-Western Railway Company. You may—and they may—depend upon it that the Newton portion of the ratepayers will not submit gently to have the money squandered without knowing the reason why ; and that when the next election comes round, the active spirits among the Earlestown Commissioners, and the "dummies "too, "of that ilk," will be made to
blush for their stewardship, and will be told to resign a position for which the Almighty never fitted them. A DISGUSTED RATEPAYER. Newton, Nov. 19, 1891.

div.head: ANOTHER COUNCIL AM
div.p: ANOTHER COUNCIL AM

Sir,—A remarkable phenomenon of human nature is the spirit of thankfulness which gushes from some minds when they rtceive the smallest mercies. Indeed,in some instances, this peculiar spirit is so fine in its grasp, and so careful to render thanks, that matters of the least im- portance are held up and dangled before the people as things for which they should bow their heads in grati- tude. The following paragraph,copied from one of your contemporaries, contains a case in point—" The follow- ing resolution was passed by the Executive Committee of the Manchester Salford,land District Temperance Union, at their meeting on Tuesday—' rhat the Execu- tive desire to express their hearty approval of the exdl- lent example set by the Warrington Town Council, in refusing to appoint a brewer to a seat on the Watch Committe of that borough,seeing that a large proportion of the criminal offences with which the police have to deal is directly traceable to the use of intoxicating drinks." Well done,good teetotallers of blanchester and Salford! How grateful must the inhabitants of Warring- ton be for such a gratifying prcnouncement on the part of their neighbours! The elevation of a molehill into a mountain would be a poor affair when compared with the feat of legerdemain which the " Executive " of the Manchester and Salford teetotallers performed, when they describect the removal of Councillor Belton from the Watch Committee as an "excellent example." Surely these gushing temperance men must have based their resolution upon an ex partereport of the proceedings of our town councillors on the occasion referred to. For it is hardly conceivable that men outside the walls of bedlam, having the whole case before them, would have " resolved "as they did. Had they known that our sapient councillors had only removed one drink. manufac- turer from the Watch Committee, and raised a 'whisky maker from that Committee to the chief magistracy of the borough, they would surely have damned the trans- action with" faint praise." I know of no body of men who are so easily pleased with " small mercies" as teetotallers. Barren resolutions and funny speeches by "Sir Wilfrid "and others are sufficient to inflite their simple souls with the liveliest gratification as if the teetotal millenium had come, while at the same time the liquor traffic is roaring and raging around those with, the force of an avalanche. But surely in the case underr notice we must attribute their resolution to ignorance of thecircumstances rather than to mere effusiveness.

I have no personal knowledge of Councillor Bolton, and I certainly have no sympathy with his occupation as a brewer and owner of IT drink shops ; but nevertheless I think he bas been harshly and unjustly dealt with by his colleagues in the Town Council. If his presence on the Watch Committee was considered to be a stumbling block that interfered with the Head Constable and his. men in carrying out the law regarding the drink shops, why was there not a sweep made of the other members of that Committee who were interested in the liquor traffic? That the action of the. Councillors was not prompted by a desire to purify the Watch Cemmittee is evident from what preceded the deposition of Councillor Bolton. They had gone about for sometime begging for a Mayor, and having found a congenial spirit in the person of a whisky manufacturer, they pitchforked him into office without one dissentient ! This official is not only chief magistrate but.is also a member, opofficia,. of every Committee of the Town Council,and, therefore,. I should think more likely to be an impediment to the order and sobriety of the town than the humble brewer with his seventeen drinking shops. What a fine sense of consistency these Councillors must have!' But where were the teetotallers and other "friends of the people."' when this abominable job was being perpetrated ? Oh, tell it not in Gath, they were present in full' force,, and joined enthusiastically in elevating a scion of the great house which owns no less than sixty-two public-houses in the borough, to the highest office which the burgesses can confer. After this 1 hope, for the sake of poor, frail humanity, that we shall see no more posturing, and hear no more speeches by our local reformers of the drinking -- usages of society. —Yours faithfully,

OBSERVER. [Our Correspondent cannot have been present at the Election of Mayor, or he would know that it is wholly inaccurate to say that the teetotallers "were present in full force and joined enthusiastically "in the pro- ceedings.—Ed. Ex. 3

MISSIONLRY SERMONEL—Missionary services were held at the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Broom-edge, on Sun- day, the Rev. C. Tinn of ()Mani, being the preacher. Another service was held on Monday evening, at which addresses were given by the Rev. C. Tinn and the Rev. G. H. Southall. A collection was taken at each service in aid of the mission fund. Ridsdale Rowley, Mr. Hesketh Meade, and Mr. James Allan (humorist). Mr. A. g. Sandiford will be the accompanist. _ _

- SUDDEN DEATH OF A CHILD.—WaItiF J. Carey, aged five weeks, son of Thomas Carey, Massey Brook Cot- tages, was found dead in bed on Saturday morning, at six o'clock. The mother rose at 5.20 to get her husband's breakfast ready. and when she returned to the room she found the child dead. The bey had been delicate since his birth. The Coroner has decided that an inqaest is not necessary.

NOT PARTED IN DEATH.—Lymm has this week lost two of its oldest inhabitants, Mr. James Hatton and his wife Ann, both in their 85th year. There were only two days between them in their birth and three in their death. The old gentleman passed away on Sunday, And his wife died on Wednesday. They passed their long span of years within sound of the church bells. They were a hard.working and industrious couple, and were highly respected in the district. The remains of the late Mr. Hatton were interred on Wednesday, and the remains of his late wife will be laid beside him on Sunday.

div.head: LATE DR. BOYLE.
div.p: THE LATE DR. BOYLE.

The 'interment of the remains of the late Dr. Royle took p ace on Monday afternoon at 215, at the Lymm Parish Church. The remains were conveyed from Scop- wick House, Elstree, the residence of his son, the Rev. Vernon Royle, by train to Lymm. The train started at four o'clock, and arrived at London-road, Manchester, considerably after, one o'clock, tbe delay being occa- sioned by a landslip on tbe railway, and the train having to he worked round Northampton. The train was met at Manchester by a number of sympathizers of the bereaved. At about 1.45 the ,train arrived at Lymtn, half an hour after the advertised time. The weather was, unfortunately, unpropitious, but in .spite of this circumstance, there was a large attendance of the pub- lic. A procession was formed, and in the centre, the remains of Dr. Royle were conveyed on an open hearse. The church was reached at two o'clock, and after the usual service, the remains were interred. The Rev. H. B. Jones (vicar of Brook- lands), and the Rev. J. P. Cort, together with the Rev. W. G.Guest, officiated at the graveside. Amongst those present were Mr. F. Royle, Mr. A. F. Royle, Rev. Vernon Royle, Mr. J. C. Royle, and Mr. F. Sweet (son-in-law), Sir J. Nolsford, Messrs. M. Fairwell Makinson (stipen- diary magistrate for Salford), N. Forster (clerk to the magistrates), Smelt (deputy-coroner), W. Touchstone (secretary of the Northern Church Defence Association). A large number of wreaths were sent.

Damm.—A man named Oakes, a labourer, was sum- moned for being drunk in Lymm.—A fine of 103. includ- ing costs was imposed. FIREWORKS.—Edward Rowles and James Worthington pleaded guilty to letting off fireworks on the 31st October within 50ft. of the highway at Statham.—The casas were dismissed.

CARELESS DRIVERS.—Joseph Robinson was summoned for being asleep whilst in charge of a horse and cart at .Bollington on the 19th Nov.—He pleaded guilty and was fined is. and costs.—John Hampson and George Henry Holt were summoned for each driving a horse and cart without reins at Partington on the 10th November and was fined ss. and costs. ASSAIILTS.—Joseph Martin, who did not appear, was summoned by a married woman named Hannah Walters, for an assault committed on the 24th October.—A fine of 20s. and costs was imposed, the alternative being a month's imprisonment.—Peter John Jackson was sum- moned for assaulting John Warren and Elizabeth Warren, man and wife, on the 24th October.—Mr. Arthur Browne, of Warrington appeared for the prosecution.—The de- fendant was bound over to keep the peace'for six months on the charge of assault against the male complainant, the other case being dismissed. OBSCENE LANGUAGE.—A youth named Wm. Dean, of Lymm, wa,s summoned for • making use of obscene language, on the 26th October. at Booth's Hill Lymm.— Mr. A. Browne, of Warrington, prosecuted. The defend- ant, who denied the charge, was fined 53. and costs. THE GREEN DRAGON INN HEATLEY.— William C. Mountain applied for tempGrary authority to sell at the Green Dragon Inn, ffeatley. Police Superintendent Walker objected to the applicant being granted the authority, on the ground that he was not already living on the premises. Further, the present holder of the license should make the application. Thomas Scatter- good then stepped forward, and said he was the present holder of the license. CONCERT AT LATCI:MO•RD.

, A concert under distinguished patronage was given on Wednesday evening, in the,-P'erish Room,. G-iappenhall-road, for a charitable object. Many of the dile of the neicwhhourhood were present, the dr4css seats being lireßilled. The othstr parts of tlr4e. room were, however, only thinly occupied. Miss. Norah Oakshott. the C. Hylton Stewart, and Mr. Carl Courvoisier,.thok part as vocalists, and the. instrarcental music • swain the hands ef Messrs. F. W. Reynolds (pianoforte), Frank H. Crossley (violin), Carl Fuchs (violoncello), and Carl Cour-- voisier (viola), the list named gentlemaa thus act- ing itt- a dual capacity. The programme consisted main!' of items of" chamber MUSIC " which, though attractive enough to the educated taste, necessarily narrowed the publiinterest in the concert. • Miss ! oakshott appeared to be suffering from a cold. Cer- tainly ,the 1 )wer and middle registers of her voice were veiled and somewhat ineffecciveit is safe how- ever, to conclude that, under favourable conditions Miss Oalitshott is capable of meritorious effort as a vocalist:, The" Gondolier°, wand4t The Angel at the windows' are of coursei.widely different in charac- ter, and 'though the singing of the first was un- doubtedi superior, the second gained an encore. This was responded to with a quaint little song eminenti•y suited to tilis-Onkshott's style and voice. The Rev: C. Hylton Stewart accompanied Miss Oak- shott on the piano, and; though often sympathetic in following the singer;. lie was occasionally too Cemonstrative, and he4did not always adhere to the. printed score. Mr. Stewart himself sang two songs ! with fair success, the best being Cotsford Dick's "The Kingdom Blessed!' Schube'ert's well-known • local moreeau. " Who. is Sylvia ?" and, (in res- • ponsw to an encore),. the song" My heart and , lute," were sung by Wt. Courvoisie in a man- ner which showed thail, alike as a vocalist and an instrumentalist he has at command true artistic taste and kidgment. 'Me duet " When the wind bloweth in from the sear between Miss Oakshott and Mr. Stewart, was a •very pleasing item. The instrumental music was of varied interest, and, with slight exceptions-imregard to particular pass- ages, the performance &tail. concerned was praise- worthy and often excelrent. Of the two pianoforte quartets that by Beethoven had the advantage in interest and that quality•graphically if inelegantly termed "go," especially in the Rondo movement with which both works- conclude. The reason of

this lies, perhaps, in thefact that in Mozart's work the pianoforte gives a less. sustained support to the strings. Mr. Crossley platysd as a violin solo, the two contrasted movements " Adagio " op 34. F. R.ies, and" Mazurka" Wieniawski, which afforded him ample scope in vegard to style, and in both of these Mr. Crossley evinced a conscientiousness of method and a degree of fervour which gained fcr him iv rapt attention. An. Carl Fuchs contributed some 'cello solos with that unimitable grace and in that finished manner which have been noted in these columns in regard to all his previous perform- ances. It is wcrthy of mention that one of the 'cello items was a " Melody," from the pen of Mr. Crossley, possessing the triple charms of simplicity, graceful- ness, and tunefulness. Mr. F. W. Reynold's piano- forte solos were characterized by a high degree of refinement of touch and interpretation.

Last evening week a paper was read before the members of the above association by Mr. Harry Manley, entitled "Chivalry." The paper wan racist instructive and interesting. The Chairman, Mr; R. E. Garnett,along with other members.complimented Mr. Manley on his able essay. The meeting closed with the usual vote of thanks to the essayist and chairmen. FOOTBALL ACCIDENT.—AB' accident °enured on Saturday during the Associntion football match between Penketh and Widnes Parish Church (let teams), at Widnes. A. Wilkinson, playing for IPenketh on the left wing, had kicked the ball, and was following it up when he was charged by one of the opposing team, and overthrown, falllteg: on his left shoulder. It was at once seen that he had sustained some injury, and he was immediately taken to Warrington and examined by Dr. T. Starkey Smith. It was then found that the cAlar bone was broken. Wilkinson was not down in the 1 team picked toplay for Penketh, bull he had volun- teered to do duty in place of a man who was unable to go. ST. MARY'S' CHORAL SOCIETY, GREAT SANKEY. In connection with the above society, a concert wegiven by the members on Mondayr evening, im the Sunday Schools, Great Sankey, in aid of the ex- penses of St.. Mary's Church Brass Band. The chair' was taken at 730 p.m., by the Rev. E. S. Jackson, vicar. nere was a very large attendance, the room being crowded to its utmost capacity. The concert was a success, both financially aid otherwise. Miss E. Jeans accompanied the whole of the pieces on the piano in a most efficient manner. The pro- gramme was as follows :—Anthem, by the choir," I will lift up' mine eyes ;" song, "The Sprig of Shillelagh, Mr. Appleton; solo violin, "'La Son- nambula," MT.. James ?ay; part song, 'The Flower Gatherirs," Misses Woods and W. Ray; cornet solo, "The Lost Chord,' the bandmaster; glee, "Boat song," the choir; duet, Overture to " Tancredi," Messrs.:Ray ; song, " Old Fashions," Miss E. Jeans; glee, "The Fbrry Maiden," the choir; quartette, "Village Chimes," the band; song, "Hearts," Miss Boardman; " The Water Nymphs," Misses Ray, Etherington, and Boardman; song, "The Dustman," Rise Woods; song, "To-morrow will be Friday,' Miss E. Jeans; solo, flute, „ Cara Jusghi:' Mr. W. Ray; glee, "Song of the Vikings," the choir. This finished the programme; and after unanimously according Mr. Jackson a hearty vote of thanks for his services in the chair, the meeting dispersed after singing the National Anthem.

div.head: MA.RRIAGE OF MISS FLORENCE CHANDLEL
div.p: MA.RRIAGE OF MISS FLORENCE CHANDLEL

At GraNenhall Parish Church, on Wednesday,l there was celebrated the marriage of Miss Florence Chandley, eldest daughter of Mr. Sylvanus Chand- ley, alderman of the borough of Warrington, to Mr.l G. H. Kirkpatrick, son df Mr. James Kirkpatrick, of Tyldesley. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. C. W. Dunlop, uncle of the bridegroom,assisted by the Rev. Canon Greeuall. The bridesmaids were Miss Hesketh, of Southport, and Miss M. Chandley, 'sister of the bride. Their dresses were sea green and white, with hats to match. The groomsman was Mr. Wm. Hesketlr, of Southport. At the conclusion of the ceremony, a merry peal was rung out from the church bells in honour of the happy occasion; and nearly 100 wedding guests were received during the day by Mr. and Mrs. Chandley at their home. The newly-united couple subsequently took their departure for Leamington, whence they intend to proceed to the Isle of Wight. We may mention that 'beautiful and useful presents were sent in by a numerous circle of friends. A NAVVY /MIND DEAD.
At half-past five on Thursday morning, a navvy, named John James, was found dead, on the bank of the Ship Canal, at Moore. He had been in delicate health for some time, and had also been drinking.
INQUEST.

Mr. Warsley, deputy-coroner, held an inquest vester- day, at the Red Lion, Mooreon the body of John 3ames, from Oswestry, who was found dead on the Ship Canal bank, at Acton Bridge, on Thursday morning. Jenkin J-ones said he was going along the banks of the Ship Canal, and saw the deceased lying on the ground with his legs crossed. He was quite dead. He gave informa- tion to the police, and the by was taken to the Red Lion. After the medical eviwence, the jury returned a verdict sf "Death from natural causes." There were no marks on the bcdy.

div.head: ANOTHER SHIP CANAL BILL.
div.p: ANOTHER SHIP CANAL BILL.

Notice has been given of another Parliamentary Bill in connection with the Ship Canal. The preamble runs as follows : "In Parliament. Session 1892. Manchester Ship Canal. (New roads in parishes of Warrington Eccles, and Flixton ; Abandonment of Works ; Acquisition of Lands compulsorily and by Agreement; Additional lands in parishes of Eastham, Stoke (detached) Ince, Frodsham Runcorn, Warrington,Great Budworth,Grap- penhall, Eccles. and Flixton ; Opening of Deviation Rail- ways Nos. 1,2, and 3, authorised by the Manchester Ship Canal Act, 1885; Alteration of Sub-section 6of Section 71 of that Act, and Sub-section (1) of Section 31 of that Act; Extension of time for completion of Warrington Dock; Exempting vessels using EntiPance Channel to Eastham Docks from Tolls to the Upper Mer- sey Navigation Commissioners; Classification of Mer- chandise and Schedule of Maximum Rates and Charges for Railways of the Company ; Terminals; Tolls for Tug- boats and Barges propelled by steam on Bridgewater and other Canals, and in respect of Craft toWed thereon ; Incorporation Repeal and Amendment of Acts.)" The reference to the proposed new dam runs as follows. _ _

_ (c) Number 3. A dam across the bed of the River Mersey in a southerly direction (with a lock and sluices thereon) commencing in the township of Warrington in the parish of Warrington in the county of Lancaster at a point on the north bank of that River about 38 chaios east of the northern end of the Bridge over that River known as Walton Girder Bridge measured along the north bank of the River and terminating in the town- ship of Walton Inferior in the parish of Runcorn in the county of Chester at a point on the south bank of the River about 41 chains east of the southern end of the last mentioned Bridge measured along the south bank of the River and wholly within those townships. The main point affecting the interests of Warring- ton is :- 11. To extend the time for the construction and completion of the "Warrington Dock" being Dock No. 4 authorised by the Act of 1885. With regard tki this proposal to extend the time beyond the three years now allowed by the Act,the Corporation of Warrington will have something to say. Is will be their duty to resist it. Warrington cannot afford t 3 be shelved in this cool fashion.

div.head: STARVING CREW RESCUED.
div.p: A STARVING CREW RESCUED.
HALIFAX, TnuresnAx.—The snhooner Lottie Beale was wrecked several days sec) on Noddy Island. Tha crew has just been rescued after spending two "days upon the rocks without food and water.
MR GLA.DSTONE AND MR. GOSCHEN..

Mr. Gladstone, writing to Mr. F. A. Channing, M.P., with referenceto Mr. Goschen's financial administration and the recent correspondence thereon, says Mr. Goschen's letter cannot be read without surprise. Mr. Gladstone goes on to dispute Mr. Goschen's claim to be the pioneer of the proposal to divide rates between owners and occupiers, and adds that Mr. Goschen may not be equally anxious to proclaim himself the pioneer of the principle of compensating owners of public-houses out of State funds.

The Earl of Onslow, Governor of Now Zealand, has resigned owing to urgent private affairs requiring his attention. A Northwich correspondent reports another:subsidence of considerable extent at Marston, caused by extensive mining for rock salt. Further accounts are to hand of the terrible sufferings of the peasantry in the interior of Russia,children perish- ing in great numbers from hunger and cold. The remains of the Marchioness of Westminster were on Thursday interred at Motcombe, Dorsetshire, in the presence of a large and representative assembly. It is rumoured in New York that Lord Stanley of Preston is about to resign the Governer-Generalship of Canada, with a view to his being appointed Viceroy of India. Thomas Fernely, aged 73, was found dead in bed near Stockport on Thursday, having been burnt to death by the upsetting of a paraffin lamp, which sct fire to the bedclothes. A Skibbereen telegram says the country people at- tacked the coastguards at the Head of Kinsale, severely injuring one, and carried away a quantity of wreckage. One marauder is in custody.

div.head: Y.M.CA. CON VERSA ZIONE.
div.p: Y.M.CA. CON VERSA ZIONE.

On Thursday evening the annual conversazione of the Warrington Y31.C.A., was held in the Co-opera- tive Hall, Sankey-street. The hall was very pleas- antly decorated-for the occasion with plants, fairy lamps, &c., and the walls were hung with curtains. There was a large attendance and a very pleasant evening was spent. Mr. J. Fairclough, J.P., presided and amongst others present were the Rev. F. K. Freeston, Counci-llor J. S. Green, Messrs. R. Wyllie, S. B. Stringer, H: iforden,C. H. Kerry, A. E. Horden, J. Critchley, Til IL Dutton, J. T. Patterson (hon. secretary), and R: E. Garnett (hon treasurer). The proceedings having been opened with a hymn and prayer the HON. SECRET'A.RY submitted his report in which '! he expressed the regret of the Committee at the resignation of Mr. T. Wallington, the late general f see., and accorded to him their hearty thanks for his arduous andtvaluable services extending over a period of nearly three years. The Association entered its new premises on the let of June, and since that time the members had steadily increased. They had now 174 members and 22 honorary members in con- nection with the institution. The Committee were desirous of iloing all in their power for the spiritual, intellectual and social improvement of the young men of the town. A shorthand class had been car- ried on by Mr: G. Brown as teacher. A class of sing- ing—tonic-sor-fa—had been formed and was con- ducted by Rev. E. Moore. Entertainments or sJcial gatherings were held every Wednesday eveningand the crowded' state of the rooms showed their popu- larity. They had a debating society ; draught and chess clubs met two nights each week ; there was a bible class conducted by Mr. S. Moss, and Eervices specially adapted for young men were conducted by Mr. C: It Kerry. The cricket and bicycle clubs were well patronised. Next year they proposed start ine, a rambling club, and they were also leek- in g forward to the formation of a tennis club. Ladies-would be enrolled as members of both of these clubs. In conclusion he asked for the co-oper- ation of all interested in the welfare of young men. , (Applause.) The- CHAIRMAN read a letter frobat Mr. J. C. Parr; regretting his inability to attend that meeting% He (the chairman) had unfortunately been prevented from attending the usual Wednes- day evening entertainment by a weekly engage- ment °miring on that night, but he could assure them that he heard repeatedly of their proceedings and always took the most lively interest in them, and in his small way he would gladly help on that valuable institution. (Applause.) He had its wel- fare at heart as he considered a home-from-home like that almost invaluable to young men compelled to reside in a strange town.. (Hear, hear and The HON. TREASVREM (Mr. E. E. Garnett-) next submitted his report. He said that at the and of the present year they shottld be about £22 ss. 4d. in debt. What they realty wanted by the end of the year was a sum of-about .£4O. The cash received was £95 us. 71., and .E 5 18s. 6d. was still due mak- ing a total of £lOl 10s. Id. As their total expendi- ture would be £123 16s. 5d., there would be the deficiency he had named of £22 ss. 44. The cash received inctuded £4O /Bs. 3d. for members subserip- tions. They also wanted a piano, and a library to be furnished.. The bedrooms, he added, were more than self-supporting, and they wished to furnish another one. An excellent programme of MIL9iC. &C., was ren- dered during the evening, including songs, violin and pianoforte solos, and recitations, the artistes being Mr. W. H. Payton, Mr. R. H. Pearson, Miss Gunton, Mr. W. S. Howard, Miss Piekton, Mr. P. 0, P. Price,
